fine-tuning-as-the-costliest-option.explain:
## What it is

Fine-tuning updates a model's weights on your labelled examples. It sits at the top of a cost ladder: a better prompt, few-shot demonstrations, retrieval, a tool call, a stronger base model, then a tune. Each rung costs more money and more calendar time, and each rung is harder to undo.

A prompt change is a pull request. A retrieval change is a document edit. A tune is a dataset, a training job, an eval harness, a serving path, and a retraining plan when the base model is retired. The GPU invoice is the visible line; the hidden line is the people who collect, clean, and re-judge examples every quarter.

Treat the ladder as a decision procedure, not a vibe. You climb a rung only when the cheaper one has a named, measured failure that it cannot close. Interviewers who say "should we fine-tune?" are testing whether you reach for weights first or last.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most "we should fine-tune" threads are a reaction to a demo that looked sloppy. The cheap work — rewriting the system prompt, adding three examples, retrieving the policy, calling a price API — has not been done, or has been done once without measurement. Shipping a tune in that state locks the team into a model version and a data pipeline they did not budget.

In interviews the question is almost always "fine-tuning versus RAG". The junior answer names both. The senior answer puts them on a ladder, prices the full cost, and refuses the tune when the failure is missing facts. Hiring managers also use "fine-tuning" as a job-description keyword; they rarely want you to have trained a 70B model. They want you to know when not to.

## How it works + one small example

Write the options as a table before anyone books a GPU.

1. Prompt and few-shot: hours, reversible, no new serving path.
2. Retrieval or a tool: days, updates by editing data, can cite and filter.
3. Stronger or cheaper base model: a config change and a re-eval.
4. Fine-tune: weeks of data work, a training recipe, hosted weights, a retrain when the base moves.

Example. A support bot quotes last quarter's shipping fees. The product lead says "fine-tune on the help centre". You run the ladder: the prompted model with the current fee table retrieved at request time scores 94% on a 200-row fee set; the same model without retrieval scores 61%. There is no residual style problem. You do not open a training job. You ship retrieval and a weekly crawl of the fee table.

A second example, where a tune is the right next cost. A ticket router must emit one of forty house labels in a strict JSON shape. The best prompt still drifts on ten of the labels after retrieval of the taxonomy. You have 4,000 labelled tickets and a held-out set. Now the residual error is behaviour, the data exists, and the cost of a small LoRA is justified against the volume of calls.

## Failure modes

1. **Tuning as seriousness.** The team trains because it feels like real ML. A week later a three-line prompt change matches the tune on the same set. The adapter is now a liability: it must be served, versioned, and retrained.

2. **Ignoring the serving and retrain tax.** The first run is cheap. The next base-model deprecation is not. If you did not put "retrain twice a year" in the estimate, you underquoted.

3. **Mixing knowledge into the tune.** Weights cannot cite, cannot respect per-user ACLs, and go stale. The model then sounds more confident about last year's policy.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Fine-tuning is the last, most expensive, least reversible rung after prompts, retrieval, tools, and a better base. I price data, evals, serving, and the next retrain before I agree to train, and I only climb when a measured residual error is about behaviour, not facts.
keyPoints: Climb prompting, retrieval, tools, then a stronger base before a tune.
The real cost is data, evals, serving, and retraining, not the GPU hour.
Prompt and retrieval edits reverse in a day; weight changes do not.
Tune only for a named residual failure the cheaper rungs cannot close.
Interviewers want the ladder and a refusal, not a training war story.
A tune that bakes changing facts will go stale and cannot cite.

questions.q: Name the cheaper rungs you try before fine-tuning and why they come first.
questions.a: A better prompt and few-shot examples, retrieval or a tool for facts, and a stronger or cheaper base model. They are faster, reversible, and do not pin you to one checkpoint. Fine-tuning is last because it needs data, evals, serving, and a retrain plan.

questions.q: A chatbot quotes outdated shipping fees. A lead wants to fine-tune weekly on the help centre. What do you do?
questions.a: Refuse the tune. Fees are changing knowledge. Retrieve the live fee table or call a pricing tool, measure on a held-out fee set, and only consider a tune if a style or format gap remains after retrieval works.

questions.q: A one-day LoRA run 'fixed' format drift, then a prompt change matches it on the same set. What was wasted?
questions.a: The serving path, the adapter version, and the future retrain. The residual error was still a prompt problem. You now own weights you did not need. Keep the prompt, delete or freeze the adapter, and write the cheaper baseline into the decision record.

questions.q: Why is the GPU invoice a poor estimate of a tune's cost?
questions.a: Curation, labelling, the eval harness, hosting a custom model, and retraining when the base is replaced usually dwarf a single run. Those costs recur. A $40 training job can become a quarter of an engineer's time.

questions.q: How do you decide a combination of retrieval plus a small tune is cheaper than a giant prompted model?
questions.a: Measure the prompted giant and the retrieved-plus-tuned small model on the same held-out set for quality, latency, and cost per thousand requests. Ship the mix only if quality holds and unit cost or latency drops enough to pay for data and retrains.

what-fine-tuning-is-good-for.explain:
## What it is

Fine-tuning is a behaviour transplant. It is good at changing **how** a model answers — tone, house format, a closed label set, a house template — and at shrinking a long instruction into the weights so each call spends fewer prompt tokens. It is also the standard way to **distil** a large teacher's style into a smaller student you can host.

It is not a knowledge pump. A few thousand pairs will not reliably install a wiki, and they will not stay current. The jobs that fit have a stable target you can write down: "always answer as this brand", "always emit this JSON", "always pick one of these forty labels", "always refuse like this".

A useful test: if you can describe the desired mapping in one page and collect a few hundred clean demonstrations of that mapping, a tune can beat a long prompt. If the mapping is "know whatever is in the CMS this week", you want retrieval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will be asked to make a cheap model act like an expensive one on a narrow slice of traffic. That is a tune or a distillation, not a bigger prompt. Ticket routing, medical-coding-style label sets, brand voice, and "fill this incident template" are the tickets that actually pay for data work.

In interviews, "what is fine-tuning good for?" is a filter. The expected phrase is **style and format, not facts**. Then they want a concrete example with volume, a closed label set, and a cost target. If you only say "customising the model" you sound like a brochure.

Interviewers want style/format/closed labels/distillation — and a volume reason. 'Customising the model' is a brochure.

## How it works + one small example

Pick a task with (1) a written spec, (2) a closed or highly regular output, (3) enough labelled examples, (4) enough volume that prompt tokens or a frontier API bill matter.

Example. A support org has forty ticket labels and 6,000 historical tickets. The prompted frontier model is 91% accurate but costs too much at 80k tickets a day and sometimes invents a forty-first label. You write the label spec, clean the 6,000 rows, hold out 800, and train a 3B LoRA. Held-out accuracy is 90%, invalid labels drop to near zero, and cost per thousand tickets falls by an order of magnitude (illustrative). The tune paid for itself in format reliability and unit cost, not in "knowing the product".

A second good use: a 1,800-token house style guide in every prompt. After a tune on 800 edited replies, you drop the guide to a short reminder. Latency and cost fall; tone holds on the eval set.

Ticket-router example: 40 labels, 6k tickets, 80k/day. Prompted frontier is 91% and invents a 41st label. A 3B LoRA hits 90% with near-zero invalid labels at a tenth the unit cost (illustrative). You did not tune to 'know the product'. You tuned a stable mapping. A ten-call-a-day tool would have kept the long prompt.

## Failure modes

1. **Unstable target.** The brand voice changes every campaign, or the label set is still being invented. The model learns last month's politics.

2. **No volume, no savings.** A ten-call-a-day internal tool does not repay data work. Keep the long prompt.

3. **Calling distillation a knowledge install.** The student copies the teacher's manner and its mistakes. You still need an eval that is not the teacher's own labels.

4. **Tuning a moving label set** that product still invents weekly.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Fine-tuning is for stable behaviour: tone, formats, closed labels, shorter prompts, and distilling a big model into a cheap one. I use it when I can write the mapping and measure it, not when I need facts that change.
keyPoints: Tuning changes how a model answers, not what it knows.
Best fits: tone, strict formats, closed labels, prompt shortening, distillation.
The task needs a written spec and a stable mapping.
Volume plus a cheaper student is a common business case.
A long house style guide is a candidate to bake into weights.
If the CMS changes weekly, retrieval still owns the facts.

questions.q: List four jobs where fine-tuning is a better fit than retrieval.
questions.a: Consistent brand tone, a strict JSON or house template, a closed classification or extraction schema, and distilling a large model into a smaller hosted one. Prompt shortening when a long instruction is stable also fits.

questions.q: How would you justify a 3B LoRA for forty-way ticket routing?
questions.a: High volume, a fixed label set, thousands of labelled tickets, and a cost or latency target. Compare the LoRA to the prompted frontier model on a held-out set for accuracy and invalid-label rate; ship if quality is close and unit cost drops.

questions.q: A PM wants to tune so the bot 'knows our 200-page product manual'. What do you say the tune is actually good for here?
questions.a: Nothing about the manual's facts. If they also need a house answer shape or tone, that slice can be tuned after retrieval supplies the page. The manual itself stays in a corpus you can edit.

questions.q: Why does baking a 1,800-token style guide into a tune save money?
questions.a: Those tokens are paid on every call. After the behaviour lives in the weights you send a short reminder. You still keep a few eval examples of the tone so you notice drift.

questions.q: When is distillation the reason to tune rather than 'better quality than GPT-x'?
questions.a: When a large teacher already hits the quality bar and you need the same mapping at lower latency or cost, or on hardware you control. You are buying capability-per-dollar, not a new skill the teacher lacked.

what-it-is-not-good-for.explain:
## What it is

Fine-tuning is a weak way to install **facts**, especially facts that change, must be cited, or must be filtered per user. A model trained on a wiki learns patterns and a few memorised strings. It will still invent, it cannot show a passage, and it cannot hide a document the caller is not allowed to see.

It is also a weak way to **create a spec**. If nobody can write what a good answer is, the dataset will be a pile of opinions and the model will average them. It will not invent product sense you do not have.

It is a weak way to **buy reasoning the base model does not have**. A LoRA on a 3B model will not suddenly do graduate proofs. It is a weak **safety system**: a narrow tune often forgets refusals the base had learned.

The slogan that belongs on the whiteboard is: retrieval for knowledge, tools for live state, prompts for reversible behaviour, tuning for stable behaviour you can already evaluate.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job the most expensive failed tunes are "we trained on the Notion export". Three months later prices moved, the model still quotes the old ones, and nobody can point a customer at a source. Legal then asks how you will unlearn a paragraph. You cannot, except by retraining.

Interviewers bait this with "how would you customise the model on our knowledge base?". The trap is to describe LoRA. The pass is to refuse, name RAG and access control, and only then mention a tune for tone if a measured gap remains.

## How it works + one small example

Classify the request before you talk about GPUs.

- Changing facts, citations, ACLs → retrieval or a tool.
- Vague "make it better" → write an eval, do not train.
- Reasoning the base cannot do → pick a stronger base, do not sprinkle adapters.
- Safety as the only goal → keep the provider's safety stack; do not overwrite it with a support-tone LoRA.

Example. A retailer wants the assistant to know this week's prices and to refuse to discuss other customers' orders. You put prices in a retrieved feed and enforce order lookup in a tool that checks the session. You do **not** fine-tune on a price CSV. If answers still sound unlike the brand after that, a small style tune can sit on top — but the CSV never enters the loss.

A second anti-example. A team fine-tunes on 3,000 wiki chunks as if they were demonstrations. The model starts answering policy questions without retrieval, cannot cite, and leaks a draft page that was in the train set. The fix is to throw the tune away and build RAG with ACL filters.

## Failure modes

1. **Stale confidence.** Tuned models often sound more sure about memorised strings. Users trust the wrong number.

2. **No citation path.** Support and compliance need a URL or a passage id. Weights do not have one.

3. **Safety erosion.** A tone tune trained only on helpful completions starts answering questions the base would have refused. If you did not keep a refusal probe set, you will ship it.

A practical sitting for what it is not good for: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-1 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of what it is not good for with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put what it is not good for on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of what it is not good for that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Fine-tuning is the wrong tool for changing facts, citations, permissions, vague goals, or missing reasoning. I use retrieval and tools for knowledge, and I will not train until someone can write what good looks like.
keyPoints: Weights are a poor store for facts that change or must be cited.
Retrieval can filter per user; a checkpoint cannot.
A fuzzy spec produces a fuzzy model — write the eval first.
A small tune rarely buys reasoning the base model lacks.
Narrow tunes can forget safety behaviour; probe refusals.
Interview line: RAG for knowledge, tuning for behaviour.

questions.q: Why is fine-tuning a company wiki a bad way to answer policy questions?
questions.a: Facts go stale, recall is unreliable, the model cannot cite a passage, and it cannot hide pages the caller must not see. Retrieval keeps the corpus editable and filterable.

questions.q: Prices change weekly and a PM proposes a weekly tune. How do you answer?
questions.a: A weekly retrain is a tax and still lags the source of truth. Call a price API or retrieve the feed. Tune only if tone or format still fails after the live data is in the prompt.

questions.q: After a 'helpfulness' LoRA, the model answers a disallowed how-to. What happened?
questions.a: Catastrophic forgetting of safety. The train set had no refusals. Restore a refusal mix, add a safety probe to the eval, and consider keeping the provider's safety layer in front.

questions.q: A stakeholder says 'just train it, we'll know good when we see it'. What is missing?
questions.a: A written definition of good and a labelled eval. Without those the dataset is un-auditable and you cannot tell a successful tune from a lucky vibe.

questions.q: Name two things retrieval can do that a fine-tune cannot.
questions.a: Cite or link the passage it used, and apply per-user access control so two callers do not see the same hidden document. It can also update by editing a file instead of retraining.

start-from-a-measured-failure.explain:
## What it is

A fine-tune starts from a **named failure** of the best non-tuned system, not from enthusiasm. You need a representative eval set, a prompted-and-retrieved baseline score, and a categorisation of the misses. Only the buckets that are about stable behaviour — format, tone, a closed skill the prompt cannot hold — are tune candidates.

"Named" means you can point at twenty examples and say the same sentence about each: "emits an extra key", "sounds like a generic chatbot", "confuses label 12 and 14". If you cannot, you are not ready to collect training data, because you do not know what an example is supposed to teach.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, unmeasured tunes cannot be defended. Finance asks what improved; you shrug. A later prompt change then beats the adapter and nobody can prove it because the original baseline was "it felt off".

Interviewers listen for the word **baseline**. If you jump to LoRA rank they mark you as someone who trains for sport. If you walk through failure buckets and a target delta they mark you as someone who can spend a GPU budget.

No baseline, no project. They want the failure buckets and which ones are tunable.

## How it works + one small example

Procedure:

1. Build 200–1,000 real inputs with expected outputs or rubrics.
2. Run the best prompt, few-shot, retrieval, and structured-output stack you can afford.
3. Tag each miss: missing context, tool needed, format, tone, label confusion, safety, other.
4. Estimate the upside of fixing only the tunable tags.
5. Write a target: "label accuracy from 86% to 93% on the held-out set, format validity ≥ 99%, refusal probe not worse than baseline".

Example. 200 misses: 120 missing document (retrieval), 30 bad JSON (schema / constrained decode), 50 tone and house-label errors. The tunable set is 50 cases. If those 50 are 25% of production pain, a tune that halves them is a 12-point win on that slice — worth a small LoRA. If they are 4% of pain, you stop.

You record the baseline numbers **before** anyone trains. The training run does not get to choose a friendlier test set later.

Of 200 misses: 120 missing context (retrieval), 30 schema (constrain decoding), 50 tone/label. Only the last 50 are tune candidates. You write that split before anyone books a GPU. The upside is bounded; you can price it.

## Failure modes

1. **No baseline.** You cannot show the tune helped or that it did not hurt general quality.

2. **Buckets never written.** The dataset becomes "more support tickets" and the model relearns retrieval failures as if they were style.

3. **Target missing.** Training continues until someone likes a sample, which is how you ship an overfit checkpoint.

4. **A vibe that 'the model is sloppy'** with no tagged misses.

Translate start from a measured failure into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-1.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for start from a measured failure than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used start from a measured failure, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of start from a measured failure in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I start from a labelled eval, a strong prompted baseline, and named failure buckets. I only train on the leftover behaviour errors, and I write the target score before the first step.
keyPoints: A tune starts from a measured miss, not a vibe.
Categorise failures; only behaviour buckets are tune candidates.
Record the prompted baseline and a target before training.
Estimate the upside from the tunable slice, not from all errors.
Do not let the training run pick a new test set afterwards.
Interviewers listen for 'baseline' before they listen for LoRA.

questions.q: What three artefacts must exist before you open a training job?
questions.a: A representative eval set, a score for the best prompted (and retrieved) baseline, and a categorisation that shows a leftover behaviour gap with a written target.

questions.q: Of 200 misses, 120 lack documents and 50 are tone. How do you bound the tune?
questions.a: Treat 50 as the tunable set. Estimate production impact of that slice and set a target only on those errors plus regression probes. Do not train to 'fix' the 120 — that is a retrieval project.

questions.q: A team reports the tune 'feels better' but baseline numbers were never saved. What can you not do?
questions.a: You cannot prove a gain, cannot detect a regression, and cannot decide to roll back. Freeze a held-out set now, score the current adapter and a re-run of the old prompt, and treat anything else as anecdote.

questions.q: Why is 'the model is sometimes wrong' not a named failure?
questions.a: It does not tell you what to put in the dataset. Named means a repeatable sentence about a cluster of examples, such as 'invents a forty-first label' or 'adds a greeting the parser rejects'.

questions.q: How does a failure taxonomy change the training mix?
questions.a: You oversample the tunable buckets and keep retrieval-miss examples out of the loss, or you turn those into retrieval tests instead. The mix should match the residual error, not the raw log distribution.

the-full-cost-of-a-tune.explain:
## What it is

The full cost of a tune is the sum of **data creation**, **training runs**, **evaluation**, **serving the custom model**, and **retraining** when the base model, the task, or the data distribution moves. The line item people quote — one GPU-hours number — is usually the smallest.

Data work is labelling, cleaning, de-duplication, PII review, and a second-pass audit. Evaluation is a held-out set, a judge or rubric, and human spot checks. Serving is either a reserved GPU, a multi-LoRA host, or a vendor fine-tune endpoint with its own price. Retraining is the tax you pay every time the base checkpoint you trained on is deprecated or a new failure class appears.

Write the sum in the same units you use for the baseline API bill: cost per thousand successful requests over a year, including one or two retrains.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, an underquoted tune gets approved and then quietly eats a person. The adapter works; the dataset does not stay clean; the base model is retired; nobody owns the recipe. Leadership thought they bought a one-off.

In interviews, listing GPU hours as the cost is a junior tell. Listing data, eval, serving, and the next retrain is the answer they want. It also shows you can talk to finance without hiding the recurring part.

GPU hours are the visible line. Data, evals, serving and the next retrain are the bill.

## How it works + one small example

Build a one-page cost sheet.

- Data: hours to spec, collect, clean, and audit (often the majority).
- Train: number of runs you will actually do (sweeps, not one lucky job) times GPU price.
- Eval: building and maintaining the set; judge calls; periodic human review.
- Serve: extra latency hardware or vendor markup versus the prompted baseline.
- Retrain: assume the base changes at least once in the next two quarters unless you have a written freeze.

Example. Prompted frontier API: $12 per 1k requests (illustrative). A 3B LoRA on one GPU: $0.40 per 1k to serve, plus $8k of engineer time to build v1, plus $3k each retrain, two retrains a year. At 2M requests/year the serve saving is large, but only if quality holds and someone actually owns the $6k/year retrain. If volume is 20k requests/year, the same $8k build never pays back — keep the API.

Put the sheet next to the quality table. A cheaper model that needs a human in the loop on 8% of traffic can erase the serve saving.

Estimate: 2 engineer-weeks to clean data, 1 to harness, $X to train (small), $Y/month to serve, 2 retrains/year when the base moves. Example: a $40 run became a quarter of an engineer. You put all five lines on the ADR. If the residual error is a prompt, this estimate should kill the project.

## Failure modes

1. **One-run thinking.** You will sweep learning rates and ranks. Budget five to twenty runs, not one.

2. **Forgetting serving.** A custom model that cannot sit on your existing gateway is a new platform project.

3. **Zeroing the retrain tax.** A deprecated base makes the adapter a paperweight. If you cannot fund a retrain, do not train.

4. **Quoting only the training SKU** to a VP.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I cost a tune as data plus many training runs plus eval plus serving plus at least one retrain, converted to cost per thousand requests over a year, and I compare that to the prompted baseline — not to a single GPU hour.
keyPoints: Full cost = data + runs + eval + serving + retraining.
People-time on data and evals usually beats the GPU invoice.
Budget a sweep of runs, not a single lucky job.
Convert everything to cost per thousand requests over a year.
A retrain when the base dies is part of v1, not a surprise.
Low volume rarely repays even a cheap adapter.

questions.q: What five cost buckets belong in a fine-tune estimate?
questions.a: Data creation and cleaning, training runs (including sweeps), evaluation, serving the tuned model, and retraining when the base or task changes.

questions.q: Volume is 15k requests a year. The LoRA would save $0.01 per request. Do you train?
questions.a: Probably not. Annual serve savings are about $150, which will not cover data work or a retrain. Keep the prompted model unless there is a non-cost reason such as data residency.

questions.q: The GPU quote was $60 but three engineers spent two weeks on labels. What was mis-estimated?
questions.a: People-time on data. The $60 was the run, not the project. Put labelling hours on the sheet and decide again with the full number.

questions.q: Why must serving appear even when training is free on leftover GPU?
questions.a: Someone has to host a custom checkpoint, keep a template aligned, and take pages when it dies. That is platform cost the prompted API already included in its unit price.

questions.q: How do you include two retrains a year in a unit-cost comparison?
questions.a: Add the expected retrain labour and GPU to the yearly total, divide by yearly successful requests, and compare that unit cost to the baseline API. If volume is uncertain, show a break-even volume.

tied-to-one-base-model.explain:
## What it is

A fine-tune is married to **one base checkpoint**. LoRA adapters are not portable across architectures or even across most version bumps of the same family. Full-weight tunes are even more stuck. When the lab ships a better base next quarter, you do not flip a model name. You rerun data through a recipe and re-prove the eval.

The durable assets are therefore the **dataset**, the **recipe** (template, hyperparameters, scripts), and the **eval suite**. The weight file is a derived artefact. Teams that treat the `.safetensors` as the product discover they have nothing to move when the base is deprecated.

Managed vendor tunes have the same marriage: the vendor's "gpt-x-mini-ft" dies when that base leaves the catalogue.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, base models move several times a year. If your product identity is "the adapter we trained in March", you will miss quality and price wins, or you will run a dead base because migration was never funded.

In interviews, "what happens when the base model is deprecated?" separates people who have shipped a tune from people who have only read a LoRA diagram. The answer is: we retrain from the versioned set; we do not migrate tensors.

An adapter is married to a base revision. Next quarter's better base is a retrain, not a rename.

## How it works + one small example

Design for remarriage.

- Pin the base by exact id and hash in the run config.
- Store the dataset, template, and eval outside the checkpoint directory.
- Write a one-command retrain that takes a new `--base` and produces a comparable eval table.
- Budget the retrain in the original cost sheet.
- Prefer adapters over full tunes when you expect to hop bases, because they are cheaper to redo — not because they transfer.

Example. You ship a LoRA on `llama-3.1-8b-instruct`. Six months later `llama-3.3-8b-instruct` scores higher as a prompted baseline. You do not "convert" the old adapter. You run the same 4,200-row set and the same eval. If the new base plus the old prompt already clears the target, you **drop the tune**. If not, you train a new adapter on the new base and compare.

Vendor example. OpenAI retires the base you tuned. Your fine-tuned model may keep serving for a while, then vanish. The export you needed was the training JSONL, not the hosted weights.

Write the retrain tax into the first estimate. Example: the catalog retires your 8B in 90 days. The durable assets are the dataset, recipe and eval. The adapter file is a souvenir. Teams that 'just change the model name' discover PEFT will not apply.

## Failure modes

1. **Weights as source of truth.** The only copy of "how we answer" is an adapter file. The data lake was never versioned.

2. **Assuming LoRA transfers.** Loading a Llama-3 adapter on Llama-3.1 or on Mistral is not a supported move. It is a new project.

3. **No freeze plan.** You cannot even stay on the old base because nobody recorded the exact revision and chat template.

4. **Treating the adapter as portable across families.**

A practical sitting for tied to one base model: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-1 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of tied to one base model with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put tied to one base model on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of tied to one base model that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A tune is glued to one base version. I treat the dataset, recipe, and eval as the product, and I assume I will retrain — or delete the tune — when a better base arrives, rather than migrating tensors.
keyPoints: Adapters and full tunes are bound to one base checkpoint.
The durable assets are data, recipe, and evals, not the weight file.
A better base next quarter means a retrain or a deleted tune.
Do not assume a LoRA loads on a cousin model.
Pin exact base id, template, and hashes in the run config.
Vendor fine-tunes die when that vendor base leaves the catalogue.

questions.q: What should you keep when a base model is deprecated?
questions.a: The versioned dataset, the training recipe including the chat template, and the eval suite. Those let you retrain on a successor. The old adapter is a souvenir.

questions.q: A new instruct model beats your prompted baseline and your old LoRA. What do you do with the adapter?
questions.a: Score the new base with the old prompt on the same held-out set. If it clears the target, retire the adapter. If not, retrain a new adapter on the new base and compare; do not try to load the old tensors.

questions.q: An engineer copies a Llama-3 LoRA onto a Mistral serve path to 'save a retrain'. What breaks?
questions.a: Shapes, residual math, and the chat template will not match. You get garbage or a load error. Retrain on the model you will serve.

questions.q: Why is a managed fine-tune still tied to one base?
questions.a: The vendor trains on a named base and serves that pair. When the base is retired the fine-tune goes with it. Your exportable asset is the training file.

questions.q: How do you make a retrain a one-command event?
questions.a: Pin dataset hash, template, seed, and package versions in a config; accept a new `--base`; write the same eval table. If any of those live only in a notebook, you do not have a recipe.

prompt-then-retrieve-then-tune.explain:
## What it is

The working order is **prompt, then retrieve (or tool), then tune**. You exhaust reversible behaviour changes and knowledge injection, write down the **residual error**, and only then collect demonstrations of that leftover mapping.

"Exhaust" does not mean months of tinkering. It means you can show a table: best prompt, best prompt plus retrieval, best prompt plus retrieval plus constrained decoding. If the residual is still a stable behaviour gap, the tune has a job. If the residual is "we never tried citations" or "the schema is not enforced", you are not done with the cheap rungs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this order stops the cargo-cult tune. Teams that skip it train the model to paper over a missing retriever, then cannot update a fact without another job.

Interviewers often walk you through a failing bot. If your first sentence is LoRA, you fail. If your first sentences are "rewrite the prompt, add retrieval, measure the leftover", you pass — even if you later recommend a tune.

Exhaust the cheap rungs and write the residual error. Opening a job first is the junior tell.

## How it works + one small example

Run a three-row bake-off on the same held-out set before anyone labels a new SFT set.

Row A: best system prompt, few-shot, structured output.
Row B: A plus retrieval or tools for any fact that lives outside the weights.
Row C: proposed tune on top of B, or on a smaller model if cost is the point.

Write the residual of B in one paragraph: "JSON valid 96%, house tone 70%, facts with retrieval 93%". The tune is aimed at the 70%, not at the 93%.

Example. An FAQ bot misses 40 of 200 questions. After a prompt rewrite, 28 remain. After retrieval of the FAQ corpus, 6 remain, all of them "sounds too robotic" on otherwise correct answers. Those 6 (and more like them) are the SFT set. You do not include the 34 that retrieval already fixed.

Time-box the cheap work: a week of prompt and retrieval iteration with daily evals is enough to write a residual. You do not need a research programme.

Checklist signed in the ADR: prompt work done, retrieval/tools tried, residual tagged as style/format not facts. Example: a policy bot's misses were stale fees. Retrieval closed them. You never opened a job. A second project had a residual JSON drift after schema constraints — that one earned a LoRA.

## Failure modes

1. **Tuning over a missing retriever.** The adapter memorizes last week's answers. Next week the CMS changes and you are stuck.

2. **No written residual.** Labellers invent a broader task than the failure you actually have.

3. **Skipping structured output.** Format errors that constrained decoding would have fixed become an expensive SFT project.

4. **Skipping retrieval** because 'we will bake the wiki in'.

On the job, prompt then retrieve then tune is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-1.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is prompt then retrieve then tune'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply prompt then retrieve then tune as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating prompt then retrieve then tune as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prompt, then retrieve or call a tool, then write the leftover error, then tune only that leftover. If I cannot show the residual of the cheap stack, I am not ready to train.
keyPoints: Order: prompt, retrieval or tools, then a tune.
Write the residual error of the cheap stack in one paragraph.
Do not put retrieval misses into the SFT set.
Constrained decoding often closes format gaps without weights.
A one-week bake-off is enough to decide; do not stall forever.
Interviewers fail you if LoRA is sentence one.

questions.q: What do you write down after the prompt-and-retrieval bake-off?
questions.a: The residual error: which metrics still miss, with examples, on the same held-out set. That paragraph is the spec for the dataset. Everything the cheap stack already fixed stays out of training.

questions.q: Format validity is 91% with free decoding and 99% with a schema. Should you tune for format?
questions.a: No. Enforce the schema at decode time. Use a tune for the leftover tone or label problem, not for a constraint the decoder can already impose.

questions.q: A LoRA 'fixed' FAQ misses that later turned out to be missing chunks. What is the recovery?
questions.a: Rebuild retrieval, re-score the prompted+retrieved baseline, and retrain only if a behaviour gap remains. Consider dropping the adapter; it was compensating for an index bug.

questions.q: Why must the three-row bake-off use one held-out set?
questions.a: Otherwise you cannot attribute the gain. A friendlier set for the tune will always make the tune look necessary.

questions.q: How long should you spend on the cheap rungs before a tune is allowed?
questions.a: Long enough to produce a measured residual, typically days to a couple of weeks with a daily eval, not an open-ended research cycle. If you cannot measure, you are not exhausting the rungs — you are avoiding the decision.

style-versus-knowledge-test.explain:
## What it is

Before you collect a single training row, classify the failure as **style or format** versus **missing knowledge**. Style and format: tone, length, JSON shape, house labels, greeting rules, refusal phrasing. Knowledge: a fact that lives in a document, a database, or an API, including facts that differ by user.

Only the first class is a default tune candidate. The second class is retrieval, a tool, or a better index. Mixed failures are common; you split the example. The knowledge goes into the retriever. The way you want the answer spoken can still go into SFT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this test is the five-minute save. It stops a two-week labelling party for a problem an endpoint already solves.

In interviews, "is this a tune?" is often this test in disguise. Say "style versus knowledge" out loud. Then apply it to their FAQ bot, their SQL assistant, or their policy helper.

If the miss is a missing fact, it is not a tune candidate. If it is tone or format, it might be.

## How it works + one small example

For each failing example ask: **if I pasted the right passage or API result into the prompt, would a competent model succeed?** If yes, it is knowledge. If the passage is already there and the model still uses the wrong voice, the wrong schema, or the wrong house label, it is style or format.

Example. "What is the refund window for SKU 44?" fails. The policy is in a doc the model never saw. Knowledge — retrieve. Same question with the paragraph in context, but the model writes a chatty essay instead of the two-sentence house template. Style — tune or a stricter prompt.

A SQL assistant that invents a column is knowledge (schema tool). A SQL assistant that writes valid SQL in the wrong dialect house style after the schema is provided is behaviour (tune or few-shot).

Write the split on the eval sheet as two columns so labellers cannot smuggle facts into demonstrations.

Tag each residual miss: knowledge vs behaviour. Example: 40 knowledge, 8 format. You retrieve. You do not train. A 40/8 split the other way, with a written spec, is a tune conversation.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling everything style.** Teams tune on "answers about refunds" and accidentally bake last year's window into the weights.

2. **Calling everything knowledge.** A real format problem is left to a 2,000-token prompt that still drifts.

3. **Not splitting mixed rows.** The demonstration contains a fact that will rot, and a tone you actually wanted. The rot comes along for the ride.

4. **A mixed bag you trained anyway** so the model became confidently wrong about last year's policy.

Translate style versus knowledge test into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-1.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for style versus knowledge test than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used style versus knowledge test, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of style versus knowledge test in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I sort every miss into style or format versus missing knowledge. Knowledge goes to retrieval or a tool; only a leftover style or format gap is allowed near a training job.
keyPoints: Style/format = how; knowledge = what, including per-user facts.
If the right passage in the prompt would fix it, do not tune.
Split mixed examples so facts do not enter the loss.
House labels and JSON shapes are format, not knowledge.
Live prices and policies are knowledge even if you have a dump.
Say 'style versus knowledge' in the interview before you say LoRA.

questions.q: What question tells you a miss is knowledge rather than style?
questions.a: If pasting the correct passage or tool result into the prompt would make a competent model succeed, the miss is knowledge. If the evidence is already there and the shape or tone is still wrong, it is style or format.

questions.q: The model has the refund policy in context but writes a long essay. Tune or retrieve?
questions.a: Style or format. Tighten the prompt or collect demonstrations of the two-sentence house template. Do not add more policy documents.

questions.q: Labellers pasted yesterday's prices into the gold answers 'so the model knows them'. What is the bug?
questions.a: They turned a knowledge problem into a stale tune. Strip prices from the demonstrations, retrieve or call the feed at request time, and keep only the wording style in SFT if needed.

questions.q: Is a closed forty-label taxonomy knowledge or format?
questions.a: Format / behaviour: a closed mapping from ticket text to a house id. The definitions can be retrieved as a short legend, but reliability of the mapping is a classic SFT job once the legend is stable.

questions.q: How do you handle an example that both misses a fact and uses the wrong tone?
questions.a: Split it. Put the fact in the retriever or tool. Write the gold answer as if the fact were already present, in the desired tone. Train on the second piece only.

retrain-tax-in-the-estimate.explain:
## What it is

The **retrain tax** is the cost of doing the work again when the base model is replaced, the tokenizer or chat template changes, the task drifts, or a new failure class appears. It belongs in the **first** estimate, not in a surprise ticket after deprecation.

A honest v1 quote looks like: build once + serve for N months + K planned retrains. K is at least one if you follow frontier or popular open bases, because those move. K is higher if your domain changes weekly.

The tax is mostly people, not GPUs: rebase the recipe, re-check the template, re-run evals, maybe relabel a slice, recertify safety probes, and redo the canary.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams that ignore the tax end up frozen on a dead base because nobody budgeted migration. That is how you pay frontier-era prices for a model the vendor is trying to turn off.

In interviews, mentioning the next base-model upgrade unprompted is a strong signal. It shows you have seen a tune survive contact with a catalogue change.

Include the next base upgrade, not only the first run. Interviewers listen for this line.

## How it works + one small example

Put two extra lines on the cost sheet.

- **Scheduled rebase:** once per base-family upgrade you intend to follow (often 1–2 per year).
- **Unscheduled rebase:** a drift trigger from production (new product line, new failure cluster) with a reserved label budget.

Example. Year-1 cost without tax: $8k to build, $2k to serve. With tax: add two rebases at $3k each (mostly eval and template work, a short LoRA run). Year-1 is $16k, not $10k. The prompted API at the same volume is $18k. The tune still wins, but the margin is thin; if rebases slip to $5k because the template changed, the API wins again.

A freeze is a valid alternative: you accept a fixed open-weight base for 18 months and do not chase every release. Write that freeze down. It is a product decision, not an accident.

Put 'retrain twice a year' (or at every catalog EOL) in the cost table. Example: year-1 looks cheap; year-2 with two catalog moves matches a full engineer-month. That number belongs on the first slide.

## Failure modes

1. **Zero K.** The estimate assumes the March checkpoint lives forever.

2. **Tax as GPU only.** The rebase is treated as a $40 job. The real work is eval and canary.

3. **Chasing every base.** You pay the tax monthly and never amortise the last adapter.

4. **A one-run business case.**

A practical sitting for retrain tax in the estimate: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-1 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of retrain tax in the estimate with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put retrain tax in the estimate on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of retrain tax in the estimate that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I put the next base-model upgrade and at least one drift retrain in the original cost, as people-time plus a short run, not as a later surprise. If we cannot fund that tax, I will not train.
keyPoints: Retrain tax = rebase when the base, template, or task moves.
Put K planned retrains in the v1 quote.
The tax is mostly eval, template, and canary work.
A written freeze on one open base is a valid way to cut K.
Chasing every new base spends the tax without amortising.
If the tax is unfunded, the cheap API is the honest choice.

questions.q: What is the retrain tax and when do you pay it?
questions.a: The cost of repeating data-to-eval work when the base, tokenizer, template, or task changes. You pay it on scheduled base upgrades and on drift triggers. It belongs in the first estimate.

questions.q: Your v1 quote omitted rebases. The base is deprecated in six months. What do you tell finance now?
questions.a: The adapter will die with the base. Either fund a rebase (recipe + eval + canary) or migrate traffic to a prompted model. Do not pretend the weight file will load on the successor.

questions.q: A team retrains on every weekly open-weight release. Quality is flat. What is wrong?
questions.a: They are paying the tax without a gain. Freeze a base until the prompted successor beats the current pair by a written margin, then rebase once.

questions.q: Why is the retrain tax mostly people-time?
questions.a: Re-checking the chat template, rerunning evals, recertifying safety, and canarying the new adapter dominate a short LoRA job on a small model.

questions.q: How does a freeze-for-18-months decision change the estimate?
questions.a: K scheduled rebases drop toward zero for that window. You accept missing some base-model gains in exchange for a stable serving path. Write the freeze date and the metric that would break it.

decline-a-tune-in-an-interview.explain:
## What it is

You should be able to **decline a fine-tune** in a hiring-manager story, especially for an FAQ or policy bot. The decline is a structured argument: the failure is knowledge, cheaper rungs are untried or already sufficient, the full cost including retrain tax exceeds the gain, and the product needs citations or ACLs that weights cannot provide.

A decline is not "fine-tuning is outdated". It is "for this failure, a tune is the wrong instrument". You can still say you have trained LoRAs on format tasks. The point is judgement.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers who build AI products are tired of candidates who fine-tune as a personality. They want someone who will protect the team from a six-week side quest. FAQ bots are the classic trap because the job description said "fine-tuning" and the actual system is RAG.

On the job the same speech saves you when a VP saw a vendor slide. You need it ready, polite, and numerical.

Be ready to refuse an FAQ bot. Facts change, citations matter, ACLs matter.

## How it works + one small example

Use a four-beat decline.

1. **Restate the failure.** "Customers get last month's return window."
2. **Name the class.** "That is changing knowledge, not tone."
3. **Show the cheaper fix.** "Retrieval on the policy corpus with citation, plus a prompt that refuses when the passage is missing. Here is a 50-question score."
4. **Price the tune they asked for.** "A tune would bake today's window, could not cite, and we would retrain at every policy edit. I will not do that."

Example interview answer. "I would not fine-tune your FAQ bot. FAQs change and need a link. I would build retrieval with ACL filters, measure exact-match and citation rate on a frozen set, and only revisit a tune if answers are factually right but off-brand after that. If you want a smaller model for cost, I would distil after the RAG path is good — not instead of it."

If they insist they have 10,000 FAQ pairs already: "Then those pairs are eval and retrieval chunks, not SFT, unless a style gap remains."

Keep a positive close: the capstone you *would* tune — a labeler or a house JSON template — so you do not sound allergic to weights.

Script: 'Your FAQ is knowledge that changes. I would retrieve the articles and eval citation validity. I would only tune if a house tone still failed after that. Fine-tuning the wiki would go stale and could not respect per-user pages.' Then stop. Do not offer a LoRA to be polite.

## Failure modes

1. **Absolute refusal.** "I never fine-tune" sounds ideological and fails the next question about LoRA.

2. **No numbers.** A decline without a 50-question sketch looks like fear of GPUs.

3. **Insulting the job description.** They listed fine-tuning because recruiters copy keywords. Redirect; do not mock.

4. **Agreeing to tune because the job description said fine-tuning.**

A practical sitting for decline a tune in an interview: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-1 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of decline a tune in an interview with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put decline a tune in an interview on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of decline a tune in an interview that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I would not fine-tune an FAQ bot: the miss is changing knowledge that must be cited, so I retrieve, measure, and only tune a leftover house style. A tune I cannot decline is a tune I should not be trusted with.
keyPoints: Decline with a class, a cheaper fix, and a cost, not a slogan.
FAQ and policy bots are the standard 'do not tune' story.
Offer retrieval plus a citation metric on a frozen set.
Keep a positive example of a tune you would run (format, labels).
Existing FAQ pairs are usually eval and chunks, not SFT.
Never say you never fine-tune; say you will not for this failure.

questions.q: Give a four-beat decline of fine-tuning an FAQ bot.
questions.a: Restate the failure (stale or uncited answers), name it as knowledge, propose retrieval with citations and a measured set, and price the tune as stale weights plus a retrain on every edit. Close with the leftover style tune you would consider later.

questions.q: The JD lists fine-tuning and the take-home is an FAQ bot. How do you handle the keyword?
questions.a: Say you can run LoRA and you have, then decline it for this task with the knowledge test. Offer a small style adapter only after RAG hits the fact metric. You satisfied the keyword without shipping the wrong system.

questions.q: You declined, and the interviewer says they already have 10k FAQ pairs. What are those pairs?
questions.a: Primarily retrieval chunks and an eval set. They become SFT only if, after retrieval, a style or format gap remains and the pairs are rewritten as demonstrations of that leftover mapping.

questions.q: Why is 'I never fine-tune' a bad decline?
questions.a: It sounds ideological. The next question will be a closed label task where a tune is right, and you will have boxed yourself in. Decline the instrument for this failure, not the instrument forever.

questions.q: What number should you be ready to sketch in a decline?
questions.a: A small frozen FAQ set (for example 50–200 questions) with accuracy and citation rate for prompted+retrieved versus a hypothetical tune, plus a one-line retrain tax when the policy changes.

specify-the-behavior-first.explain:
## What it is

A dataset without a written behaviour spec is a pile of opinions. **Specify the behaviour first**: one page that says what a good answer is, what a bad answer is, the output shape, the missing-info rule, and the tone. Every later example is accepted or rejected against that page.

The spec is not a prompt. It is an acceptance test. Labellers, synthetic teachers, and you in six months must be able to apply the same rules. If two reviewers cannot agree on a row using only the spec, the spec is unfinished and you must not scale collection.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most dirty SFT sets come from "just export the good chats" with no definition of good. You then spend the training budget amplifying whoever happened to be on shift.

In interviews, "how do you build a fine-tune set?" should start with a spec, not with Unsloth. It shows you treat data as a product with QA, not as a dump.

A written spec is what every example is checked against. Without it you are collecting vibes.

## How it works + one small example

Write the spec as bullets a new hire can apply.

- Task sentence: "Classify the ticket into exactly one of forty labels and a one-line reason."
- Output contract: JSON keys, allowed enums, max reason length.
- Missing info: empty ticket → `other`.
- Tone: no greeting, no apology stack.
- Hard no: never invent an order id.

Then collect **ten gold rows** by hand that pass, and five that fail with a reason. Those fifteen rows are the quiz you give every labeller and every filter script.

Example. Without a spec, logs include "sure! I'd be happy to help — this looks like billing :)" as gold. With a spec, that row is rejected for greeting and emoji. The model never learns to talk like a weekend intern.

Pin the spec next to the dataset version. When the product changes the label set, the spec version bumps and you do not silently mix v1 and v2 rows.

One page: inputs, allowed outputs, tone, refusal rules, JSON keys. Example: 'always one of 40 labels, never invent, one-sentence rationale'. Raters use that page. Examples that fail it never enter train. A spec written after collection is a retrofit and you will relabel.

## Failure modes

1. **Spec written after 2,000 rows.** You will not relabel. The spec becomes fan fiction.

2. **Spec is a slogan.** "Be helpful and on-brand" cannot accept or reject a row.

3. **Two specs.** Prompt-eng has one, labelling has another. The model averages the fight.

4. **A Slack thread as the spec.**

A practical sitting for specify the behavior first: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-2 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of specify the behavior first with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put specify the behavior first on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of specify the behavior first that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write a one-page acceptance spec before I collect a row, quiz it on ten gold and five fail examples, and I will not scale labelling until two people apply it the same way.
keyPoints: The behaviour spec is an acceptance test, not a prompt.
Write output shape, missing-info rule, and hard nos first.
Ten pass and five fail examples are the labeller quiz.
If two reviewers disagree, stop collecting and fix the spec.
Version the spec with the dataset; do not mix v1 and v2 rows.
Interviewers want spec-before-Unsloth, not a dump of chats.

questions.q: What belongs on the one-page behaviour spec before collection?
questions.a: The task sentence, output contract, missing-info rule, tone constraints, and hard nos. Plus a handful of pass and fail examples so a new hire can apply it without a meeting.

questions.q: Two labellers disagree on 30% of a sample. What do you do?
questions.a: Stop scaling. The spec is unfinished. Add decision rules for the disputed cases, relabel the sample, and only resume when agreement is usable.

questions.q: You exported 'thumbs-up' chats as gold and trained. Outputs are chatty. Root cause?
questions.a: No acceptance spec. Thumbs-up meant 'user was satisfied', not 'matches the house template'. Write the spec, filter the export, and retrain.

questions.q: Why is the spec versioned with the dataset?
questions.a: When labels or tone rules change, old rows become wrong. A version pin lets you exclude v1 from a v2 train and explain a checkpoint.

questions.q: How do you use the spec on synthetic teacher data?
questions.a: Run the same accept/reject rules in a filter script, then spot-check. The teacher is not exempt; it is another labeller with a known bias.

where-examples-come-from.explain:
## What it is

SFT examples come from **production logs**, **expert demonstrations**, or **filtered synthetic data**. Each source has a bias. Logs match real traffic but include errors, policy breaches, and the old prompt's bad habits. Experts are clean and on-spec but expensive and often too tidy. Synthetic data is cheap and broad but collapses toward the teacher's phrasing and the teacher's mistakes.

You almost always mix: logs for coverage of real phrasing, experts for the gold mapping on hard cases, synthetic for rare slots you cannot wait to observe. You never mix without labelling the source on each row so you can ablate later.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a log-only set teaches the model to sound like last quarter's slightly broken bot. An expert-only set looks great on a polished eval and dies on typos. A synthetic-only set is a clone of one teacher.

Interviews want you to name the three sources and one bias each. Bonus if you say you tag source on every row.

Logs, expert demos, synthetic — each is biased. Name the bias.

## How it works + one small example

Build a source policy.

- Logs: keep rows where a human edited the answer to the spec, or where a judge plus a human spot-check passed. Drop raw model dumps.
- Experts: write the hard 10% — boundary labels, refusals, empty input — not 4,000 easy paraphrases.
- Synthetic: seed from real prompts, generate with a teacher, filter with the spec and your evals, cap how many clones share an n-gram.

Example. 3,000 rows: 2,200 human-edited productions (source=`log_edit`), 300 expert hard cases (`expert`), 500 teacher variants of rare labels (`synth`, teacher id pinned). An ablation that drops `synth` tells you whether the rare labels still hold.

Bias to expect: logs under-represent new products; experts over-represent complete sentences; synthetic under-represents insults, code-switching, and empty inputs unless you force them.

Logs: real, messy, possibly wrong. Experts: clean, expensive, not the tail. Synthetic: fast, clone-prone, teacher-biased. Example: you take 70% cleaned logs, 20% expert edge cases, 10% filtered synthetic, and you measure n-gram overlap so the teacher does not clone itself.

## Failure modes

1. **Raw log dump.** You train on the bug you are trying to leave.

2. **Synthetic majority without filters.** The student becomes a phrasing clone and fails real traffic.

3. **Untagged mix.** You cannot debug a regression to a source.

4. **100% synthetic** because it was free.

Time-box where examples come from to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-2 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on where examples come from', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether where examples come from would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for where examples come from that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I mix edited logs for real phrasing, expert rows for hard cases, and filtered synthetic rows for rare slots, and I tag the source on every line so I can ablate.
keyPoints: Three sources: logs, expert demos, filtered synthetic.
Logs match traffic but copy old bugs; edit before they are gold.
Experts are clean and too tidy — use them on the hard tail.
Synthetic is cheap and clone-prone; filter and diversity-check.
Tag source on every row so you can ablate.
Do not let any one source be 100% without a reason.

questions.q: Name one bias of logs, experts, and synthetic data.
questions.a: Logs copy the old system's errors and miss new products. Experts look unlike messy users. Synthetic repeats the teacher's phrasing and mistakes and lacks rude or empty inputs unless you force them.

questions.q: You have 200 expert rows and noisy logs. How do you grow the set?
questions.a: Keep human-edited logs that pass the spec. Use the 200 as seeds for teacher variants on rare labels, filter hard, and hold out real traffic for test. Do not duplicate the 200 twenty times.

questions.q: After a synth-heavy train, production typos fail. What was the source bias?
questions.a: Synthetic and expert rows were too clean. Add messy log_edit rows and a typo slice to the eval. Retrain or mix in more logs.

questions.q: Why tag source on every training row?
questions.a: So you can drop or down-weight a source when an ablation or a production slice says that source is hurting, without rebuilding the whole lake.

questions.q: When are raw model-to-user logs acceptable as gold?
questions.a: Almost never, unless a later human edit or a trusted judge-plus-audit accepted them against the spec. Raw dumps train yesterday's failures.

match-the-chat-template.explain:
## What it is

Instruction models were trained with a **chat template**: special tokens that mark system, user, assistant, and end-of-turn. Your SFT rows must be rendered with **that same template**. A mismatch is silent. Loss still falls. The served model then never stops, ignores the system prompt, or talks like a base model.

The template is part of the tokenizer and the model's card, not a style choice. Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, and vendor APIs each have their own. If you train with `"User:"`/`"Assistant:"` and serve with the official Jinja template, you trained a different language than you serve.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the number-one "it worked in the notebook" bug. The notebook concatenated strings; vLLM applied `tokenizer.apply_chat_template`. The eval in the notebook used the same broken concat, so it looked fine.

Interviewers love "the model rambling in production". The first suspicion is template or EOS, not rank.

Train with the template the base expects. A mismatch silently degrades train and serve.

## How it works + one small example

One rule: **the function that builds messages for training is the function that builds messages for eval and for serve**. Call `apply_chat_template` (or the vendor equivalent) in all three places. Store the template string or its hash in the run config.

Example. Training row as messages `[{role:system,...},{role:user,...},{role:assistant,...}]`, rendered with the 3.1 Llama template that inserts `<|eot_id|>`. Serve with vLLM's default for that tokenizer. Do not hand-write `<|im_start|>` because a blog used it for a different family.

Check: decode a training batch and look for the special tokens you expect. Check: generate with the served stack and confirm it emits the stop token. A five-minute "wrong template in staging" drill should be in the runbook — you want to recognise the failure shape (ramble, doubled roles, ignored system) before production.

Render every row with the official template; store the template hash on the dataset version. Example: you trained with a generic ChatML on a Llama-3 instruct base. Loss fell; serve rambled. Re-render + retrain fixed it. The GPU was not the bug.

## Failure modes

1. **Train without EOS / eot.** The model never learns to stop.

2. **System prompt only at serve.** The model never saw a system role in SFT and shrugs.

3. **Multi-turn rows flattened to one user string.** You lose turn structure the template was built for.

4. **A notebook that concatenates 'User:'** by hand.

Make match the chat template falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-2.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For match the chat template, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair match the chat template with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for match the chat template and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I render every train, eval, and serve call with the base model's official chat template and the same stop tokens. A template mismatch looks like a bad tune and is usually just a different language at serve time.
keyPoints: The chat template is part of the model, not decoration.
Train, eval, and serve must call the same render function.
Missing end-of-turn tokens teach the model to ramble.
Do not copy another family's special tokens from a blog.
Hash the template in the run config with the tokenizer revision.
Ramble-in-prod is a template bug until proven otherwise.

questions.q: What is a chat template and why must SFT match it?
questions.a: It is the special-token wrapping the base model was trained to see for roles and end-of-turn. If SFT uses a different wrapping, the model learns a dialect you will not speak at serve time, so loss lies and generations look broken.

questions.q: Notebook loss is low; vLLM rambles. First check?
questions.a: Compare `apply_chat_template` output for a train row with the served prompt. Look for missing eot/eos and different role tags. Fix the render function; do not raise rank.

questions.q: How do you keep train and serve aligned as people add features?
questions.a: One shared message-building module imported by the trainer, the eval job, and the gateway. Pin tokenizer revision and template hash in the run file.

questions.q: Why is flattening a multi-turn chat into one 'User:' string risky?
questions.a: The model never practises the official turn tokens. At serve, real multi-turn history uses those tokens and the model leaves the distribution it trained on.

questions.q: What should a staging 'wrong template' drill show you?
questions.a: The failure shape: endless generation, repeated role tags, or a system prompt that is ignored. You want that picture in the runbook so on-call does not start a retrain.

loss-on-responses-not-prompts.explain:
## What it is

Supervised fine-tuning should teach the model to **produce the assistant reply**, not to memorise the user prompt. You **mask the prompt tokens** in the loss (labels = -100 on non-assistant tokens) so gradients flow only through the response, including its end-of-turn token.

If you train on the full sequence, a long retrieved context or a long system prompt dominates the loss. The model gets very good at copying the prompt and only weakly better at the answer. It can also learn to emit user-side text at serve time.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, RAG-style SFT without masking is a common silent failure: train loss looks healthy because the model predicts the already-known context. The skill you wanted barely moves.

Interviews: "why do we mask the prompt?" is a standard SFT question. Answer: so the gradient is about the behaviour you will ask for at inference.

Mask prompt tokens so gradients hit the assistant span. Otherwise you train the model to copy the user.

## How it works + one small example

Use the trainer's completion-only / assistant-only loss flag (TRL `DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM`, or equivalent assistant-mask in the chat template). Verify by printing a label tensor: prompt positions are ignored, assistant tokens are not, EOS is not.

Example. Prompt is 1,800 retrieved tokens plus a question; gold answer is 40 tokens. Unmasked, ~98% of the loss is "predict the documents". Masked, 100% of the loss is the 40-token house answer plus stop. The same batch now trains the skill.

For multi-turn rows, mask every user and system span; unmask every assistant span you want to imitate. If an earlier assistant turn is context only, mask it too — otherwise you spend capacity relearning old replies.

TRL/SFT: labels = -100 on prompt tokens. Spot-check a batch in a debugger. Example: forgetting the mask made the model echo the ticket text. Training loss looked healthy because copying is easy.

## Failure modes

1. **No mask on RAG SFT.** Loss falls, skill does not.

2. **Masking the EOS.** The model never learns to stop.

3. **Masking the whole assistant span by off-by-one.** You train on nothing useful and underfit while celebrating a tiny loss.

4. **Full-sequence loss** on a long retrieved context.

On the job, loss on responses not prompts is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-2.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is loss on responses not prompts'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply loss on responses not prompts as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating loss on responses not prompts as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I mask every non-assistant token so the loss is the reply I will ask for at inference, and I always keep the stop token in the loss. If most of the sequence is retrieved context, an unmasked loss is a lie.
keyPoints: Loss belongs on assistant tokens, including EOS.
Long prompts otherwise dominate and the skill barely moves.
Use the trainer's completion-only / assistant-mask path.
Print labels once and confirm prompt positions are ignored.
In multi-turn, only unmask the assistant spans you want to teach.
A tiny loss with no mask often means you predicted the context.

questions.q: Why mask prompt tokens in the SFT loss?
questions.a: Inference never asks the model to generate the prompt. Gradients should concentrate on the assistant response and its stop token. Otherwise long contexts dominate the loss and the skill you care about is a rounding error.

questions.q: Train loss is low on RAG-style rows but answers stay wrong. First suspicion?
questions.a: Unmasked loss on the retrieved documents. Check the label mask. Switch to completion-only loss and re-score the skill metric.

questions.q: Should the end-of-turn token be masked?
questions.a: No. If EOS is masked the model is not trained to stop. Keep it in the assistant span.

questions.q: A multi-turn example has an earlier assistant mistake you do not want copied. What do you mask?
questions.a: Mask that earlier assistant span (treat it as context) and unmask only the final corrected reply, or rewrite the history so the bad turn is not there.

questions.q: How do you verify the collator is masking correctly?
questions.a: Dump one batch: token ids, labels, and a decode of unmasked positions. You should see only assistant text and stop tokens contributing to loss.

few-clean-beats-many-noisy.explain:
## What it is

For a **narrow** task, a few hundred **clean, representative** examples usually beat thousands of noisy ones. Noise here means wrong labels, mixed specs, duplicates, truncated replies, and near-copy synthetic clones. Each noisy row pulls the model toward a different mapping; the average is mush.

Clean means it passes the spec, is unique enough, and covers the cases you actually see — including the tail, not only the easy mode. Representative means the mix matches the residual error, not a convenience export.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people equate "more data" with "more serious". A 20k dump of thumbs-up chats will lose to 400 audited rows on a forty-label router. You need the courage to delete.

Interviews: saying "quality over quantity for SFT" is expected; saying "and I measure with a 50-row audit every version" is senior.

A few hundred clean rows often beat thousands of near-duplicates for a narrow task.

## How it works + one small example

Set a quality gate before you grow.

- Target a few hundred to a few thousand **accepted** rows for a narrow skill, not 50k raw.
- After each ingest, run the cleaner (dupes, contradictions, truncations, clone n-grams).
- Hand-audit 50 rows; if error rate > your threshold (say 4%), do not train.
- Grow by adding **missing slices**, not by duplicating what you already have.

Example. v1: 350 expert+edited rows, audit error 2%, held-out accuracy 89%. v2: +8,000 raw logs, audit error 11%, accuracy 84%. You revert to v1 and only add the 200 cleaned logs that fill rare labels. Volume was not the lever; coverage of the tail was.

When you truly need scale (a broad assistant), you still clean first. You just accept that "few" becomes "few tens of thousands of clean rows", not "a million unfiltered traces".

Quality pass: drop clones, contradictions, truncated answers. Example: 8k scraped rows, 1.1k after clean, better val than the 8k. You report both sizes so nobody 'helps' by adding the junk back.

## Failure modes

1. **Duplicates as free data.** The model overfits a phrasing and the eval leaks.

2. **Growing before the audit passes.** You industrialise a 11% error factory.

3. **Easy-only cleanliness.** You deleted the hard cases because they looked messy, then the tail dies.

4. **Scraping more** as the only improvement plan.

Time-box few clean beats many noisy to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-2 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.
