When they ask you to 'go deeper on few clean beats many noisy', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether few clean beats many noisy would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for few clean beats many noisy that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

For a narrow tune I would rather train on 400 rows that pass a spec and a 50-row audit than on 20,000 noisy chats. I grow by filling missing slices, not by dumping logs.
keyPoints: Narrow SFT: hundreds of clean rows beat thousands of noisy ones.
Clean = spec pass, unique, covers the real mix including the tail.
Audit a fixed sample every dataset version before you train.
Grow by missing slices, not by duplicates or raw dumps.
Delete is a data skill; more is not automatically better.
Broad assistants still need cleaning; the number just scales up.

questions.q: Why can 400 clean rows beat 20,000 noisy chats on a narrow task?
questions.a: Noisy rows teach contradictory mappings, so the model averages mush. Clean rows agree on one spec. For a closed skill the signal in a few hundred agreements is enough; the extra volume is mostly error.

questions.q: v2 added 8k logs and accuracy fell. What do you check first?
questions.a: The 50-row audit error rate and per-label coverage versus v1. If audit error jumped or hard cases were diluted, revert and add only cleaned tail rows.

questions.q: How do you decide the set is allowed to grow?
questions.a: The spec is stable, the audit error is under threshold, and you can name the slice the new rows add. If you cannot name the slice, you are collecting comfort, not coverage.

questions.q: When is 'few hundred' the wrong scale?
questions.a: When the task is a broad open-ended assistant rather than a narrow mapping. You still clean, but you need much more diversity. Do not use the narrow-task slogan to under-collect a general model.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants to hit 50k rows this sprint. What do you offer instead?
questions.a: A coverage map of slices and a plan to add the empty ones with audit gates. Report accepted rows, not ingested rows.

cleaning-bad-examples.explain:
## What it is

Cleaning is a pipeline, not a hope. You remove **duplicates**, **contradictions** (same prompt, different gold), **wrong labels**, **truncated** replies (hit max tokens, cut mid-JSON), and **synthetic clones** that repeat the same sentence frames. You also drop rows that fail the spec even if a human once liked them.

Every dropped class gets a count in the dataset card so you can see whether the cleaner is eating the tail.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, uncleaned sets cause mysterious "the model contradicts itself" reports that are just two golds fighting. Truncated JSON in train produces truncated JSON in prod.

Interviews: walk through a concrete cleaner, not "we preprocess".

Duplicates, contradictions, wrong labels, truncations, cloned synthetic phrasing — all out.

## How it works + one small example

Implement as deterministic steps with logs.

1. Normalise whitespace and hash the prompt (and optionally the answer) to drop exact dupes.
2. Group by normalised prompt; if golds disagree, send to a human or drop the group.
3. Schema-validate structured golds; drop or repair.
4. Detect truncation: no EOS, unmatched braces, ends mid-word after a length cap.
5. N-gram / embedding near-dupe collapse for synthetic batches.
6. Spec filter: greetings forbidden? drop them.

Example. 6,400 ingested → 410 exact dupes, 88 contradictions, 120 invalid JSON, 64 truncations, 900 synth clones, 70 spec fails → 4,748 accepted. The card shows you almost wiped two rare labels in the clone collapse, so you restore 40 unique expert rows for those labels.

Do not "clean" by deleting every long or angry user prompt. That is policy, not hygiene, and it hides production.

Automated filters plus a 50-row hand audit every version. Example: two gold labels for the same ticket; you pick from the spec and you log the conflict rate. Conflict rate > 5% means the spec is unclear, not that you need a bigger model.

## Failure modes

1. **Contradiction kept as two truths.** The model samples both.

2. **Cleaner eats the tail.** Rare labels vanish; aggregate accuracy rises; hard-case accuracy falls.

3. **Repair by regex until gold is fiction.** You trained on a sentence no user will trigger.

4. **Cleaning once** and never again after a dump lands.

A practical sitting for cleaning bad examples: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-2 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of cleaning bad examples with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put cleaning bad examples on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of cleaning bad examples that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I run a logged cleaner for dupes, contradictions, bad labels, truncations, and synth clones, I publish drop counts, and I check that rare slices survived before I train.
keyPoints: Drop dupes, contradictions, wrong labels, truncations, synth clones.
Log drop counts by class on the dataset card.
Schema-validate structured golds before they enter train.
Watch the cleaner so it does not delete rare labels.
Hygiene is not 'delete long or angry users'.
Contradictory golds become a self-contradicting model.

questions.q: List five classes of bad SFT rows and why each hurts.
questions.a: Duplicates overfit a phrasing and leak. Contradictions teach two mappings. Wrong labels invert the skill. Truncations teach unfinished JSON. Synthetic clones shrink diversity and hide eval leakage.

questions.q: After cleaning, aggregate accuracy rose but a rare label died. What happened?
questions.a: The cleaner or clone collapse removed the few examples of that label. Compare per-label counts before and after and restore unique gold for the tail.

questions.q: How do you handle two different golds for one normalised prompt?
questions.a: Do not keep both. Send the group to a human with the spec, or drop the group. Training on both is how the model learns to flip a coin.

questions.q: What is a cheap truncation detector?
questions.a: Missing EOS, unmatched brackets in structured output, or a reply that ends at the generation cap mid-token. Those rows teach the model to stop early.

questions.q: Why publish drop counts instead of silently deleting?
questions.a: So a reviewer can see if 'cleaning' was actually 'deleted the hard 8%'. The card is part of the dataset version.

balancing-edge-cases.explain:
## What it is

If you train on the raw log distribution, the model learns that the **easy majority is always right**. **Balance** the set so difficult, rare, and high-cost slices have enough mass: empty inputs, ambiguous labels, refusals, multilingual, long tickets, the one product line that causes refunds.

Balance is not fake uniformity. It is **enough** of each slice that the loss cannot ignore it, plus eval metrics per slice so you notice when a majority accuracy hides a tail collapse.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a router that is 94% overall and 40% on "chargeback" will still page you. The majority class was over-sampled by nature.

Interviews: "how do you stop the model always picking the common label?" — class weights, oversampling the tail, and slice metrics, not a bigger rank.

If 95% of rows are the easy label, the model learns to always emit it.

## How it works + one small example

Build a slice table before the split.

- Define slices that matter: label, language, length bucket, refusal, tool-use, the original failure mode.
- Set a minimum train count per slice (even 30–50 can matter on a narrow task).
- Upsample the tail or set loss weights; downsample endless easy "how-to" if it is 70% of logs.
- Keep the **natural** mix on the held-out test so you do not fool yourself with an artificial test prior.

Example. Chargeback is 3% of logs and 30% of money. You upsample chargeback to 12% of train, keep test at 3%, and report both overall and chargeback accuracy. A tune that lifts overall 1 point and drops chargeback 8 points is a fail, not a ship.

Write the balancing rule in the dataset card so v2 does not "accidentally" return to the raw prior.

Upsample rare-but-costly classes or down-sample the easy majority, and report slice n. Example: 'legal hold' is 1% of logs and 40% of the pain. You target 15% of train. Val stays natural so you do not lie to yourself.

## Failure modes

1. **Balanced test set.** You celebrate a number that production will never show.

2. **Upsampled junk.** You duplicated three bad chargeback rows twenty times.

3. **No slice metrics.** Only the mean is reviewed; the tail burns.

4. **Balancing the test set** and celebrating a fake win.

Translate balancing edge cases into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for balancing edge cases than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used balancing edge cases, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of balancing edge cases in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate balancing edge cases more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for balancing edge cases more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used balancing edge cases more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of balancing edge cases more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I give hard and expensive slices enough train mass to be learned, I keep the test mix honest, and I refuse a mean score that hides a tail drop.
keyPoints: Raw logs over-teach the easy majority.
Set a minimum train count for slices that matter.
Upsample clean tail rows; do not clone three junk examples.
Keep the held-out prior close to production.
Report slice metrics, especially the expensive ones.
Write the balancing rule into the dataset version.

questions.q: Why does a raw-log mix produce a model that ignores edge cases?
questions.a: The loss is dominated by frequent easy rows, so parameters move to win the majority. Rare slices contribute too little gradient to be learned unless you upsample or reweight them.

questions.q: Chargeback is 3% of traffic and 30% of loss. How do you balance?
questions.a: Raise its share in train (or its loss weight) using clean examples, keep test near 3%, and gate the ship on chargeback accuracy as well as the mean.

questions.q: Overall +2, payments slice −8. Ship?
questions.a: No. The mean hid a costly regression. Block, inspect those failures, and add clean payments rows or drop the checkpoint.

questions.q: Why not also rebalance the held-out test to be uniform?
questions.a: You would no longer estimate production risk. Uniform test is a diagnostic; the gate should reflect traffic and cost.

questions.q: What is the danger of upsampling by simple duplication?
questions.a: You overfit a handful of phrasings and can leak those copies into eval if you split badly. Prefer new unique tail examples or careful weighted sampling with a leak scan.

leak-free-splits.explain:
## What it is

Split into **train, validation, and held-out test** so that **near-duplicates do not cross**. A leak is not only an exact copy. It is a paraphrase, a shared ticket id, a shared document, or a synthetic child of a test parent. Leaks make test scores look like production and then production falls off a cliff.

The held-out test is frozen. You may look at it when you are ready to ship, not every time you tweak rank.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 98% test / 70% production is almost always leakage or a mismatched template. The leak is the more embarrassing one because it is your process.

Interviews: "how do you split?" should include grouping keys and a near-dupe scan, not `train_test_split(random_state=42)` on rows.

Near-duplicates across train and test are leakage. Hash normalised prompts.

## How it works + one small example

Split by a **group** that must stay together: user id, ticket id, document id, or seed prompt id for synthetic children. Then run a **normalised-prompt hash** and, if you can, an embedding near-dupe pass across the three sets. Any hit moves to train or is dropped from test — test stays pure.

Example. You generate five teacher paraphrases per seed. If any paraphrase is in test, all siblings and the seed are in test — or none are. A random row split puts siblings on both sides and the model "discovers" the paraphrase.

Order of operations: clean → group split → near-dupe scan → lock test hashes in the dataset card. New rows are assigned by the same rules; they do not "refresh" test.

Normalise (lower, collapse space, strip ids), hash, and refuse any test item whose hash or close cousin is in train. Example: a paraphrase of a test ticket in train inflated the score 6 points. After the scan, you knew the real number.

## Failure modes

1. **Random row split on paraphrases.** Instant leak.

2. **Tuning on test.** The held-out set dies the tenth time you peek.

3. **IDs stripped before split.** You can no longer group.

4. **A random 80/20 on raw rows** with repeated customers.

Make leak free splits falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-2.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For leak free splits, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair leak free splits with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for leak free splits and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make leak free splits more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-2.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For leak free splits more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair leak free splits more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for leak free splits more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split by group, scan normalised near-duplicates across train and test, and I freeze the test hashes. A 98% test score with a production slump is a leak until I prove otherwise.
keyPoints: Train, validation, and a frozen held-out test.
Split by group (ticket, user, seed), not by isolated rows.
Near-dupe and paraphrase leaks count as leaks.
Synthetic children stay with their seed on one side.
Lock test hashes; do not refresh test with new rows.
Peeking at test every run spends the holdout.

questions.q: What is a near-duplicate leak in an SFT split?
questions.a: A train row that is an exact or paraphrased copy of a test prompt, or a synthetic child of a test seed. The model memorizes the sibling and the test score stops predicting production.

questions.q: You have five teacher paraphrases per seed. How do you split?
questions.a: Assign the whole sibling group to one split. Never put two paraphrases of the same seed on opposite sides.

questions.q: Test is 98%, production is 70%. What do you suspect and do?
questions.a: Leakage or a template mismatch. Re-run the near-dupe scan, split by group, and re-evaluate on fresh traffic. Do not celebrate the 98%.

questions.q: Why freeze test hashes in the dataset card?
questions.a: So later ingest cannot quietly move a near-dupe of a test item into train, and so reviewers can replay the split.

questions.q: When may you look at the held-out test?
questions.a: When you are choosing whether to ship a candidate already selected on validation. Not on every hyperparameter idea.

pii-licensed-content.explain:
## What it is

Training data is **eaten into weights**. If you would not want the model to repeat a string word for word, that string should not be in the set. That includes **personal data** (names, emails, account ids, health, addresses), **secrets**, and **licensed or copyrighted** text you do not have the right to train on — vendor docs with restrictive terms, books, news, other models' outputs when their terms forbid it.

A tune is not a search index. You cannot reliably delete one paragraph later. The cleanup is before the job.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is legal and trust, not polish. A model that completes a customer's phone number from a log export is an incident. A model that recites a licensed manual is a letter from a publisher.

Interviews: mention PII redaction and licence checks without being asked. It reads as production experience.

If you would not want the model to repeat it, it does not belong in train.

## How it works + one small example

Run a review **before** the split is locked.

- Automated: email/phone/id regexes, secret scanners, known-licence classifiers if you have them.
- Human: a sample of logs, especially long pastes.
- Policy: drop or replace PII with stable placeholders (`{{email}}`) **consistently** in prompt and gold so the mapping still makes sense.
- Licence: keep a source list. Teacher outputs need their own terms check (see distillation).

Example. A support export has order ids and emails. You replace them with typed placeholders and keep the house tone. The model learns the template, not Ms. Alvarez's address. You store the raw export in a restricted bucket that the trainer cannot read.

If a row cannot be redacted without destroying the task (a medical letter that *is* the PII), you do not train on it in an ordinary LoRA. That is a different compliance project.

Scan for emails, account numbers, licensed paragraphs. Example: a help article copied verbatim became a regurgitation risk. You drop or rewrite. A customer name in a rationale is PII even if the label is fine.

## Failure modes

1. **Redact the prompt, leave the gold.** The model learns to re-insert the email.

2. **"It's internal, so it's fine."** Internal still has employees and customers.

3. **Training on a vendor PDF whose terms forbid it.** You cannot un-eat it cheaply.

4. **'We'll redact later'** after the job has run.

Translate pii licensed content into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for pii licensed content than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used pii licensed content, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of pii licensed content in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If I would not want the model to quote a string, I do not train on it. I redact PII consistently, scan for secrets, and I check licences — including teacher outputs — before the job.
keyPoints: Weights can regurgitate training strings; treat that as likely.
Redact PII in both prompt and gold, consistently.
Scan for secrets before the trainer sees the files.
Licensed text and some teacher terms are off-limits.
You cannot reliably unlearn one paragraph after the fact.
Internal logs still contain other people's data.

questions.q: Why is a fine-tune a worse place to store PII than a database?
questions.a: You cannot query-delete one row from weights, and the model may reproduce the string for a new user. A database has access control and erasure. Redact before training.

questions.q: You redacted emails in prompts but left them in gold replies. What happens?
questions.a: The model is trained to emit emails. It will invent or leak them. Redact both sides with the same placeholder scheme.

questions.q: A row is a medical letter that is inherently PII. Options?
questions.a: Do not put it in an ordinary SFT set. Either run a compliance-approved pipeline or drop the row. Placeholders that destroy the task are not a fix.

questions.q: What licence question do you ask about synthetic teacher data?
questions.a: Whether the teacher's terms allow using outputs to train a competing or replacement model. If not, pick another teacher or human data.

questions.q: Where should the raw unredacted export live?
questions.a: In a restricted store the training job cannot read. The trainer sees only the redacted, versioned set.

versioning-the-dataset.explain:
## What it is

A tuned checkpoint is unexplained unless you can point at **exactly** the rows, the spec, the template, and the training config that made it. **Version the dataset** like code: an id, a hash of the accepted rows, the spec version, the split hashes, the cleaner version, and a card with counts and audit error.

"We used the support export" is not a version. Two months later nobody can reproduce the run or answer which bad row caused a regression.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, versioning is how you rebase onto a new base model without folklore. It is also how you revert: restore `ds-2026-03-12` and the matching recipe.

Interviews: "how do you track experiments?" should mention dataset hash next to learning rate, not only W&B screenshots.

Every trained artefact points at a dataset hash and a config hash. Otherwise you cannot retrain.

## How it works + one small example

One folder or table per dataset version:

- `spec.md` (or its hash)
- `accepted.parquet` + SHA-256
- `splits.json` with group ids and prompt hashes
- `card.md`: source mix, drop counts, slice counts, 50-row audit error
- pointer from the training run: `dataset=ds-2026-03-12@sha256:...`

Example. Adapter `router-lora-17` says `dataset=ds-2026-03-12`, `base=llama-3.1-8b-instruct`, `template=llama3.1@rev`. A bad chargeback answer is reproducible: load those rows, find the gold, see the error, ship `ds-2026-03-18` with the fix, train `router-lora-18`.

Do not overwrite a version in place. Snapshots are cheap; arguments about what changed are not.

DVC or a hashed tarball in object storage: `tickets-sft-v7`. The run file stores that hash. Example: v8 silently added 200 bad rows; you rolled to v7 because the hash was in the decision record.

## Failure modes

1. **Mutable 'latest'.** Today's train is not yesterday's and nobody noticed.

2. **Hashing the raw dump, not the accepted set.** The cleaner moved; the hash lied.

3. **Config in a chat thread.** The run cannot be replayed.

4. **'final_final.csv'** on a laptop.

On the job, versioning the dataset is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-2.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is versioning the dataset'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply versioning the dataset as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating versioning the dataset as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, versioning the dataset more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-2.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is versioning the dataset more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply versioning the dataset more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating versioning the dataset more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every checkpoint points at an immutable dataset hash, spec version, and split file. If I cannot name those, I do not have a model I can retrain or debug.
keyPoints: Version rows, spec, splits, and cleaner — not a folder called latest.
Hash the accepted set the trainer actually reads.
The run config stores dataset id + sha256 + template + base.
Never overwrite a version; snapshot and bump.
A dataset card with audit error is part of the version.
Rebase and rollback both depend on this pin.

questions.q: What artefacts make a dataset version reproducible?
questions.a: The spec, the accepted-row file and its hash, the split hashes, the cleaner version, and a card with counts and audit error. The training run stores those pointers next to the base and template.

questions.q: A production miss looks like a wrong gold. How do you confirm?
questions.a: Resolve the adapter's dataset hash, find the nearest train row, and read the gold against the spec. If the gold is wrong, bump a new dataset version; do not hotfix weights by hand.

questions.q: Two runs claim the same dataset name but different metrics. First check?
questions.a: Compare sha256 of the accepted files and the split files. A mutable 'latest' or an unhashed cleaner change is the usual cause.

questions.q: Why hash accepted rows rather than the raw ingest?
questions.a: The trainer never sees the raw ingest. Reproducibility is about the tensor input. Raw hashes hide cleaner drift.

questions.q: How does dataset versioning make a base-model rebase cheaper?
questions.a: You rerun the same hashed set and eval on the new base instead of reconstructing folklore from Slack. The comparison is fair.

gold-spec-before-collection.explain:
## What it is

**Gold-spec before collection** means the acceptance rules exist as a checklist an example must pass, and logs that miss them are **rejected**, not "cleaned later". It is the operational form of specify-the-behaviour-first: the spec is in the intake filter, not in a slide.

Collection UIs, log exporters, and synthetic jobs all call the same `accept(row)` function. If it returns false, the row never enters the lake.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "we'll filter in a notebook next week" is how 50k dirty rows become the set because next week never comes. Putting the spec at the door is cheaper than a heroic cleaner.

Interviews: this is the difference between a data dump and a labelling operation.

Write acceptance rules, then reject logs that miss them. Collection without a spec is a junk pile.

## How it works + one small example

Turn the spec into predicates.

- `has_allowed_label`
- `json_valid` / `schema_valid`
- `no_greeting` / `no_pii_regex`
- `not_truncated`
- `reason_length <= 20 tokens`

Hook them in the export job. Show labellers the failing predicate. Track reject rates per predicate so a sudden spike means the product changed or the logger broke.

Example. After a prompt change, production answers grow greetings. Reject rate on `no_greeting` jumps from 4% to 40%. You do not quietly accept them. You either fix production or you stop exporting until humans edit. The train set stays on-spec.

The ten gold / five fail quiz is the unit test for `accept()`.

Rules: required keys, max length, no PII, label in the enum. A linter drops rows at ingest. Example: 30% of logs failed the enum; you never paid to train on them.

## Failure modes

1. **Accept-all, filter-later.** The lake becomes the product.

2. **Predicates only on synthetic.** Logs sneak around the spec.

3. **Silent rejects.** Labellers do not learn; they repeat the fail.

4. **Collect first, invent rules later** and relabel for a month.

Translate gold spec before collection into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for gold spec before collection than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used gold spec before collection, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of gold spec before collection in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate gold spec before collection more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for gold spec before collection more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used gold spec before collection more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of gold spec before collection more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compile the behaviour spec into an accept() used at intake. Rows that miss it never enter the lake, and I watch reject rates so a broken logger cannot fill the set.
keyPoints: The spec is an intake filter, not a later notebook.
One accept() for logs, experts, and synthetic jobs.
Show labellers which predicate failed.
Watch reject-rate spikes as a data-quality alert.
Unit-test accept() on the ten gold and five fail rows.
Filter-later is how dirty lakes become training sets.

questions.q: What does gold-spec before collection change about intake?
questions.a: Every source goes through the same accept() predicates derived from the spec. Failures are rejected at the door with a reason, not stored for a mythical later clean.

questions.q: Reject rate on no_greeting jumps from 4% to 40% after a prompt change. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not relax the predicate to fill the set. Fix the producer or switch to human edits. Investigate the spike; it is a data alert.

questions.q: Synthetic jobs use accept() but the log exporter does not. Risk?
questions.a: The lake's majority becomes unspecced logs. The filter is theatre. Put the exporter on the same function.

questions.q: How do you unit-test the intake filter?
questions.a: The ten passing golds must accept; the five known fails must reject with the expected predicate. Run that in CI when the spec changes.

questions.q: Why show labellers the failing predicate?
questions.a: So they correct the same mistake next time instead of submitting another silent reject. The spec stays alive.

near-duplicate-leak-scan.explain:
## What it is

A **near-duplicate leak scan** hashes **normalised** prompts (and sometimes answers) so a paraphrase of a test item cannot sit in train. Normalise: lowercase where safe, strip punctuation and greetings, collapse whitespace, maybe drop digits that are only ids. Then hash. Optionally embed and block pairs above a similarity threshold.

This is the mechanical twin of leak-free splits. The split assigns groups; the scan catches what grouping missed — a human rewrite of a test ticket, a synth paraphrase with a new seed id.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the difference between an honest 81% and a vanity 96%. After you have been burned once, the scan is a required CI step on every dataset version.

Interviews: naming "normalised prompt hash" is concrete enough to be believed.

Hash normalised prompts so a paraphrase of a test item never lands in train.

## How it works + one small example

Pipeline:

1. Build a canonical string per row (`norm(prompt)`).
2. Exact-hash collision across splits → move or drop.
3. Optional: MinHash or embedding k-NN; review pairs over a threshold.
4. For synthetic rows, also hash the **seed** and block if the seed is in test.
5. Write surviving test hashes into `splits.json`.

Example. Test has "I was charged twice on order 8891". Train has "Charged 2x, order 8891 — please help". After digit-preserving normalisation the order id still links them; your group key should have caught 8891. If ids were stripped, the embedding pass still flags the pair. You move the train sibling out.

Re-run the scan whenever you add rows. New synth is the usual leak source.

After the split, run a near-dup pass (hash + embedding similarity). Anything over a threshold moves to train or is dropped from test — you choose, you record. Example: 40 test items were cousins of train; removing them dropped the headline 3 points. That was honesty.

## Failure modes

1. **Hashing raw text only.** "Please help" vs "pls help" evades an exact hash.

2. **Aggressive normalisation that collides unrelated tickets.** Too many false merges; you empty the test set.

3. **Scan once at v1.** v3 synth leaks into the frozen test's neighbourhood.

4. **Only exact-string dedup.**

A practical sitting for near duplicate leak scan: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-2 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of near duplicate leak scan with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put near duplicate leak scan on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of near duplicate leak scan that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for near duplicate leak scan more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-2 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.
