Worked habit: put near duplicate leak scan more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of near duplicate leak scan more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I normalise prompts, hash them, and block train rows that collide with test — including paraphrases and synth children — every time the dataset version bumps.
keyPoints: Normalise then hash; exact raw hashes miss paraphrases.
Keep a group key (order id, seed) in addition to the hash.
Re-run the scan on every ingest, especially synthetic.
Embedding near-dupe is a second pass, not a replacement.
Tune normalisation so you do not collide unrelated rows.
A vanity 96% is often a missed paraphrase leak.

questions.q: What does a near-duplicate leak scan do that a random split does not?
questions.a: It catches paraphrases and synthetic children that do not share a row index. Random splits assume independence; language data is full of rewrites.

questions.q: Train has a polite rewrite of a test ticket. How should the scan treat it?
questions.a: As a leak. Move the train row or drop it. If they share an order id, the group split should have kept them together; the scan is the backstop.

questions.q: After adding 2k synth rows, test score jumps 7 points. First check?
questions.a: Re-run the leak scan against the frozen test hashes and seed ids. Synth is the usual silent leak. If hits appear, remove them and re-score.

questions.q: Why preserve order ids while stripping greetings in normalisation?
questions.a: Greetings are style; ids are the group key that proves two rows are the same case. Stripping ids makes true leaks look novel.

questions.q: When do embedding near-dupes need a human?
questions.a: When similarity is high but the task differs (two refund tickets with different outcomes). Auto-blocking those would shrink diversity; review the band above the threshold.

synthetic-diversity-checks.explain:
## What it is

Teacher-written examples collapse. **Synthetic diversity checks** measure how much the new rows are clones — repeated n-grams, repeated templates, tiny edit distance — and **drop the clones** before they dominate the loss.

Diversity is not "many files". It is many **distinct** phrasings, entities, and slice tags. A teacher asked to "write more chargeback tickets" will emit the same four sentences with new numbers. That is one example with makeup.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, undiverse synth is how students fail the first weird user. It is also how you leak: clones of a test seed look new to a sloppy hash.

Interviews: "risks of synthetic SFT" should include clone collapse and teacher error, not only "might be wrong".

Measure n-gram overlap across teacher rows and drop clones.

## How it works + one small example

Measure, then drop.

- Self-BLEU / n-gram overlap inside the synth pool and against train.
- Template detection: same opening 8 tokens.
- Entity diversity: unique SKUs, locales, error codes.
- Slice caps: no more than N synth rows per seed or per label.

Example. 1,000 teacher rows → 620 share one of three openings ("Of course, I can help with your refund…"). You drop those 620, keep 180 that start differently and pass the spec, and you change the teacher prompt to forbid the house greeting the teacher loves.

Pair this with the leak scan: a clone of a test item is both a diversity fail and a leak.

Self-BLEU / unique-trigram rate on the synthetic slice. Example: 2k teacher rows collapsed to ~300 templates. You keep one per template and you ask the teacher for new seeds, not more temperature on the same seed.

## Failure modes

1. **Diversity by count.** 5,000 rows, 12 templates.

2. **Dropping until the tail is gone.** You needed those 40 ugly rows more than the 600 clones.

3. **No teacher prompt constraint.** You fight the same greeting every batch.

4. **Temperature 1.2 as a diversity strategy** with one prompt.

Make synthetic diversity checks falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-2.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For synthetic diversity checks, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair synthetic diversity checks with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for synthetic diversity checks and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make synthetic diversity checks more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-2.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For synthetic diversity checks more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair synthetic diversity checks more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for synthetic diversity checks more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I measure n-gram and template overlap on teacher rows, drop clones, cap per seed, and I will not let 5,000 files hide twelve sentences.
keyPoints: Synthetic data collapses to a few templates unless you check.
Measure n-gram overlap, openings, and entity diversity.
Cap synth rows per seed and per label.
Drop clones; keep the ugly unique tail.
A clone of a test seed is also a leak.
Fix the teacher prompt if the same greeting keeps appearing.

questions.q: What is a synthetic diversity check looking for?
questions.a: Clone collapse: repeated n-grams, identical openings, low entity variety, too many children per seed. Those rows waste loss and can leak paraphrases into test.

questions.q: 620 of 1,000 teacher rows start with the same greeting. Action?
questions.a: Drop them, forbid that opening in the teacher prompt, and keep only rows that pass the spec and look distinct. Do not keep them for 'volume'.

questions.q: Diversity filtering removed most chargeback synth. What did you lose?
questions.a: The tail you were trying to grow. Restore unique expert or log_edit chargeback rows and loosen the filter only for that slice, or prompt the teacher with more seeds.

questions.q: Why cap children per seed?
questions.a: Many paraphrases of one seed are still one situation. They overweight that situation and leak if any sibling is in test.

questions.q: How do diversity checks interact with the leak scan?
questions.a: Run both. Diversity drops clones inside train; the leak scan blocks remaining near-dupes of test. Neither replaces the other.

label-audit-sample.explain:
## What it is

A **label audit** is a **fixed-size hand review** (fifty rows is a good default) of every dataset version, with the **error rate recorded** on the card. It is not browsing until you feel good. It is a sample with a protocol: who reviews, against which spec, how disagreements are resolved, and what error rate blocks training.

Fifty is enough to catch a 10% disaster with high probability and cheap enough to do every bump. It will not catch a 0.5% poison; that is what automated predicates are for.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the cheapest quality metric you will ever have. Teams that skip it train on a 12% wrong set and then debug the model for a week.

Interviews: "how do you know the set is clean?" — accept() plus a 50-row audit with a recorded rate. That sentence is complete.

Hand-review a fixed 50-row sample every dataset version and record the error rate.

## How it works + one small example

Protocol:

1. Draw 50 rows **stratified** by slice (not 50 easy ones).
2. A reviewer who did not write the rows applies the spec blindly.
3. A second reviewer on disagreements.
4. Error rate = definite fails / 50. Threshold e.g. 4% (2 rows) blocks the train.
5. Write the rate, the reviewer ids, and links to the fail rows on the card.

Example. v7 audit: 4/50 fail (wrong label, truncated JSON, PII, greeting). You fix those classes in the cleaner, redraw 50, get 1/50, train. You do not "fix the four and call it 0/50" without a redraw — that is grading your own homework.

Trend the rate across versions. A climbing audit error means intake is drifting even if accept() has not changed.

Two reviewers, same 50, conflict log. If error rate > 2% (illustrative), stop training and fix the pipeline. Example: v9 audit was 8% wrong; you never launched that job. The sample is versioned next to the set.

## Failure modes

1. **Unstratified sample.** You never see the tail.

2. **Author reviews their own rows.** The rate is fiction.

3. **No block threshold.** The audit is a ritual; you train anyway.

4. **Auditing only the first version** and trusting automation after.

Translate label audit sample into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for label audit sample than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used label audit sample, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of label audit sample in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate label audit sample more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-2.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for label audit sample more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used label audit sample more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of label audit sample more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every dataset version gets a stratified 50-row hand audit, the error rate goes on the card, and I will not train if it misses the threshold. Fixing the sample without redrawing does not count.
keyPoints: Fixed 50-row (or similar) audit every dataset version.
Stratify so the tail is in the sample.
Reviewers are not the authors of those rows.
Record the error rate; a threshold blocks the train.
After fixes, redraw; do not grade the same 50 again as 0%.
Trend the rate — climbing means intake is drifting.

questions.q: What does a label audit sample produce that accept() does not?
questions.a: A measured human error rate on a stratified sample, including mistakes no predicate knows about yet. accept() is automated and blind to new failure classes.

questions.q: Audit is 4/50. You fix those four rows. Can you train?
questions.a: Not on the strength of '0/50 on the same sample'. Redraw a new stratified 50. The original four taught you classes to clean, not the new rate.

questions.q: Audits are always 50 easy how-to tickets. What is wrong?
questions.a: The sample is not stratified. The tail can be 20% wrong while the audit stays clean. Force slice quotas.

questions.q: Why record reviewer ids on the card?
questions.a: So you can see self-review, measure inter-rater issues, and reproduce who called a row good when a production incident traces to it.

questions.q: Pick a block threshold and justify it for a forty-label router.
questions.a: Something tight like 4% (2/50). A 10% wrong set will move decision boundaries. Automated predicates should already have removed the obvious fails, so 4% remaining is a real process problem.

what-sft-changes.explain:
## What it is

**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** continues training a pretrained or already instruction-tuned model so that next-token prediction on your **target responses** becomes more likely. It does not add a new head for your task. It **nudges** existing weights (or a LoRA sitting on them) toward the demonstrations.

What moves: the mapping from a class of prompts to a class of replies — tone, format, a closed label set, a house template. What barely moves: large new factual stores, general reasoning the base never had, and safety you did not include in the mix.

SFT is imitation. If the gold is wrong, the model becomes fluently wrong. If the gold is a distribution of styles, the model averages them. The ceiling is the data plus the base, not the learning-rate schedule.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you need a mental model that stops magical thinking. Teams expect SFT to "teach the wiki" or "make it smarter". It taught the reply shape. Retrieval still owns the wiki.

Interviews: "what does SFT actually optimise?" — token-level loss on the assistant span. Then: it is capped by demonstration quality, and it can forget behaviours you did not replay.

SFT raises likelihood of the target tokens. It nudges; it does not install a wiki.

## How it works + one small example

Mechanically: render the chat, mask the prompt, minimise cross-entropy on assistant tokens. After a few hundred to a few thousand steps the model is more likely to emit your JSON and less likely to emit the generic assistant preamble.

Example. Base instruct model, forty labels. Before SFT it invents label 41 and writes a paragraph. After SFT on 800 clean rows it emits `{"label":"billing","reason":"..."}` and stops. It did not learn new billing law; it learned the mapping and the shape.

A second picture: you SFT on only polite refunds. The model becomes unwilling to refuse a fraudulent refund request. That is not "more helpful"; it is imitation of a one-sided mix. You change the mix, not the optimiser.

You start from an instruction model, you minimise loss on the assistant spans, you get a model that prefers your mapping. Example: after two epochs the router emits house labels; it does not 'know' next week's SKU. If you needed facts, you retrieved.

## Failure modes

1. **Expecting knowledge install.** You evaluate with teacher labels and think you got smarter.

2. **Imitating a mess.** Loss falls; the product is a fluent mess.

3. **Forgetting the rest of the assistant.** Narrow SFT without replay of refusals and general asks.

4. **Calling SFT 'teaching the model everything we know'.**

Time-box what sft changes to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-3 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on what sft changes', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether what sft changes would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for what sft changes that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

SFT is next-token imitation of your assistant spans. It reliably changes format and tone and is capped by the demonstrations; it is a weak way to add facts or new reasoning.
keyPoints: SFT minimises loss on target assistant tokens.
It nudges behaviour; it does not bolt on a new task head.
Ceiling = data quality + base capability.
Good at tone, format, closed mappings; weak at facts.
A one-sided mix is imitated, including missing refusals.
If gold is wrong, the model becomes fluently wrong.

questions.q: What quantity does SFT actually minimise?
questions.a: Cross-entropy on the tokens of the target assistant responses (ideally with prompts masked). There is no separate classification head unless you added one.

questions.q: After SFT the model formats JSON perfectly but still invents policy. What did SFT change?
questions.a: The reply shape and maybe tone. Policy facts were never a good SFT target. Put policy in retrieval and stop expecting the loss to install it.

questions.q: Loss is excellent and the model is fluently off-brand. Cause?
questions.a: The gold is off-brand. SFT imitated it. Fix the spec and the rows; do not lower the learning rate to 'add creativity'.

questions.q: Why is SFT a poor way to add reasoning the base lacks?
questions.a: A short imitation stage does not create new circuits for proofs or long-horizon planning. You need a stronger base, more pretraining, or a different method — not 800 rows of hoped-for brilliance.

questions.q: How can SFT reduce safety?
questions.a: If the mix has no refusals, likelihood of the old refusal style falls. The model imitates the helpful-only gold. Replay safety and probe it.

hyperparameters-that-matter.explain:
## What it is

The first knobs that actually move an SFT run are **learning rate**, **epochs** (or steps), **batch size** (and **gradient accumulation**), and **sequence length**. Rank and optimiser bells matter later. Most failed first runs are "LR too high, loss exploded" or "LR too low / too few steps, nothing moved" or "sequence length chopped the answer".

Learning rate is the one to sweep first. Epochs on a small clean set should be small; repeating 400 rows for 10 epochs is how you memorise. Batch size changes noise and memory; accumulation fakes a larger batch when VRAM is tight. Sequence length must fit the **rendered** prompt plus answer; otherwise you train on truncated gold.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people copy a blog's 2e-4 and 3 epochs for a different model size and data scale. The run looks busy and the eval is flat.

Interviews: list these five, say you sweep LR before architecture, and mention that tokens-per-batch = microbatch × accumulation × sequence.

LR, epochs, batch, seq length, grad accum — in that order of attention. Sweep LR first.

## How it works + one small example

A first grid for a 7–8B LoRA on a few hundred to a few thousand rows (illustrative, not a law): LR in {5e-5, 1e-4, 2e-4}, 1–2 epochs, microbatch 1–4, accumulate to an effective 16–32, sequence length from a percentile of your rendered lengths (e.g. 99th) not from a meme 4096 if your rows are 600 tokens.

Example. Run A: LR 5e-4, loss spikes, garbage. Run B: LR 5e-5, 1 epoch, val skill +6 points. Run C: same LR, 5 epochs, train loss tiny, val skill −2 (overfit). You keep B. You did not touch rank yet.

Log tokens/second and effective batch. If accumulation is 32 and you think you have batch 32 but only 40 steps/epoch, you are barely updating — count **optimizer steps**, not dataloader rows.

Start with a small LR grid, one epoch, watch val. Example: 2e-4 diverged; 2e-5 learned. You did not touch rank until LR was stable. Seq length must cover your real tickets or you silently truncate gold.

## Failure modes

1. **Sweeping rank before LR.** You attribute an LR miss to LoRA.

2. **Epochs as a badge.** More passes on 300 rows is memorisation.

3. **Sequence length below the gold.** You train the model to stop mid-JSON.

4. **Copying a blog's 3e-4** on a different base and precision.

Translate hyperparameters that matter into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for hyperparameters that matter than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used hyperparameters that matter, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of hyperparameters that matter in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I sweep learning rate first, keep epochs low on a small clean set, set sequence length from real rendered lengths, and I count optimiser steps — not folklore from a different model.
keyPoints: First knobs: LR, epochs/steps, batch, accumulation, sequence length.
Sweep LR before rank or architecture.
Few clean epochs; many epochs on a tiny set overfit.
Sequence length must fit rendered prompt plus gold.
Effective batch = microbatch × accumulation.
Count optimiser steps, not just dataset passes.

questions.q: Which hyperparameter should you grid first on a new SFT job?
questions.a: Learning rate. It decides whether the run explodes, crawls, or learns. Rank, epochs, and fancy optimisers are later, once an LR shows a real skill bump.

questions.q: 400 rows, 10 epochs, train loss near zero, val skill down. What do you change?
questions.a: Cut epochs (or steps) and maybe LR. You memorised the 400. Early-stop on the skill metric and add data only if underfit remains.

questions.q: Answers in train are 800 tokens but max length is 512. Symptom?
questions.a: Truncated gold, often mid-structure. The model learns to stop early. Raise length, pack smarter, or shorten the gold — do not ignore it.

questions.q: Why does gradient accumulation exist?
questions.a: To reach a larger effective batch when VRAM only fits a microbatch of 1–2. The optimiser sees the accumulated gradient as one larger step.

questions.q: Your epoch is 40 optimiser steps. Is that enough to judge two epochs?
questions.a: Maybe not; you have very few updates. Either the data is tiny (then one epoch plus a small LR sweep is enough) or accumulation is so high you are under-stepping. Report steps, not only epochs.

full-vs-parameter-efficient.explain:
## What it is

**Full fine-tuning** updates every weight. **Parameter-efficient** methods (LoRA, QLoRA, and cousins) freeze the base and train a small add-on. For a **narrow** task, full updates are rarely necessary: they cost more memory, more storage, more time, and they are easier to overfit and easier to forget with.

Full FT still exists: research, or a broad domain shift where adapters underfit even at high rank. That is not the default for an 8B house-label router.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, full FT of a 70B is a cluster conversation. LoRA is a single-GPU conversation. Choosing full FT because it "sounds more real" is how teams blow the budget and then cannot host the result.

Interviews: trade quality, memory, time, and storage. Say when you would still full-tune (you probably would not).

Updating every weight is rarely needed for a narrow task and is expensive to store and serve.

## How it works + one small example

Compare on the same data and eval.

- Memory: full FT keeps optimiser states on all params; LoRA keeps them on the adapter. QLoRA also quantises the frozen base.
- Storage: full copy of the model versus tens of megabytes of adapter.
- Serving: full FT is one blob; LoRA can stay swappable on a shared base.
- Quality: for style/format, LoRA usually matches full FT closely enough that the extra cost loses.

Example. 8B labeler, 2k rows. Full FT needs a much larger GPU (or heavy offload) and writes 16GB of weights. LoRA rank 16 on attention fits a 24GB card and writes 50MB. Held-out accuracy differs by 0.4 points. You ship the adapter.

If LoRA rank 64 plus MLP still underfits a broad rewrite task, *then* you discuss full FT or a bigger base — after you have proved the adapter ran out.

PEFT (LoRA) for almost all product tunes. Full FT when you have a research reason and the GPUs. Example: a 8B full FT is a full 8B artefact per version; a rank-16 LoRA is megabytes. You can still lose to a bad dataset either way.

## Failure modes

1. **Full FT on a 400-row set.** You will memorise and forget.

2. **Assuming LoRA cannot work** because a paper used full FT on a different problem.

3. **No serve plan for a full copy.** You trained something you cannot host.

4. **Full FT to look serious.**

On the job, full vs parameter efficient is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-3.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is full vs parameter efficient'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply full vs parameter efficient as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating full vs parameter efficient as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

For a narrow task I default to LoRA or QLoRA: enough quality, far less memory and storage, swappable. I only consider full fine-tuning after adapters underfit a task that actually needs it.
keyPoints: Full FT updates all weights; PEFT trains a small add-on.
Narrow tasks rarely need full FT.
PEFT wins on memory, disk, time, and multi-tenant serving.
Compare quality on the same eval before paying for full FT.
Tiny data plus full FT is a memorisation machine.
If you cannot host a full copy, do not train one.

questions.q: Why is full fine-tuning rarely necessary for a narrow house task?
questions.a: The behaviour lives in a low-dimensional change. Adapters can represent that change. Full FT spends memory and storage and overfits small sets without a matching quality win.

questions.q: When would you still consider full FT?
questions.a: After high-rank LoRA (attention + MLP) underfits a broad domain shift, and you can afford to train and host the full copy. Not as the first experiment on 800 rows.

questions.q: You full-tuned an 8B on 400 rows. Train loss is zero, general chat is broken. Diagnosis?
questions.a: Overfit full FT plus catastrophic forgetting. Switch to LoRA, cut epochs, add a forgetting probe, and accept that 400 rows do not justify touching every weight.

questions.q: Name three costs full FT pays that LoRA usually does not.
questions.a: Optimiser memory on all parameters, storing a second full checkpoint, and losing cheap multi-adapter serving on one base.

questions.q: A stakeholder says PEFT is 'not real training'. How do you answer?
questions.a: Show the same-set eval of LoRA versus a full run if you have it, plus the memory and serve numbers. Real is what ships and can be retrained, not what updates more tensors.

a-first-sft-run-with-trl.explain:
## What it is

A first SFT job should be **small, scripted, and boring**. Use a library such as **TRL**'s `SFTTrainer` (or equivalent) with a config file: model id, dataset hash, template, LR, batch, max length, seed. Confirm that **train and validation loss both move down** and that a **skill metric** on a few samples improves. If only train loss falls, you are not done celebrating.

The point of the first run is not a leaderboard. It is to prove the pipes: data renders, mask is correct, the job is reproducible, and you can read logs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, notebook-only first runs cannot be replayed by the next person. TRL (or Axolotl, Unsloth, a vendor API) is the difference between a souvenir and a recipe.

Interviews: you should be able to name a stack and what you look at on run one (loss on both splits, a couple of generations, no OOM).

A small TRL job whose train and val loss both fall is the hello-world — not a ship.

## How it works + one small example

Minimal path:

1. One YAML/CLI: base, dataset, template, LR, epochs, seed, output dir.
2. Overfit a **four-row** sanity set until the model reproduces them. If it cannot, the template or mask is wrong — fix before the real set.
3. Real run: train + val loss, sample generations each N steps, save checkpoints.
4. Commit the config. Do not leave the LR in a chat.

Example. Four-row overfit fails: the model never emits the JSON key. You find the collator was not completion-only and max length cut the gold. Fix, overfit succeeds, then run the 800-row job. Val loss follows train for an epoch and you keep that checkpoint.

TRL specifics change; the discipline does not: config in git, hash of data, one command.

One file: dataset hash, template, LR, max steps. Confirm val loss tracks train. Read 20 outputs. Example: train fell, val rose at step 400 — you already have an early-stop point. A first run that only prints train loss is incomplete.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping the four-row overfit.** You debug a 2-hour job that could have failed in three minutes.

2. **Watching only train loss.** You miss under/overfit.

3. **Unpinned packages.** Next week the same config is a different trainer.

4. **Declaring victory on train loss alone.**

On the job, a first sft run with trl is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-3.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is a first sft run with trl'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply a first sft run with trl as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating a first sft run with trl as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

My first SFT run is a config-file TRL (or similar) job: four-row overfit to prove the pipes, then a real run where train and val loss both fall and I can replay the command.
keyPoints: First run proves pipes, not a leaderboard.
Use a config file: base, data hash, template, LR, seed.
Four-row overfit before the long job.
Train and val loss should both move; sample outputs too.
Pin package versions with the config.
If you cannot rerun the command, it was a notebook souvenir.

questions.q: What should a first TRL SFT run prove?
questions.a: That data renders with the right template and loss mask, the job is reproducible from a config, train and val loss move, and generations look like the task. Not that you beat a paper.

questions.q: The four-row overfit cannot reproduce the JSON. Where do you look?
questions.a: Chat template, completion-only mask, and max sequence length truncating gold. Do not start a hyperparameter sweep on the full set yet.

questions.q: Why pin TRL/transformers versions in the run file?
questions.a: Trainer defaults and template code move. An unpinned rerun is a different experiment with the same YAML name.

questions.q: Train loss falls, val loss never does, on run one. Meaning?
questions.a: Leak, too few unique val rows, or you are already overfitting / the val set is a different task. Fix data and split before you sweep rank.

questions.q: Why is a CLI/YAML better than a notebook for the first real run?
questions.a: Someone else can replay it, CI can run it, and the config can be stored next to the checkpoint. A notebook hides cells you forgot to run.

reading-the-loss-curves.explain:
## What it is

Loss curves are a **health check**, not a ship metric. **Underfit**: train and val stay high, skill does not move — raise steps or LR (carefully), or the task is too hard for the base. **Overfit**: train keeps falling, val rises or skill falls — stop earlier, lower LR/epochs, more unique data. **Unstable**: loss spikes or NaNs — lower LR, check for bad rows (huge tokens, broken mask), try grad clipping.

A smooth falling train loss can still be a bad product. Always pair curves with the skill metric.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people screenshot a pretty train curve and ship. Val has been rising for an hour.

Interviews: sketch the three shapes and the first action for each. Mention that generation quality can diverge from loss.

Underfit: both high. Overfit: train down, val up. Unstable: spikes — lower LR.

## How it works + one small example

Look at train loss, val loss, and **one task number** on the same plot cadence.

Example. Steps 0–200: both losses fall, format-valid 70→91%. Steps 200–400: train 0.4→0.15, val 0.35→0.55, format-valid 91→88%. You take the step-200 checkpoint. That is overfitting; more steps would have looked "better" on train.

Unstable example: a spike every time a 8k-token row hits a 2k max length and the mask goes empty. You filter those rows; the spikes vanish. The curve was telling you about data, not about LoRA.

Log in a comparable unit (loss per token). Changing packing mid-run makes curves incomparable.

Screenshot both curves in the run page. Example: a spike every 50 steps was a bad batch of truncated rows, not 'the model'. You cleaned; the spikes left. You do not increase epochs on an overfit curve.

## Failure modes

1. **Smoothing away spikes.** You miss the bad batch.

2. **Different val every run.** Curves cannot be compared.

3. **Trusting loss after a template change.** You may have started measuring a different token set.

4. **Smoothing the val curve away** in a blog screenshot.

Translate reading the loss curves into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for reading the loss curves than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used reading the loss curves, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of reading the loss curves in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate reading the loss curves more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for reading the loss curves more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used reading the loss curves more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of reading the loss curves more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read train versus val loss for underfit, overfit, and instability, and I still pick checkpoints from the task metric. A pretty train curve is not a ship decision.
keyPoints: Underfit: both losses high, skill stuck.
Overfit: train down, val up or skill down — stop earlier.
Unstable: spikes/NaNs — lower LR, inspect bad rows.
Pair curves with a task metric every time.
Use a fixed val set so runs compare.
Loss after a template change is a new measurement.

questions.q: How do you recognise overfitting on SFT curves?
questions.a: Train loss keeps falling while validation loss rises or the task metric worsens. Take an earlier checkpoint and reduce LR or epochs.

questions.q: Both losses are high and flat after an epoch. First knobs?
questions.a: Confirm the mask and template, then try a higher LR in a small grid or more steps. If still flat, the base or the data may be wrong for the task — do not just add rank blindly.

questions.q: Loss spikes on the same step numbers each epoch. Suspicion?
questions.a: A bad row or a length/mask edge at those indices. Inspect that batch; do not only lower LR.

questions.q: Why is val loss not enough to pick a checkpoint?
questions.a: It can fall while the product skill (exact label, schema, refusal) does not, or while generations get worse. Use the skill metric.

questions.q: You changed packing and the loss halved instantly. Did you win?
questions.a: Probably not; you changed how loss is averaged or which tokens are seen. Recheck the skill metric on the same eval.

catastrophic-forgetting.explain:
## What it is

**Catastrophic forgetting** is when a narrow tune **gains the skill and loses abilities the base already had**: general instruction following, languages you did not train, tool-calling format, and especially **safety refusals**. The loss never mentions those abilities, so they can fade.

It is not rare. A support-tone LoRA that never saw a disallowed request will answer it more often. A JSON-only tune will become rude when asked a normal question.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you ship a "better router" that fails a compliance probe. The task metric looked great because you did not measure the rest.

Interviews: name forgetting, give a safety example, and say you keep a **probe set** with a fail threshold.

The model gains the skill and loses general ability. Probe it.

## How it works + one small example

Keep a small **forgetting probe**: 50–200 prompts the tune should still handle — general asks, a few languages if you serve them, tool-call format, and the safety suite. Run it on base, prompted baseline, and every checkpoint. Fail the run if a probe slice drops more than a written delta (for example 5 points or any new critical jailbreak).

Mitigations: mix a little replay data (refusals, general chat), lower LR / fewer epochs, prefer LoRA over full FT, stop when the **task** metric plateaus.

Example. Task accuracy 86→93%. Refusal probe 96→71%. You do not ship. You add 80 refusal demonstrations, drop a half epoch, and land 92% task / 94% refusal. The first checkpoint was a trap.

Keep a 50-item general set. Fail the run if it drops past a written threshold. Example: router +8, general −6, refusals worse. You mix 200 general/safety rows or you drop rank. Task-only joy is how you ship a specialist that cannot follow 'reply in JSON'.

## Failure modes

1. **No probe.** You learn about forgetting from a customer.

2. **Probe is only English chit-chat.** You miss the safety slice.

3. **Replaying so much general data** that the narrow skill never appears.

4. **No general probe** because the task metric was pretty.

A practical sitting for catastrophic forgetting: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of catastrophic forgetting with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put catastrophic forgetting on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of catastrophic forgetting that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for catastrophic forgetting more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of catastrophic forgetting more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put catastrophic forgetting more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of catastrophic forgetting more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat forgetting as expected: a small general and safety probe runs on every checkpoint, and a written drop fails the run even if the task metric is up.
keyPoints: Narrow SFT can erase general skill and refusals.
The train loss will not warn you; those tokens are absent.
Keep a probe set and a fail threshold.
Replay a little safety/general data; prefer LoRA and early stop.
A task win plus a probe crash is a failed run.
Full FT forgets faster than a small adapter on the same data.

questions.q: What is catastrophic forgetting in SFT?
questions.a: The model gains the narrow trained skill and loses prior abilities such as general following, formats you did not replay, or safety refusals, because those behaviours were not in the loss.

questions.q: Task +7, refusal probe −20. Ship?
questions.a: No. Fail the run. Mix refusal replay, reduce LR/epochs, and require the probe to hold within the written delta.

questions.q: Why does a support-only mix increase unsafe answers?
questions.a: Every gradient step makes 'always answer helpfully in this tone' more likely and never rehearses 'refuse'. Likelihood of the old refusal style decays.

questions.q: What belongs on a forgetting probe set?
questions.a: General instructions, any languages you serve, tool or schema formats the product still needs, and the safety/refusal suite. Small but fixed across runs.

questions.q: Name two knobs that reduce forgetting besides adding replay data.
questions.a: Lower learning rate or fewer epochs/early stop on the task metric, and using LoRA instead of full fine-tuning so fewer base weights move.

read-outputs-not-just-loss.explain:
## What it is

A lower loss does **not** guarantee better answers. You must **read sample outputs** from each checkpoint on a fixed prompt sheet: happy path, tail, empty input, injection, and a couple of production traces. Loss is an average of token surprises. Users experience sentences.

Reading is scheduled, not "if I have time". Five prompts every checkpoint is enough to catch ramble, dropped fields, newly rude tone, or a model that learned to say "here is the JSON" and then not emit it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the eval script can be green because it regexes a key that is now wrapped in markdown. A human eye sees it in ten seconds.

Interviews: "loss went down, would you ship?" — no, show generations and the task metric.

Lower loss is not a better answer. Read samples at each checkpoint.

## How it works + one small example

Keep `prompts/sheet.jsonl` in the repo. The trainer samples it each checkpoint and writes a markdown diff. You read the diff before you look at W&B.

Example. Loss 1.1→0.4. Sheet shows: empty ticket now returns a novel; a billing ticket doubles the JSON; a refusal prompt is answered. The "best loss" checkpoint is unusable. An earlier checkpoint with loss 0.6 is the product.

Automate what you can (schema valid, refusal regex) but do not delete the read. Automation misses the new failure class until you add it — reading is how you discover the class.

Every N steps, dump 15 greedy outputs on a fixed pack (task, schema, refusal). Example: loss still falling while JSON grew a preamble. You picked the earlier checkpoint. Loss would have picked the last.

## Failure modes

1. **Only train-set samples.** Of course they look good.

2. **Different prompts each time.** You cannot compare checkpoints.

3. **Reading only the winner after the fact.** You already discarded the better earlier step.

4. **Picking the last epoch by habit.**

In interviews, follow the definition of read outputs not just loss with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put read outputs not just loss on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

In interviews, follow the definition of read outputs not just loss more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read a fixed prompt sheet at every checkpoint. Loss is a health signal; the sheet is the product. I will not ship a loss winner I have not watched answer.
keyPoints: Loss is token surprise, not user-visible quality.
Sample a fixed sheet every checkpoint.
Include tail, empty, injection, and refusal prompts.
Do not sample only the training set.
Reading discovers new failure classes for the eval.
The best-loss step is often not the best sheet.

questions.q: Why can loss fall while answers get worse?
questions.a: Loss averages token likelihood. The model can assign mass to fluent but wrong structures, ramble after a likely preamble, or drop a rare slice that barely affects the mean.

questions.q: What belongs on the checkpoint prompt sheet?
questions.a: A fixed mix of happy path, hard tail, empty/missing info, prompt-injection, and refusal/safety. Same sheet every run so you can diff.

questions.q: Automation says schema-valid 100% but a reader sees JSON inside a paragraph. Next step?
questions.a: Tighten the metric to require a parse of the whole reply, and treat the read as a new test. Do not ignore the read because the old regex passed.

questions.q: Why is sampling train rows a weak read?
questions.a: Those answers were in the loss. You want prompts the model should generalise to, including ones you refuse to train on.

questions.q: When do you read — after the run or during?
questions.a: During, at each checkpoint, so you can keep an earlier step. After-the-fact reading cannot recover a discarded checkpoint.

choosing-a-checkpoint.explain:
## What it is

The checkpoint you keep is the one that **wins on validation behaviour**, not the last step and not the lowest train loss. You evaluate saved steps on the **task metrics** and the **forgetting probes**, pick on validation, and **confirm once** on the frozen test.

Last-step bias is strong because jobs end and people take the final folder. That folder is often the most overfit.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the cheapest quality win in the file. Teams already saved the better step and then served `checkpoint-final`.

Interviews: "always take the last epoch" is a fail. "Val skill plus probes, confirm on test once" is a pass.

Keep the checkpoint that wins the **task metric** on val, not the lowest loss and not the last step.

## How it works + one small example

Save every N steps. For each save: val task metrics, probe metrics, maybe the prompt-sheet score. Rank by a **pre-written** rule: e.g. maximise val label-F1 subject to format-valid ≥ 99% and refusal drop ≤ 3 points. Ties go to the earlier step.

Example. Steps 100/200/300: F1 0.88/0.91/0.90, refusal 0.95/0.94/0.82. The rule picks 200. Step 300 is "newer" and worse. Test is run **once** on 200: F1 0.90. You ship 200.

Do not peek at test to break a val tie. Change the val rule if you must, and accept that you spent a bit of statistical honesty.

Save every epoch (or every N steps). Score the skill. Example: epoch 1 is +5, epoch 2 is +5.2 with a refusal drop, epoch 3 overfits. You ship epoch 1 or 2 per the kill criteria, never epoch 3 because 'it finished'.

## Failure modes

1. **Final folder default.** Overfit served.

2. **Picking on test.** You spent the holdout.

3. **No pre-written rule.** You pick the chart you like after seeing numbers.

4. **Always taking step -1.**

Translate choosing a checkpoint into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for choosing a checkpoint than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used choosing a checkpoint, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of choosing a checkpoint in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I choose the checkpoint from validation task metrics and probes with a rule I wrote before the run, I prefer the earlier tie, and I touch the held-out test once to confirm.
keyPoints: Do not default to the last step or lowest train loss.
Score every save on val skill and forgetting probes.
Write the selection rule before you see the numbers.
Prefer the earlier checkpoint on a tie.
Confirm the winner once on frozen test.
Serving checkpoint-final is a process bug.

questions.q: Why is the last step a bad default checkpoint?
questions.a: It is often the most overfit: train loss is lowest and val skill or probes have already turned. Earlier saves are usually the product.

questions.q: Val F1 peaks at step 200; step 300 has lower train loss and a worse refusal probe. Which do you keep?
questions.a: Step 200 if it meets the pre-written constraints. Train loss is not the objective. Confirm 200 on the frozen test once.

questions.q: You used the test set to choose between three val-tied checkpoints. What did you spend?
questions.a: The holdout. The test number is now optimistic. Next time break ties with a val rule or an earlier step.

questions.q: What belongs in a pre-written selection rule?
questions.a: The primary task metric, hard constraints (schema, refusal delta), and a tie-break (earlier step). Written before the curves exist.

questions.q: How often should you save if the job is two epochs?
questions.a: Often enough to have mid-epoch choices — every N steps, not only epoch ends — because the peak can sit between epochs.

learning-rate-sweep-first.explain:
## What it is

A **learning-rate sweep** is the first experiment, before you change epochs, rank, or architecture. Three or five LRs on a short run will tell you the basin: too high (spikes, garbage), too low (flat skill), just enough (skill moves, val holds).

Changing three knobs at once is how you learn nothing. LR is the knob that most often turns a "LoRA does not work" story into a working one.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, rank debates burn days while the LR is an order of magnitude off. A 2-hour sweep would have ended the debate.

Interviews: "I sweep LR first" is a compact seniority signal.

A three-point LR grid beats an architecture hunt. Do it first.

## How it works + one small example

Protocol: fix data, template, rank, epochs=1 (or a fixed step budget), seed. Grid LR (log-spaced). Compare val skill and curve health. Pick the LR, **then** touch the next knob.

Example. Rank-16 LoRA looks "dead" at 1e-6 (skill +0.2) and "broken" at 1e-3 (NaNs). At 1e-4 skill +7. You keep 1e-4. Only then do you try rank 8 vs 32. Rank 8 at 1e-4 matches rank 16; you take 8. If you had raised rank at 1e-6 you would have concluded you need full FT.

Log the sweep as a table in the runbook so the next rebase starts from a known basin, not from a blog.

2e-5 / 5e-5 / 1e-4 (illustrative) at fixed rank and data. Pick the one with a stable val skill. Example: you wasted two days sweeping rank on a diverging LR. The cheap grid would have told you on morning one.

## Failure modes

1. **One LR from a tweet.** Different model size, different effective batch.

2. **Sweeping LR and rank together.** Uninterpretable.

3. **Choosing the LR with best train loss.** That is the memoriser.

4. **Sweeping rank, alpha and epochs** on a broken LR.

A practical sitting for learning rate sweep first: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of learning rate sweep first with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put learning rate sweep first on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of learning rate sweep first that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for learning rate sweep first more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-3 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of learning rate sweep first more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put learning rate sweep first more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of learning rate sweep first more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I grid a few learning rates on a short fixed setup before I touch epochs or rank. Most 'adapters do not work' stories are an LR miss.
keyPoints: Sweep LR before epochs, rank, or architecture.
Hold other knobs fixed; use a short step budget.
Log-spaced grid: find explode vs dead vs useful.
Pick on val skill, not train loss.
Write the winning LR down for the next rebase.
Do not copy an LR from a different batch size or model.

questions.q: Why sweep learning rate before rank?
questions.a: A bad LR makes every rank look dead or unstable. You will mis-blame capacity. Find an LR that moves val skill, then change rank.

questions.q: Skill is flat at 1e-6 and NaN at 1e-3. What do you try?
questions.a: Points in between (3e-5, 1e-4, 3e-4) on the same short budget. That is the point of a log grid.

questions.q: Two knobs changed and the run improved. What can you not say?
questions.a: Which knob did it. Revert to a one-knob sweep or you will carry a superstition into the next model.

questions.q: Should the LR winner be the lowest train loss?
questions.a: No. Lowest train loss is often the highest LR that still runs, and it overfits. Use val skill and curve health.

questions.q: You changed batch size after the LR sweep. What now?
questions.a: Revisit LR. Effective batch changes the noise and often the right LR. A short re-sweep is cheaper than a wrong production run.

early-stop-on-the-skill-not-the-loss.explain:
## What it is

**Early-stop on the skill**, not on the loss. Token loss can keep falling after the label-F1, schema rate, or win-rate you care about has peaked. If you wait for loss to flatten you often sit in the overfit region.

The stop signal is the validation **task metric** (with probe constraints). Patience is measured in evals without improvement, not in "loss still going down, so we continue".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, extra epochs are cheap GPU and expensive quality. The last 30% of the job is where forgetting and format drift show up.

Interviews: this pairs with checkpoint choice. Same idea: the objective is the product metric.

Stop when the task metric plateaus even if loss still falls.

## How it works + one small example

Define `skill = val_F1` (or exact-match, or rubric). Stop when skill has not improved by ε for P evaluations, **or** when a probe breaches, even if loss is still falling.

Example. Val F1: 0.84, 0.89, 0.91, 0.91, 0.90. Loss: still declining at the last two points. You stop after the second 0.91 (or keep that checkpoint). Continuing to chase 0.12 train loss buys a 0.82 refusal probe.

If the skill is noisy, average two eval seeds or require a repeat before stopping — do not switch back to loss because it looks smoother. Smooth is not the goal.

Patience on the skill (e.g. 2 evals with no gain). Example: loss kept dropping by memorising phrasing; skill was flat from step 300. You stopped. Serving the later step made tone weirder, not better.

## Failure modes

1. **Patience on loss.** You stop when the model is most overfit, or never stop.

2. **Skill computed on train.** You will never stop.

3. **No ε.** You chase 0.0001 F1 forever.

4. **'One more epoch'** as a culture.

Make early stop on the skill not the loss falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-3.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For early stop on the skill not the loss, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair early stop on the skill not the loss with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for early stop on the skill not the loss and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make early stop on the skill not the loss more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-3.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For early stop on the skill not the loss more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair early stop on the skill not the loss more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for early stop on the skill not the loss more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I stop when the validation skill plateaus or a probe fails, even if loss is still falling. Extra loss after the skill peak is usually overfitting.
keyPoints: The stop signal is val skill, not train or val loss.
Loss often falls after the product metric has peaked.
Patience = evals without a real skill gain.
A probe breach can stop the run even if skill is up.
Do not early-stop on training-set skill.
Write ε and patience before the job starts.

questions.q: Why not early-stop when validation loss flattens?
questions.a: Val loss can keep falling (or look smooth) after the task metric has peaked or probes have failed. The product does not buy those extra nats.

questions.q: F1 has been 0.91 for three evals, loss still dropping. Action?
questions.a: Stop and keep the first 0.91 checkpoint (or the rule's winner). Do not spend the rest of the epoch on overfit.

questions.q: You early-stopped on train exact-match. What goes wrong?
questions.a: Train exact-match rises as you memorise. You stop at maximum memorisation. Use a held-out val skill.

questions.q: How can a safety probe stop a run that is still 'learning'?
questions.a: If refusals drop past the written threshold you abort even though task loss is falling. Learning the narrow skill at the cost of safety is a failed run.

questions.q: What is ε in early stopping here?
questions.a: The minimum skill improvement that counts as progress, set before the run, so noise does not reset patience forever.

forgetting-probe-set.explain:
## What it is

A **forgetting probe set** is a small, **fixed** bundle of general-ability and safety items that every run must not destroy. It is versioned like the task eval. You fail the run if a slice drops past a **threshold** you wrote before seeing the numbers.

Small means you can afford to run it every checkpoint. Fixed means you do not swap in friendlier questions after a scare.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the regression suite for capabilities you are not training. Without it, forgetting is an anecdote from Slack.

Interviews: naming a probe set and a numeric fail line is the grown-up version of "watch out for catastrophic forgetting".

A small general-ability set that can fail the run. Do not train on it.

## How it works + one small example

Contents (example): 40 general instructions, 20 format/tool items the product still needs, 40 safety/refusal items, 10 language items if you serve them. Metrics: pass rate per slice. Thresholds: e.g. no slice more than 5 points below the base, no new critical safety fail.

Example. Base refusal 97%. Checkpoint refusal 91% (over the 5-point budget) → run failed, even at record task F1. You mix 60 refusal rows, retrain, land 95% / still-good F1, ship.

Store probe ids in git. Do not harvest production jailbreaks into the probe and also into train without a split policy — you will teach the probe.

50–100 items, frozen. Threshold in the ADR. Example: −3 points fails. You saw −4, you mixed data, you re-ran. Training on the probe would have hidden the drop.

## Failure modes

1. **Probe equals train replay.** You measure memorisation of the replay.

2. **Moving threshold after a bad number.** The suite became politics.

3. **One blended score.** Safety can collapse while trivia holds the mean.

4. **A probe you quietly added to train.**

Translate forgetting probe set into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for forgetting probe set than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used forgetting probe set, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of forgetting probe set in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate forgetting probe set more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-3.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for forgetting probe set more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used forgetting probe set more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of forgetting probe set more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep a versioned probe set for general skill and refusals, I fail the run if a slice drops past a pre-written threshold, and I never judge forgetting by vibe.
keyPoints: A small fixed probe runs on every checkpoint.
Slices: general, still-needed formats, safety, languages.
Pre-write the drop that fails the run.
Do not bury safety in a blended mean.
Do not train on the probe items.
Version probe ids like you version the task eval.

questions.q: What is a forgetting probe set for?
questions.a: To measure abilities you are not targeting — general following, leftover formats, safety — and to fail a run when they drop past a written threshold.

questions.q: Task F1 is a record but refusal slice is −8 against a −5 budget. Outcome?
questions.a: Failed run. Do not ship. Add replay or reduce training and try again. The record F1 is irrelevant if the probe fails.

questions.q: The probe items were added to the SFT mix 'to help'. What happens to the metric?
questions.a: It stops measuring forgetting and starts measuring memorisation of the probe. Keep probe and train disjoint.

questions.q: Why slice the probe instead of one average?
questions.a: A blended score lets a collapse in refusals hide behind stable trivia. Gates are per slice.

questions.q: How big should the probe be?
questions.a: Small enough to run every checkpoint (tens to a couple of hundred items), large enough to see a 5-point drop. Fixed across experiments.

reproducible-sft-config.explain:
## What it is

A reproducible SFT config **pins** the things that change answers: **seed**, **dataset hash**, **chat template** (and tokenizer revision), and **package versions** (transformers, trl, peft, torch, cuda). The run file is the source of truth; the blog post is not.

Reproducible does not mean bitwise identical on every GPU forever. It means another engineer can get the **same eval table within noise** from the file and the data pin.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, unreproducible tunes cannot be rebased or audited. "It worked on my 4090 in March" is not an incident response.

Interviews: list the pins. Seed-only is not enough.

Pin seed, dataset hash, template, package versions in the run file. Otherwise it is a story.

## How it works + one small example

The run file contains:

- `base_model` + revision
- `dataset` + sha256
- `template_hash` / tokenizer rev
- `seed`, LR, batch, accum, max_len, rank, targets
- `pip freeze` or a lock file
- command line

Example. Six months later you rebase. You check out the old file, swap `base_model`, keep the dataset hash, and compare eval tables. If the template key is missing you cannot even reproduce the *old* number, so you cannot say the new base won.

Set seeds for Python, numpy, and torch; turn on deterministic flags where they do not kill throughput. Record the GPU type. If a vendor trainer has no seed, record the job id and the exported artefact hash.

One YAML: all of the above plus GPU type. Example: a 'same' rerun used a new TRL that changed packing; scores moved. The YAML diff explained it. A notebook with hidden cells would not.

## Failure modes

1. **Seed in the file, data not hashed.** You reproduced the RNG, not the experiment.

2. **Template living only in a notebook cell.** Serve drift is guaranteed.

3. **Unpinned TRL.** Defaults moved; your LR now means something else.

4. **Repro by memory.**

Time-box reproducible sft config to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-3 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on reproducible sft config', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether reproducible sft config would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for reproducible sft config that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on reproducible sft config more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether reproducible sft config more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for reproducible sft config more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The run file pins seed, dataset hash, template, and package versions. If those are missing I cannot rebase, audit, or claim two runs are the same experiment.
keyPoints: Pin seed, dataset hash, template, tokenizer rev, packages.
The run file must be enough to replay the eval table.
Seed-only is not reproducibility.
Record GPU and trainer job id for vendor runs.
A rebase needs the old pins to make a fair comparison.
Unpinned libraries silently change defaults.

questions.q: What four pins belong in a reproducible SFT config?
questions.a: Seed, dataset hash, chat template/tokenizer revision, and package versions (plus the obvious base id, LR, and batch). Together they let someone replay the eval table.

questions.q: Two runs share a seed but differ by 8 F1 points. First check?
questions.a: Dataset hash, template hash, package versions, and effective batch. Seed equality is the weakest pin.

questions.q: Why record tokenizer revision, not only model name?
questions.a: A tokenizer or template update changes tokenisation and stop tokens. You would train and serve different strings under the same model name.

questions.q: Is bitwise GPU determinism required?
questions.a: No. Same eval table within noise is the goal. Bitwise flags are optional and often slow. Do not confuse them with the pins that actually drift.

questions.q: How does a pinned config make a base-model deprecation survivable?
questions.a: You rerun with a new base id against the same hashes and compare. Without pins you cannot tell a real win from a changed template.

lora-adapters.explain:
## What it is

**LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) **freezes** the pretrained weights and trains small **low-rank matrices** that are added to selected layers, usually the attention projections. If a frozen map is `W`, LoRA learns `A` and `B` so the effective map is `W + (alpha/r) * B A`, with `r` much smaller than the full dimension.

You store and serve the tiny adapter, not a second copy of the base. At train time the optimiser only sees the adapter parameters (plus maybe a few norms). At inference you add the adapter (or merge it) and the model behaves as if those layers were slightly retuned.

LoRA is the default PEFT method for LLM instruction and style tunes because the quality-to-memory ratio is high on narrow tasks.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, LoRA is how a single 24–48GB GPU becomes a training machine for 7–13B models, and how thirty tenants share one base at serve time. If you cannot explain it, you cannot debug a "we loaded the wrong adapter" incident.

Interviews: draw `W + BA`, say what is frozen, name rank, and say adapters are base-specific.

Freeze the base, train low-rank BA on selected layers. That sentence is the interview.

## How it works + one small example

Pick target modules (start with `q,k,v,o` or the house default), pick `r` (8–16 is a common start), pick `alpha` (often 2r or a house default), train, save the adapter folder.

Example. 8B instruct, rank 16 on attention. Trainable parameters are a few tens of millions, not 8B. The adapter is tens of megabytes. You attach it in PEFT or vLLM by name. Swap to a second tenant's adapter without unloading the base.

Sanity check: with `r` approaching the full width you have almost-full FT in a clumsy form. If you need that, admit you want more capacity and measure; do not sneak up to `r=256` by habit.

W' = W + (α/r)BA. You pick r, α, targets (usually q,k,v,o first). Example: r=16 on attention of an 8B fits a single 24GB card with QLoRA. You can dump the adapter in megabytes and share the base.

## Failure modes

1. **Thinking adapters port across bases.** They do not.

2. **Training LoRA but serving the base only.** The eval was on the adapter; prod is unadapted.

3. **Forgetting alpha.** Rank without scale is an incomplete description.

4. **Calling any PEFT method 'LoRA'** including full FT.

Make lora adapters falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-4.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For lora adapters, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair lora adapters with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for lora adapters and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Only adapter params are trained and stored.
Default PEFT for narrow LLM behaviour changes.
Adapters do not load on a different base.
Rank and alpha both belong in the config.
Serve must actually attach the adapter you evaluated.

questions.q: What does LoRA freeze and what does it train?
questions.a: It freezes the pretrained weight matrices and trains small low-rank factors A and B that are added to chosen layers, scaled by alpha/r. The base stays a shared artefact.

questions.q: Why can many tenants share one GPU with LoRA?
questions.a: One base resides in memory; each tenant is a small adapter you swap or batch. Full fine-tunes would be one full copy each.

questions.q: Eval used the adapter; the gateway loaded only the base. Symptom?
questions.a: Production looks like the untuned model. Check adapter id in traces. This is a deploy bug, not a training miss.

questions.q: Write the effective LoRA map in one line.
questions.a: W' = W + (alpha / r) * B A, with W frozen and r << d.

questions.q: When is raising rank the wrong next step?
questions.a: When the run has not yet had a proper LR sweep, or when the failure is template/data. Rank is capacity; it does not fix a wrong dialect or dirty labels.

qlora-on-a-quantized-base.explain:
## What it is

**QLoRA** loads the **frozen base in a quantized** form (commonly 4-bit) so the same LoRA tune **fits on a much smaller GPU**. Adapters still train in higher precision. The memory win is the base weights and their absence from the optimiser, not a 4-bit adapter.

QLoRA is a training trick. Serving may use 4-bit, 8-bit, or 16-bit after you **merge or attach** and **re-evaluate**. A 4-bit train does not automatically license a 4-bit serve win.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how an 8B or 13B tune happens on one consumer GPU. It is also how people ship a quality drop they never measured, because they served a different precision than they evaluated.

Interviews: 4-bit frozen base, high-precision adapters, re-eval after dequant/serve path.

Load the frozen base in 4-bit, train LoRA in higher precision. Fits a much smaller GPU.

## How it works + one small example

Load the base with the library's 4-bit config (NF4/double quant as documented), attach LoRA, train. Estimate VRAM from quantized weights + LoRA + activations (activations still scale with batch and length).

Example. 8B FP16 base ≈ 16GB weights alone; 4-bit ≈ 4GB plus overhead. LoRA and a short sequence now fit in 16–24GB. You train, then eval three ways: adapter on 4-bit base, adapter on 16-bit base, merged-then-quantized GGUF. The winner is an empirical table, not a slogan.

Watch paged/optimizer settings and gradient checkpointing; they often matter more to OOM than the adapter rank.

nf4 + LoRA is the usual story; check current bitsandbytes/PEFT docs. Example: 8B QLoRA on a 16GB card that cannot hold 16-bit full FT. You still merge on 16-bit later if you can, then re-quant for serve.

## Failure modes

1. **Eval only in the 4-bit trainer.** Serve is 16-bit or GGUF and the number moves.

2. **Assuming 4-bit serve is free.** Quantization error can erase a small tune gain.

3. **OOM on long sequences blamed on 4-bit.** Activations, not the frozen weights, blew up.

4. **Serving the 4-bit train view** without a serve eval.
