QLoRA quantises the frozen base so LoRA fits on a small GPU. I still train adapters in higher precision, and I re-evaluate the actual serve precision because a 4-bit train is not a 4-bit trophy.
keyPoints: QLoRA: 4-bit frozen base + higher-precision LoRA.
Memory win is the base, not a tiny optimiser on all weights.
Re-eval after you dequantise or export for serve.
Activations still grow with batch and sequence length.
A 4-bit train does not guarantee a 4-bit production win.
Checkpointing and microbatch often fix OOM before rank does.

questions.q: What does QLoRA quantise, and what stays high precision?
questions.a: The frozen base weights are stored quantized (often 4-bit). The LoRA adapters and their gradients stay in higher precision so the update is not 4-bit junk.

questions.q: Why re-evaluate after merging to 16-bit or exporting GGUF?
questions.a: Quantisation and merge order change numerics. The trainer's 4-bit number can shrink or vanish on the serve path. Measure the path you will ship.

questions.q: QLoRA OOMs only on the longest 5% of rows. Cause?
questions.a: Activation memory scales with sequence length. Shorten, checkpoint, or microbatch those rows. The 4-bit base already did its job.

questions.q: Is QLoRA an inference method?
questions.a: It is primarily a training-time memory method. You may also serve quantized, but that is a separate eval. Do not conflate the two.

questions.q: When would you skip QLoRA and train LoRA in 16-bit?
questions.a: When you have the VRAM and the 4-bit train/eval gap has bitten you, or when the stack's 4-bit kernels are unstable for that architecture. Memory is the reason to use it, not fashion.

rank-alpha-target-modules.explain:
## What it is

The LoRA settings that matter first are **rank (r)**, **alpha**, **target modules**, **dropout**, **compute precision**, and **quantization type** if you QLoRA. Rank is adapter capacity. Alpha scales the update (`alpha/r`). Targets decide which matrices receive adapters. Dropout regularises small sets. Precision/quant decide memory and numerics.

Defaults are not magic. A rank-8 adapter on `q` and `v` only is a different model from rank-64 on attention plus MLP.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people copy `r=64, alpha=16` from a repo that solved a different task and then declare LoRA weak. The settings were the experiment.

Interviews: define each knob in one sentence and say you sweep rank on a held-out curve after LR is stable.

r is capacity; α scales the update; targets are which matrices get BA. Dropout and quant type also matter.

## How it works + one small example

Start conservative: attention projections, r=8 or 16, alpha=16 or 32, dropout 0.05–0.1 on small data, 4-bit NF4 if QLoRA. Sweep rank after LR. Add MLP (`up/down/gate`) only if the eval still misses and generations look underfit (not noisy).

Example. r=4, q/v only: format still drifts. r=16, q/k/v/o: format locks, labels good. r=64 + MLP: train loss lower, val flat, serve heavier. You keep r=16 attention.

Write `alpha/r` in the card. Two runs with r=16, alpha=16 versus r=16, alpha=32 are different step sizes, not the same adapter with a typo.

Start r=8 or 16 on attention; α ≈ 2r as a common default (verify in your trainer). Add MLP if the eval still misses. Example: r=64 did not beat r=16 on your set and overfit faster. The curve is the argument, not a blog's r=64.

## Failure modes

1. **Tiny rank, blaming LoRA.** Under-capacity.

2. **Huge rank on 300 rows.** Over-capacity, overfit.

3. **Silent target mismatch** between train config and serve config.

4. **r=64 because a tweet said so.**

Targets: start with attention; add MLP if still underfit.
Dropout helps tiny sets; it is not a substitute for cleaning.
Precision and quant type change memory and numerics.
Sweep rank after LR, on a held-out curve.
Train and serve must name the same target modules.

questions.q: What does LoRA rank control?
questions.a: The inner dimension of A and B, hence adapter capacity and size. Too small underfits; too large on a tiny set overfits and costs serve memory.

questions.q: r=16, alpha=16 versus r=16, alpha=32. What changed?
questions.a: The scale alpha/r doubled, so the same learned factors hit the residual harder. It is not the same recipe.

questions.q: Underfit on a hard rewrite with q,v rank 4. First capacity change?
questions.a: Add the rest of attention and/or raise rank a step. Add MLP only if that still misses. Do not jump to full FT yet.

questions.q: Why list target modules in the run card?
questions.a: Serve and later rebases must attach the same set. A missing `o_proj` at serve is a silent quality drop.

questions.q: When does LoRA dropout help?
questions.a: On small, slightly noisy sets where the adapter memorizes phrasing. It will not fix a wrong spec or a leak.

adapters-vs-full-fine-tuning.explain:
## What it is

The trade-off is **quality versus memory, time, storage, and serving flexibility**. Adapters usually keep enough quality on narrow tasks while winning every operational axis. Full fine-tuning can edge quality on broad shifts and then lose on host cost and multi-tenant serving.

Do not treat the trade-off as religious. Run the same data and eval if the decision is expensive. Treat "I have not tried LoRA" as incomplete, not as a preference for full FT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this decision is money. A full 70B tune you cannot host is a write-off. An adapter you can multi-serve is a platform.

Interviews: table the four axes and give one case for each side.

Quality, memory, time, storage. For narrow tasks adapters usually win on the last three and tie quality.

## How it works + one small example

Write the table before the job.

| | Adapter | Full FT |
| Memory | Small GPU / QLoRA | Large GPU or ZeRO |
| Time | Hours | Longer |
| Storage | MB | Full copy |
| Serve | Multi-LoRA, swap | One blob |
| Quality | Usually enough | Maybe higher on broad shifts |

Example. Ten house styles on one 8B. Adapters: one base, ten files, vLLM extra-LoRA. Full FT: ten 16GB blobs or a nightmare merge. Quality on a tone eval differs by a point. Adapters win.

Counter-example. You are adapting a base to a new language with millions of tokens and you have a cluster. Full FT (or continued pretrain) may be the real job. That is not a ticket router.

Table it. Example: full FT +0.4 at 20× storage and no multi-tenant serve. You keep LoRA. A research paper might still want full FT; a product router does not.

## Failure modes

1. **Full FT for a style tweak.** Operational waste.

2. **Adapter-only dogma** on a true domain rewrite you have already seen underfit.

3. **Ignoring serve.** The cheaper train produces the unhostable artefact.

4. **Full FT 'for quality'** with no compare.

Narrow style/format: adapters almost always win ops.
Full FT can win broad domain shifts at high cost.
Multi-tenant almost forces adapters.
A quality edge that you cannot host is not a win.
Measure both on the same eval if the spend is large.

questions.q: Name four operational axes where adapters usually beat full FT.
questions.a: Peak memory, train time, storage of the artefact, and the ability to serve many variants on one base. Quality is the remaining axis and often close on narrow tasks.

questions.q: You need 25 per-customer tones on one 8B. Which path?
questions.a: One LoRA per customer, multi-adapter serving. Full FT would be 25 full copies and a serving disaster.

questions.q: High-rank LoRA plus MLP still underfits a language-shift with lots of data. Next?
questions.a: Now discuss full FT or a better multilingual base, with a host plan. You have evidence adapters ran out.

questions.q: Why is 'full FT is more serious' a weak argument?
questions.a: Serious is a measured gain you can serve and retrain. Updating more tensors is not a quality proof.

questions.q: How does rollback differ?
questions.a: Adapter rollback is a pointer change to another small file. Full FT rollback is swapping large blobs or keeping two full models hot.

peft-with-unsloth-or-axolotl.explain:
## What it is

**Unsloth**, **Axolotl**, TRL, and vendor UIs are **front ends** over PEFT. The skill is not the logo. The skill is a **configuration file someone else can rerun**: base, data, template, LoRA knobs, seed, output. The tool should emit that file and a checkpoint you can load outside the tool.

Pick a tool because it supports your base, your GPU, and export. Do not pick it because a thread said it is 2× faster without checking the eval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, tool lock-in shows up when the wizard cannot export an adapter that vLLM loads, or when the YAML is not in git.

Interviews: name one stack, then immediately talk about the config and the eval — not the marketing speedup.

A config file someone else can rerun is the artefact, not a hero notebook.

## How it works + one small example

Requirements for whatever you pick:

- Config in version control
- Dataset hash recorded
- Official chat template, not a built-in surprise
- Export to standard PEFT adapter or merged weights
- Same eval script as production thinking

Example. Axolotl YAML pins model, `lora_r`, datasets, `sequence_len`. You run it on a rented 24GB box, push the adapter to the registry, eval with the house script, serve with vLLM. A year later Unsloth is fashionable; you replay the **eval**, not the brand.

Four-row overfit still applies. A faster trainer that cannot overfit four rows has a template bug.

Axolotl/Unsloth/TRL YAML: data path, hash, template, LR, rank. Example: a new hire reruns v7 from the file and matches ±0.3. That is a platform. A Colab with 40 hidden cells is not.

## Failure modes

1. **Clicky UI, no YAML in git.** Souvenir.

2. **Tool-specific template** that serve does not use.

3. **Speed without eval.** You trained the wrong thing faster.

4. **A GUI click** with no exported config.

estimating-gpu-memory.explain:
## What it is

GPU memory is roughly **weights + optimiser states + activations + overhead**. Weights scale with parameter count and precision (16-bit ≈ 2 bytes/param; 4-bit ≈ 0.5). Optimiser states apply to **trainable** params (large in full FT, small in LoRA). **Activations** scale with batch × sequence length × layers × hidden size, and they are why long rows OOM a job that "should fit" from the weight math.

Estimate before you rent. A wrong estimate is a surprise bill or a weekend of OOMs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is how you pick a 16 vs 24 vs 80GB box and whether QLoRA is required. Guessing from a tweet about a different length is how you burn credits.

Interviews: name the four terms and say activations, not adapter rank, usually blow long-context jobs.

Params, precision, seq, batch, plus LoRA overhead and KV. Estimate before you rent.

## How it works + one small example

Back-of-envelope for QLoRA 8B, r=16, seq=2048, microbatch=1: ~5–6GB 4-bit weights+overhead, a small LoRA optimiser, and several GB of activations (more with no checkpointing). If you raise seq to 8192 or batch to 4, activations dominate; checkpoint or shorten.

Example. Job OOMs at 90% of steps. Those steps are the long tail. You enable gradient checkpointing, set a length cap at the 95th percentile, or pack short rows together. You do not blindly rent an 80GB box for a rank issue.

Always add fragmentation headroom (a few GB). Peak is not average.

Back-of-envelope then a 10-step probe. Example: you almost rented an H100 for an 8B QLoRA that fits a 24GB box at seq 2k batch 4. The probe would have shown it. OOM at step 2 is a sizing fail, not a training fail.

## Failure modes

1. **Estimating from weights only.** You forget activations and Adam.

2. **Blaming LoRA rank for a length OOM.**

3. **No headroom.** The job dies at the last batch.

4. **Renting the biggest card** as the estimate.

keyPoints: Memory ≈ weights + optimiser + activations + overhead.
Precision and who is trainable dominate the first two terms.
Activations scale with batch × sequence length.
Long-row OOM is usually activations, not rank.
Gradient checkpointing trades time for activation memory.
Leave headroom; peaks are not averages.

questions.q: Which term usually causes OOM on the longest examples?
questions.a: Activations, which grow with sequence length (and batch). The 4-bit base does not suddenly get larger on long rows.

questions.q: QLoRA 8B fits at length 2k and dies at 8k. First fixes?
questions.a: Gradient checkpointing, smaller microbatch, or a length cap / packing policy. Renting 80GB is the last move.

questions.q: Why is full-FT memory so much higher than LoRA at the same batch?
questions.a: Adam-style optimiser states on every parameter, plus gradients for every parameter. LoRA keeps those states only on the adapter.

questions.q: Your estimate used average length, not the 99th percentile. What happens?
questions.a: The job OOMs on the tail. Estimate with a high percentile or a hard cap you actually enforce.

questions.q: What does gradient checkpointing trade?
questions.a: It recomputes activations in the backward pass to save memory, so steps slow down. That is often cheaper than a larger GPU.

tracking-runs.explain:
## What it is

A run you cannot compare is a story, not an experiment. **Track** dataset version, config (including template and seed), git commit, GPU, and **evaluation results** in one place — a tracker, a spreadsheet, or a table in the repo. The adapter file name is not a tracker.

Comparison means the same held-out set and the same judge. If those moved, you are not allowed to say "this run won".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, two weeks of LoRA folklore collapse when someone asks which rank won. The answer is in Slack and contradicts W&B.

Interviews: "how do you organise experiments?" — one table keyed by run id with data hash and metrics.

Dataset version, config, eval — in a tracker or a folder. Memory is not a tracker.

## How it works + one small example

Minimum columns: `run_id`, `dataset_hash`, `base`, `template_hash`, `r`, `alpha`, `lr`, `steps`, `val_skill`, `probe`, `notes`. Attach the config path.

Example. Twelve runs. The table shows r=8 and r=16 tied on val, r=64 worse on probes. You pick r=8. Without the table you would have shipped the last run because it finished on Friday.

If you use a hosted tracker, still dump a JSON next to the checkpoint. Hosted UIs get deleted; the artefact should carry its own card.

W&B/MLflow/a signed folder: three ids and the slice table. Example: v4 vs v6 is a page, not a Slack guess. You do not 'kind of remember v5 was better on tone'.

## Failure modes

1. **Metrics without data hash.** You compare different tests.

2. **Renaming folders by vibe.** `final_v2_real` is not an id.

3. **Private tracker, no card on the artefact.** The next owner is blind.

4. **Local folders named run2_real.**

Make tracking runs falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-4.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For tracking runs, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for tracking runs and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every run is a row: data hash, config, and the same eval numbers. If I cannot sort that table I am not experimenting, I am collecting folders.
keyPoints: Track data hash, config, and eval together.
Same held-out set and judge to compare runs.
Put a card next to the checkpoint, not only in a UI.
Run ids, not final_v2_real folder names.
The table, not the last finished job, picks the winner.
If the eval moved, you lost the right to compare.

questions.q: What three things must a run record to be comparable?
questions.a: Dataset version/hash, the full config (base, template, knobs, seed), and metrics on the same held-out eval. Missing any one makes 'this run won' rhetoric.

questions.q: Two runs differ by 3 points but used different test files. What can you say?
questions.a: Nothing about the knobs. Re-score both on one frozen set or throw the comparison out.

questions.q: Why dump a JSON card next to the adapter?
questions.a: So the artefact is self-describing when the tracker is gone, and so serve and rollback can read adapter id, base, and template without a wiki.

questions.q: Who wins if Friday's run is not the best row in the table?
questions.a: The best row, subject to the pre-written rule. Recency is not a metric.

questions.q: What happens if only train loss is tracked?
questions.a: You will pick memorisers. Track val skill and probes, not just loss.

diy-vs-managed-fine-tuning.explain:
## What it is

**DIY** means you train an open-weight (or licensed) model on your GPUs or a rented box and you **keep the weights**. **Managed** means you send data to a provider's fine-tune API and you get a hosted model name back. The axes are **data boundary**, **base catalogue**, **export**, **price shape**, and **ops burden**.

Neither is morally better. A bank that cannot leave the VPC does DIY. A team that wants a hosted GPT-class tune and accepts no export uses managed. A team that wants both often discovers they cannot have both.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is a legal conversation disguised as ML. Sending logs to a tune API may be forbidden. Keeping weights may be required for residency — or impossible if the only good base is closed.

Interviews: list the axes. Mention that managed tunes die with the vendor base.

DIY: any open base, you own files, you own GPUs. Managed: catalog bases, maybe no export, no GPU pager.

## How it works + one small example

Decision checklist:

- May the data leave the boundary? If no → DIY open weights.
- Must you export weights? If yes → DIY or a vendor that returns files.
- Do you need that closed model family? If yes → managed, with a deprecation plan.
- Who pages when training breaks? If you have no GPU people → managed or don't tune.

Example. Health notes cannot leave the VPC. You QLoRA an open 8B on an internal box, eval inside, serve inside. The JD said "OpenAI fine-tuning"; you decline that path in the design review and write why.

Counter-example. A consumer app wants a cheap hosted style tune on a closed small model, data is already in that vendor's logs under existing terms. Managed is fine; you still keep the JSONL.

Pick from export and ops. Example: no GPU team → managed, accept retrain-as-exit. Need the adapter on vLLM in a second cloud → DIY. Both still need the same eval.

## Failure modes

1. **Managed with no export, then procurement change.** You cannot leave.

2. **DIY with no one to operate GPUs.** The adapter is a local file on a laptop.

3. **Ignoring terms on training data** in either path.

4. **Managed because it felt official** without the export question.

On the job, diy vs managed fine tuning is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-4.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is diy vs managed fine tuning'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply diy vs managed fine tuning as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating diy vs managed fine tuning as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I choose DIY when data or weights must stay mine, and managed when the catalogue and ops are worth the lock-in. I will not send regulated logs to a tune API to save a weekend.
keyPoints: DIY: you keep weights and the data boundary.
Managed: hosted name, limited catalogue, often no export.
Ask data-residency and export before you talk LR.
Managed tunes still die when that base is retired.
Keep the JSONL even if you never see tensors.
No GPU operators means DIY is unfinished, not cheaper.

questions.q: When is managed fine-tuning the wrong default?
questions.a: When data cannot leave the boundary, when you must possess weights, or when you cannot accept the vendor retiring the base. Then DIY on an allowed open-weight model.

questions.q: Client data must stay on-prem. Which path?
questions.a: DIY with an open-weight base inside their environment. A managed API sends data out even if the brochure says it is not used for training.

questions.q: You have a managed tune and no export. The vendor doubles prices. Options?
questions.a: Retrain elsewhere only if you kept the JSONL and an eval. The hosted artefact is not portable. That risk should have been on the original sheet.

questions.q: What do you still keep if you use a managed API?
questions.a: The training file, the spec, the eval, and the decision record. Those outlive the hosted model name.

questions.q: DIY 'saved money' but the only GPU is an engineer's laptop. What did you buy?
questions.a: A single point of failure and a model you cannot page. Budget hosted GPUs or do not tune.

rank-versus-quality-curve.explain:
## What it is

A **rank-versus-quality curve** is a held-out plot of skill (and maybe probe health) against `r`. You pick the **smallest rank that holds the gain**. Bigger is not better; it is more overfit risk and more serve cost.

The curve is only valid at a **fixed LR and data**. Mixing knobs forges a cartoon.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, defaulting to r=64 "to be safe" makes multi-LoRA heavier and can hurt val. The curve is a one-afternoon experiment that pays every serve hour.

Interviews: "how do you choose rank?" — sweep, smallest that plateaus.

Sweep r on a held-out set; pick the smallest r that holds the gain. Interviewers want the curve, not a favourite rank from a tweet.

## How it works + one small example

After the LR sweep, train r ∈ {4,8,16,32,64} with the same steps and data. Plot val skill and adapter size. Pick the elbow.

Example. r=4: +3 F1. r=8: +7. r=16: +7.2. r=32: +7.1, refusal −2. You pick 8. The extra rank was vanity.

If the curve never plateaus and generations still miss structure, you may need more targets (MLP) or more clean data — not r=256 as a first reflex.

r ∈ {4,8,16,32}. Plot the task skill and the forgetting probe. Example: 8 and 16 tie on the task; 32 overfits and nicks refusals. You ship 8. A larger r is not a promotion, and you write the curve in the run page so the next person does not re-litigate it.

## Failure modes

1. **One rank, folklore.** 

2. **Picking the peak train-loss rank.**

3. **Changing LR at each rank** so the curve is noise.

4. **Monotonic 'bigger is better'** on rank with no plot.

Translate rank versus quality curve into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-4.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for rank versus quality curve than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used rank versus quality curve, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of rank versus quality curve in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate rank versus quality curve more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-4.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for rank versus quality curve more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used rank versus quality curve more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of rank versus quality curve more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I sweep rank on a held-out skill curve and take the smallest r that holds the gain. Extra rank after the elbow is serve cost and overfit.
keyPoints: Plot val skill against rank at fixed LR and data.
Choose the smallest r that holds the gain (the elbow).
Larger r can hurt probes and serve memory.
If the curve never elbows, look at targets or data, not r=256 first.
Do not change LR at each rank if you want a readable curve.
Record the curve in the decision record.

questions.q: How do you choose LoRA rank with a curve?
questions.a: Train a small grid of ranks at a fixed LR and dataset, plot held-out skill, and pick the smallest rank at the elbow where the gain holds.

questions.q: r=8 and r=32 match on val; r=32 is slightly worse on refusals. Pick?
questions.a: r=8. It holds the gain and is kinder to probes and serve.

questions.q: The curve climbs through r=64 with no plateau. Next thought?
questions.a: Maybe under-capacity, but also check data quality and whether MLP targets are needed. Do not jump to full FT until those are tried.

questions.q: Why fix LR across the rank sweep?
questions.a: Otherwise you cannot attribute the change to rank. A lucky LR at r=32 will look like 'more rank is better'.

questions.q: How does the curve help multi-LoRA serving?
questions.a: Smaller adapters are cheaper to keep hot and to swap. The elbow often saves memory at no quality cost.

which-layers-to-adapt.explain:
## What it is

Start adapters on **attention projections** (`q`, `k`, `v`, `o` as the architecture names them). **Add MLP** (gate/up/down) only if the held-out eval still misses and the sheet looks underfit — not as a default from a maximal YAML.

Attention adapters often capture style and format. MLP adapters add capacity for heavier rewrites and can add overfit on small sets.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "adapt everything" is a common copy-paste. It doubles adapter size and sometimes does nothing for a labeler.

Interviews: attention first, MLP if needed, measure.

Start with attention projections; add MLP only if the eval still misses.

## How it works + one small example

Two-point experiment after LR and a first rank: (1) attention only, (2) attention + MLP. Same r. Compare val skill, probes, and adapter size.

Example. Label router: attention-only matches attention+MLP within 0.3 F1 and is half the file. You keep attention-only. A creative rewrite task: attention-only still drifts on structure; adding MLP locks it. You add MLP for that task only.

Document the target list. Serve must attach the same list.

q_proj/k_proj/v_proj/o_proj first. Example: adding MLP +0.2 and +30% train time. You did not add it. If format still drifts, try MLP before you jump to full FT.

## Failure modes

1. **MLP by default on 400 rows.** Extra overfit.

2. **Different targets at serve.** Silent drop.

3. **Adapting embeddings first.** Rarely the first lever for SFT style.

4. **Adapting every linear** on the first run.

A practical sitting for which layers to adapt: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-4 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of which layers to adapt with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put which layers to adapt on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of which layers to adapt that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for which layers to adapt more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-4 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of which layers to adapt more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put which layers to adapt more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of which layers to adapt more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I adapt attention first and I add MLP only when the eval still looks underfit. Copy-pasting 'all linear layers' is a size bill, not a strategy.
keyPoints: Default targets: attention projections.
Add MLP only after an eval miss that looks like underfit.
More targets = larger adapter and more overfit risk.
Train and serve must list the same modules.
A labeler often does not need MLP adapters.
Measure a two-point A/B, do not theorise.

questions.q: Which layers do you adapt first, and why?
questions.a: Attention projections. They are the usual sweet spot for style and format changes and keep the adapter small. MLP is extra capacity you add only if needed.

questions.q: Attention-only underfits a heavy rewrite; labels are fine. What do you add?
questions.a: MLP targets on the same rank, then re-eval. Do not jump to full FT until that A/B is done.

questions.q: Serve omitted mlp adapters you trained. Symptom?
questions.a: Quality between base and the notebook eval. The missing targets never load. Fix the serve config.

questions.q: Why not adapt every linear layer on a 300-row set?
questions.a: You add parameters the data cannot constrain. Attention-only is enough for many narrow tasks and regularises for free.

questions.q: How do you record the decision?
questions.a: Put the target module list and the two-point table in the run card so a rebase does not 'helpfully' switch to all-linear.

merge-versus-keep-separate.explain:
## What it is

**Keep the adapter separate** when you need to **swap**, **multi-serve**, or **roll back** without touching the base. **Merge** (`W := W + BA`) when you need a **single file** for a runtime that cannot load PEFT (some GGUF/Ollama paths, simple servers) or when you will never swap.

Merge is a one-way convenience copy. Keep the unmerged adapter and the recipe anyway. Merged weights are a serve artefact, not the source of truth.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, merging ten customer tones into ten full models is how you run out of disk. Keeping adapters separate is how vLLM earns its keep. Merging one house model for a laptop demo is fine.

Interviews: say when each wins, and that you re-eval after merge.

Merge for a single simple deploy; keep separate to swap. Keep the adapter either way.

## How it works + one small example

Decision:

- Many variants, one base → keep separate, multi-LoRA.
- One variant, simple host → merge, then quantise if needed.
- Always keep the adapter + config in the registry even if you serve merged.

Example. You merge for an Ollama drop, re-run the eval on the merged (and quantized) file, and still store `adapter.zip`. A month later you need a second tone; you did not paint yourself into ten merged blobs.

Merge in **high precision**, then quantise. Merging into already-quantized weights stacks rounding error.

Twenty tenants → separate on vLLM. One Ollama demo → merge then GGUF. Example: you merged and deleted the adapter; you cannot fork a second tone. Restore from backup if you still have it.

## Failure modes

1. **Merge-only, adapter deleted.** You cannot rebase cheaply.

2. **Merge into 4-bit, then wonder why eval dropped.**

3. **Separate adapters but a server that cannot load them.** You shipped an unloadable artefact.

4. **Merging as cleanup.**

Make merge versus keep separate falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-4.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For merge versus keep separate, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair merge versus keep separate with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for merge versus keep separate and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make merge versus keep separate more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-4.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For merge versus keep separate more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair merge versus keep separate more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for merge versus keep separate more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep adapters separate for swap and multi-serve, I merge when the runtime wants one file, and I always keep the unmerged adapter as the source of truth after a high-precision merge.
keyPoints: Separate: swap, multi-LoRA, cheap rollback.
Merge: single-file runtimes, one-off deploys.
Merged weights are a serve artefact; keep the adapter.
Merge in high precision, then quantise.
Re-evaluate after merge; numerics move.
Do not delete the recipe when you merge.

questions.q: When do you keep a LoRA separate versus merge it?
questions.a: Keep separate for multi-tenant swap and rollback on one base. Merge when the runtime needs a single blob. In both cases keep the unmerged adapter stored.

questions.q: Why merge in 16-bit before making a GGUF?
questions.a: Merging into already quantized weights adds rounding error on top of quantisation error. Merge high precision, then quantise once, then eval.

questions.q: You deleted the adapter after a merge and the base was updated. Cost?
questions.a: A full retrain from data, and you cannot even serve the old pair if the merged blob was tied to the old base. The adapter was the cheap artefact.

questions.q: Thirty tones, one 8B, vLLM. Merge?
questions.a: No. Separate adapters and multi-LoRA serving. Merging would be thirty full models.

questions.q: Does merge change the need to match the chat template?
questions.a: No. The template is independent of whether BA has been added into W. Mismatch still rambles.

qlora-precision-traps.explain:
## What it is

A **4-bit train is not a 4-bit trophy**. Traps: evaluating only inside the trainer; serving dequantised 16-bit without re-scoring; merging into quantized weights; mixing NF4 train with a different serve quant; assuming tokens/sec at 4-bit equals quality at 4-bit.

The honest artefact is a **table**: train precision × serve precision × metric. Ship the cell you measured.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the "QLoRA win" disappears in Ollama and people blame LoRA. The path changed.

Interviews: this is an easy debug story. Tell it.

A 4-bit train does not guarantee a 4-bit serve win. Re-eval after dequant/merge/requant.

## How it works + one small example

After QLoRA, score at least:

1. Adapter + 4-bit base (trainer-like)
2. Adapter + 16-bit base
3. Merged 16-bit
4. The actual export (GGUF/Q4, vendor host, etc.)

Example. (1) 0.91 F1, (2) 0.90, (3) 0.90, (4) 0.84. The tune is real; the export ate it. You serve 16-bit adapter or a milder quant, or you accept 0.84 if cost demands it — **explicitly**.

Also trap: `torch_dtype` mismatches and kernels that silently upcast. Record dtypes in the card.

Path: train QLoRA → merge on 16-bit → eval → then quantise for serve → eval again. Example: 4-bit serve dropped schema 4 points; 8-bit held. You ship 8-bit. Trusting the train loss for the serve artefact is the trap.

## Failure modes

1. **One number from the trainer UI.**

2. **Double quantisation** (train 4-bit, merge 4-bit, export 4-bit) without a row on the table.

3. **Comparing QLoRA quality to an FP16 full FT trained with a different recipe.**

4. **One number for train and serve precision.**

Translate qlora precision traps into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-4.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for qlora precision traps than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used qlora precision traps, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of qlora precision traps in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate qlora precision traps more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-4.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for qlora precision traps more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used qlora precision traps more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of qlora precision traps more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I re-score QLoRA on the serve precision I will actually use. A 4-bit training win that dies in GGUF is a serving choice, not a proof that LoRA failed.
keyPoints: Re-eval after dequant, merge, and export.
Ship the measured cell, not the trainer screenshot.
Do not merge into already-quantized weights.
4-bit speed is not 4-bit quality.
Record dtypes and quant types in the card.
If export kills the gain, serve a milder precision or drop the tune.

questions.q: Why can a QLoRA eval in the trainer overstate production quality?
questions.a: Production may dequantise, merge, or re-quantise with a different scheme. Those steps change numerics. Only the serve-path score is the product.

questions.q: Trainer F1 0.91, GGUF Q4 F1 0.84. Options?
questions.a: Serve the 16-bit adapter, pick a milder quant, or decide the 0.84 still beats the prompted baseline on cost. Do not silently ship Q4.

questions.q: You merged BA into a 4-bit W then exported. Likely issue?
questions.a: Stacked quantisation error. Merge in 16-bit, then quantise once, then measure.

questions.q: What belongs on a QLoRA precision table?
questions.a: Rows for trainer 4-bit, 16-bit attach, merged 16-bit, and the real export, each with the same eval. Plus dtypes and quant names.

questions.q: Is a 4-bit serve always the point of QLoRA?
questions.a: No. QLoRA's point is training memory. Serve precision is a separate product choice.

demonstrations-vs-preferences.explain:
## What it is

**Demonstration** data says "this is the answer": one prompt, one gold completion. That is SFT. **Preference** data says "this is better than that": one prompt, a **chosen** reply, a **rejected** reply. That is DPO and friends.

Demonstrations need you to write the correct string. Preferences need you to **compare** two strings on a named quality — tone, concision, refusal, helpfulness — even when several replies would be acceptable. If you can write one right answer, prefer SFT. If the quality is a ranking among valid answers, prefer preferences.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people collect likes/dislikes and then run SFT on the likes only. They threw away the contrast that DPO needs, or they run DPO on pairs that are just "right vs wrong JSON" and should have been SFT.

Interviews: define both in one breath and say which failure each fits.

Demos show one answer. Preferences say A is better than B. Different data, different jobs.

## How it works + one small example

Classify the target.

- Unique gold (label, schema, exact extract) → demonstration / SFT.
- Many valid answers, you care which is better (shorter, kinder, firmer refusal) → preference / DPO.
- You have both: SFT first to get into the valid set, DPO to rank inside it.

Example. Ticket label: one right enum. Demonstration. Brand voice among three valid paragraphs: preference. "Valid JSON vs invalid JSON": that is not a preference problem; it is SFT or constrained decoding. Using DPO there wastes raters on a check a parser can do.

When you only have thumbs-up logs, you still do not have preferences. You have noisy demonstrations. To get pairs you must attach a worse alternative, not invent a reject by deleting a word.

SFT needs a gold string. DPO needs a pair that differs on the quality you named. Example: you have gold JSON — SFT. You have two fluent answers and humans prefer the terse one — DPO. Using DPO pairs as SFT gold by taking only the winner is valid; the other way (SFT-only data as fake pairs) is how you teach length.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling any two strings a preference.** They must differ on the quality you named.

2. **SFT on likes, ignoring dislikes.** You lost the contrast.

3. **Preferences on invalid vs valid format.** Use SFT or a decoder constraint.

4. **Calling every CSV 'preference data'.**

Time-box demonstrations vs preferences to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on demonstrations vs preferences', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether demonstrations vs preferences would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for demonstrations vs preferences that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Demonstrations show the one answer; preferences rank two answers on a named quality. I use SFT when I can write gold, and DPO when I need to choose among valid replies.
keyPoints: Demo = one gold string; preference = chosen vs rejected.
SFT fits unique gold; DPO fits ranking among valid answers.
Thumbs-up logs are not pairs until you add a real reject.
Format validity is rarely a preference problem.
Typical stack: SFT first, preferences second.
Pairs must differ on the quality you care about.

questions.q: What extra field does preference data have that SFT data does not?
questions.a: A rejected response as well as a preferred one, for the same prompt, differing on a named quality. SFT only has one demonstration.

questions.q: You can write the exact JSON gold. DPO or SFT?
questions.a: SFT (and/or constrained decoding). DPO is for ranking among already-valid answers, not for teaching a schema.

questions.q: You SFT'd on thumbs-up chats and ignored thumbs-down. What did you throw away?
questions.a: The contrast that would have made preference tuning possible, and a signal about what users disliked. Down votes are not automatically a reject string either — you still need a pair.

questions.q: When is a thumbs-up not a demonstration of the spec?
questions.a: When users upvote 'got my refund' rather than 'matched the house template'. Likes are outcome, not spec.

questions.q: How do you turn two valid drafts into a preference row?
questions.a: Name the quality (e.g. concision), pick chosen/rejected accordingly, and confirm they do not also differ in facts or length you do not want to teach.

building-preference-pairs.explain:
## What it is

A preference example is a **prompt + preferred + rejected** that differ in the **quality you named** and as little else as possible. If they also differ in length, factuality, or formatting, the model may learn the confound.

Construction is a design problem. You sample two replies (from SFT, from two prompts, from a teacher), you label which is better on the rubric, you discard ties and confounded pairs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, sloppy pairs are why DPO makes the model verbose or sycophantic. The rejected was just shorter.

Interviews: "how do you build pairs?" should mention the named quality and confound control.

Prompt, preferred, rejected — and they differ on the named quality, not on a random extra paragraph.

## How it works + one small example

Recipe:

1. Name one quality per dataset version (tone, concision, refusal calibration).
2. Generate two candidates from the SFT model (or SFT vs base).
3. Rater chooses; ties go to the bin.
4. Filter: both schema-valid if the product requires it; similar length (or length-normalise); same facts.
5. Spot-check that a third person can see the quality gap.

Example. Quality = concision. Chosen is 60 tokens, rejected is 180, same facts, both polite. Good. Another pair: chosen is 200 tokens with extra facts, rejected is 50 and also wrong. You taught "longer and more facts win", not concision. Drop it.

Do not build rejects by randomly shuffling words. The contrast should be a realistic bad habit of your model.

Write a construction rule. Example: preferred is the spec-correct terse reply; rejected is a verbose but still polite one. If they also differ in facts, you taught facts-via-preference, which is messy. Filter those out.

## Failure modes

1. **Random reject.** The model learns noise.

2. **Unnamed quality.** Raters each use a private rubric.

3. **Chosen invalid, rejected valid.** You inverted the product.

4. **Rejected = random model sample** with no rubric.

Translate building preference pairs into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for building preference pairs than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used building preference pairs, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of building preference pairs in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate building preference pairs more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for building preference pairs more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used building preference pairs more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of building preference pairs more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build pairs that differ on one named quality and I throw away ties and confounded length or fact gaps. A random reject is not a preference.
keyPoints: A pair is prompt + chosen + rejected on one named quality.
Keep facts and validity equal; isolate the quality.
Control length or you will teach verbosity.
Realistic rejects beat scrambled text.
Ties and unclear gaps get dropped.
Filter both sides through the same schema if the product needs it.

questions.q: What three fields make a preference example?
questions.a: The prompt, a preferred response, and a rejected response that differ in the quality you named. Missing any one is not DPO data.

questions.q: Chosen is longer and more factual than rejected. You wanted tone. Problem?
questions.a: Confound. The model can win by being longer or stuffing facts. Rebuild so facts and length match and only tone differs.

questions.q: How do you get a realistic reject?
questions.a: Sample a second reply from the current SFT model or an earlier checkpoint that shows the bad habit (ramble, over-refuse). Do not scramble tokens.

questions.q: Why drop ties?
questions.a: A pair with no perceptible gap trains noise and wastes beta. Ties mean the quality is not identifiable in that example.

questions.q: Both replies invalid JSON, quality is 'helpfulness'. Ship the pair?
questions.a: No. Teach validity with SFT or constraints first. Preference among invalid outputs will not yield a parser-friendly model.

sources-rater-agreement.explain:
## What it is

Preferences can come from **human raters**, **model judges**, or **production feedback** (thumbs, edits, re-asks). Every source is noisy. You must measure **how often raters agree** — with each other, or with a gold rubric — and **stop labelling** if agreement sits near chance.

A judge model is a rater with a known bias (length, self-preference). Production thumbs measure user satisfaction, not your spec. Humans drift without a rubric.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 2,000 pairs with 52% agreement is expensive coin-flip data. DPO will faithfully learn the coin.

Interviews: mention inter-rater agreement and a pause rule.

Humans, judges, or prod thumbs — measure agreement. Near-chance labels are noise.

## How it works + one small example

Protocol:

- Written rubric with 3–5 bullets and examples.
- Overlap set: 10–20% of pairs seen by two humans (or human vs judge).
- Report percent agreement and a chance-corrected score if you can.
- Pause if agreement is near 50–60% on a binary choice; fix the rubric.
- If you use a judge, calibrate it on the overlap and watch length bias.

Example. Two raters on 200 pairs: 58% agree. You thought you were labelling "professional tone"; they were labelling "would I send this". You rewrite the rubric with three must-have / must-not, rerun, hit 81%, then scale.

Production thumbs: use them as a source of prompts and maybe as a weak prior, not as raw chosen/rejected without a spec pass.

Cohen's κ or simple pairwise agree. Pause if κ ≈ 0. Example: two raters agree 52% on 'tone'. You stop labelling and you fix the rubric. Training on that pile teaches coin flips.

## Failure modes

1. **One rater, no overlap.** You cannot see noise.

2. **Judge-only, uncalibrated.** You distill the judge's length love.

3. **Scaling at 55% agreement.** You industrialise a coin.

4. **One rater, 10k pairs, no audit.**

A practical sitting for sources rater agreement: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of sources rater agreement with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put sources rater agreement on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of sources rater agreement that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for sources rater agreement more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of sources rater agreement more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put sources rater agreement more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of sources rater agreement more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat every preference source as noisy, I measure agreement on an overlap set, and I pause labelling if agreement stays near chance until the rubric is clear.
keyPoints: Sources: humans, judges, production feedback — all noisy.
Write a rubric; measure overlap agreement.
Pause near chance; do not scale a coin flip.
Calibrate judges; they love length and themselves.
Thumbs are satisfaction, not a spec.
Report agreement on the dataset card.

questions.q: Why measure inter-rater agreement before scaling DPO labels?
questions.a: If raters do not agree, there is no stable quality to learn. DPO will fit noise. Agreement is the gate on whether the pair set exists.

questions.q: Binary pairs, 55% two-human agreement. Action?
questions.a: Pause. Rewrite the rubric with concrete must/must-not examples, retrain the raters, re-label the overlap. Do not order another 5,000 pairs.

questions.q: A judge prefers the teacher's own long answers. Risk?
questions.a: Self-preference and length bias. Your DPO will make the student wordier and closer to that teacher, not necessarily better on the rubric.

questions.q: What is an overlap set?
questions.a: A slice labelled by two sources (two humans, or human and judge) so you can compute agreement and calibrate. Typically a fixed fraction of each batch.

questions.q: Can production thumbs be chosen/rejected as-is?
questions.a: Usually not. A thumb is not a second string, and it may not match the spec. Use thumbs to mine prompts or to filter, then build real pairs.

avoiding-length-bias.explain:
## What it is

Raters and judges **prefer longer answers**. If your pairs let length vary with quality, DPO teaches **verbosity**. **Avoid pairs that differ in irrelevant ways**, especially length, extra hedging, or added facts you did not ask to reward.

Control length at construction (similar token counts) or at analysis (length-controlled win rate). If win rate soars and average tokens double, you did not win.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the most common DPO foot-gun. The eval judge loves the new essays. Users do not. Latency and cost rise.

Interviews: name length bias and the control. Easy points.

If preferred is always longer, you taught length. Control it.

## How it works + one small example

Tactics:

- When sampling candidates, cap `max_tokens` similarly.
- Drop pairs whose length ratio exceeds a threshold (e.g. 1.5×) unless length **is** the quality (concision).
- Report win rate **and** mean tokens. Use length-controlled comparisons if you have them.
- For concision as the quality, invert the usual bias: chosen should be shorter, and facts must match so you are not rewarding deletion of content.

Example. After DPO, pairwise win +15 vs SFT, mean length 80→170. You recompute wins in length buckets; the gain vanishes. You rebuild pairs with matched lengths and a concision rubric; win +6, length 80→75. That is a real tone win.

Never use "add more detail" as an implicit quality unless the spec says so.

Match length buckets or penalise length in the pair filter. Example: raw prefs made the model ramble +40%. After length-matching, DPO improved tone without the ramble. A length histogram of preferred vs rejected belongs on the data card.

## Failure modes

1. **Celebrating win rate only.**

2. **Chosen always the longer sample** because raters were rushed.

3. **Length-penalising at train but not at eval**, or the reverse — inconsistent story.

4. **Never looking at token-length histograms.**

A practical sitting for avoiding length bias: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of avoiding length bias with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put avoiding length bias on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of avoiding length bias that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for avoiding length bias more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of avoiding length bias more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put avoiding length bias more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of avoiding length bias more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat length as a confound until proven otherwise: match it in pairs, report tokens next to win rate, and I will not ship a 'better' model that only learned to ramble.
keyPoints: Judges and humans like long answers.
If length covaries with chosen, DPO teaches verbosity.
Match lengths or use length-controlled win rates.
Always report mean tokens with quality.
When concision is the goal, chosen should be shorter at equal facts.
A +15 win with 2× tokens is a suspect win.

questions.q: What is length bias in preference tuning?
questions.a: The tendency of raters and judges to pick the longer reply, so DPO increases token count even when the named quality was tone or helpfulness.

questions.q: Win rate +15, mean tokens doubled. How do you read it?
questions.a: Suspect length bias. Slice wins by length or rebuild matched-length pairs. Do not ship on the raw win rate.

questions.q: How do you build pairs when the quality is concision?
questions.a: Keep facts equal and let chosen be shorter on purpose. Drop pairs where the short one deleted a required fact — that is a different error.

questions.q: Why cap both candidates with a similar max_tokens?
questions.a: So you do not systematically offer a long essay against a stub. The rater should choose on the quality, not on who hit the cap.

questions.q: Name an irrelevant difference other than length.
questions.a: Extra facts, markdown decoration, or a greeting the judge likes. Control or randomise those so they do not become the learned rule.

dpo-intuition.explain:
## What it is

**Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** raises the **likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones**, while a **frozen reference** model (usually the SFT checkpoint) keeps the policy from drifting too far. You do not train a separate reward model and you do not run a PPO loop. The preference pair becomes a classification-style loss on the two likelihoods.

**Beta** scales how hard you penalise divergence from the reference. Higher beta: stay close to SFT. Lower beta: chase the preference harder, risk collapse or verbosity.

Intuition is enough for an interview: push chosen up, rejected down, stay near SFT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, DPO is the preference method you can actually run. People still say RLHF when they mean DPO. Correcting that politely is useful; pretending you implemented PPO last week is not.

Interviews: no need for the full derivation. Need reference, beta, and the chosen/rejected likelihood picture.

Raise likelihood of preferred relative to rejected, against a frozen reference. No RL loop required.

## How it works + one small example

You start from an SFT model. You freeze a copy as reference. For each pair you compute log-probs of chosen and rejected under policy and reference. The loss rewards the policy for increasing the chosen–rejected gap relative to the reference, scaled by beta.

Example. SFT already emits valid JSON. Pairs contrast terse vs rambling JSON. After DPO, P(terse) rises relative to P(ramble) on those prompts. If beta is tiny, the model may leave the JSON dialect entirely to chase the judge. If beta is huge, nothing moves.

You still eval with the same held-out pairs and with the task/probe suite. DPO loss going down is not a ship signal.

You do not need to derive the paper. Say: implicit reward from the pair, KL to the SFT reference via β. Example: β too small, the model drifts and rambles; β too large, nothing moves. You sweep β after SFT exists.

## Failure modes

1. **No reference / beta ≈ 0.** Policy drift, reward hacking of the pairs.

2. **DPO from a base instruct without SFT** on your task. Off-policy pairs, weak anchor.

3. **Treating DPO as knowledge install.** Same failure as SFT, plus pair noise.

4. **Explaining DPO as 'RLHF with extra steps'** and stopping there.

Time-box dpo intuition to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on dpo intuition', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether dpo intuition would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for dpo intuition that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

DPO increases the likelihood of chosen replies versus rejected ones while a frozen SFT reference, scaled by beta, limits how far the policy can wander. I explain it without a PPO story.
keyPoints: Push chosen up, rejected down, stay near a frozen reference.
No separate reward model and no PPO loop required.
Beta: higher stays closer to SFT; lower chases pairs harder.
Usually run on top of SFT, not instead of it.
DPO loss is not the product metric.
Off-policy pairs on a raw base are a weak start.

questions.q: In one sentence, what does DPO do?
questions.a: It raises the likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones while a frozen reference model, scaled by beta, penalises drifting too far from the SFT policy.

questions.q: What does a higher beta do?
questions.a: It keeps the policy closer to the reference (usually SFT). Updates that would move far from SFT are penalised more. Lower beta lets it chase the pairs harder.

questions.q: Why is a frozen reference necessary?
questions.a: Without an anchor the policy can drive rejected likelihood to zero in degenerate ways or leave the language the pairs assumed. The reference is the KL-like tether.

questions.q: DPO loss fell, users say answers went weird. First checks?
questions.a: Beta too low, length bias, off-spec pairs, or no SFT warm start. Look at generations and probes, not the DPO loss curve.

questions.q: Do you need to derive the RLHF equivalence in an interview?
questions.a: No. State the chosen/rejected likelihood picture, the reference, and beta. Offer the 'implicit reward' one-liner only if they ask.

dpo-after-sft.explain:
## What it is

Preference tuning **usually follows SFT** rather than replacing it. SFT puts the model **on-distribution**: it already speaks the house format, so chosen and rejected are both plausible completions. The SFT checkpoint is a **sensible reference**. DPO then ranks among those completions.

Running DPO on a raw base with pairs from a different model is possible and often disappointing: the reference is a stranger, the pairs are off-policy, and you spend the method teaching format it never had.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, skipping SFT is how you get a DPO run that invents a new dialect. The pairs were all valid JSON; the base was not.

Interviews: "why SFT then DPO?" — on-policy pairs and a reference that already does the task.

Preference usually follows SFT. DPO on a raw base is a common way to get slop.

## How it works + one small example

Sequence:

1. SFT until schema/task is in the acceptable band.
2. Sample pairs from that SFT model (on-policy).
3. Freeze it as reference; DPO a copy.
4. Compare DPO vs SFT on the same held-out pairs and probes.

Example. SFT: format-valid 99%, tone 70%. You build 1,500 tone pairs from SFT samples. DPO: tone 82%, format 98.5%, probes hold. You ship DPO. If format had been 80%, you would have stayed on SFT longer — DPO is a poor schema teacher.

If you must DPO a vendor model you cannot SFT, say so: you are preference-tuning their instruction model, and your reference is their hosted snapshot, not your house SFT.

SFT first so the model can produce the format; DPO to pick among fluent options. Example: DPO-from-base invented keys; SFT-then-DPO kept schema and improved tone. You do not skip SFT to save an hour.

## Failure modes

1. **DPO first.** Format still broken; pairs are theatre.

2. **Pairs from a giant teacher, reference is a tiny SFT.** Severe off-policy.

3. **Replacing SFT data with pairs** when you still need unique gold.

4. **DPO-only because the paper demo did.**

A practical sitting for dpo after sft: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of dpo after sft with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put dpo after sft on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of dpo after sft that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for dpo after sft more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of dpo after sft more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put dpo after sft more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of dpo after sft more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I SFT until the model is in the valid band, sample pairs from that model, and only then DPO against that frozen reference. Preferences rank; they do not replace demonstrations.
keyPoints: SFT first: on-distribution replies and a sane reference.
Sample pairs from the SFT model when you can.
DPO is weak at teaching a schema from scratch.
Off-policy teacher pairs on a raw base often disappoint.
Always A/B DPO against the SFT checkpoint.
If you cannot SFT a closed model, say the reference is theirs.

questions.q: Why run SFT before DPO?
questions.a: SFT puts replies on-distribution so pairs are realistic, and it gives you a frozen reference that already speaks the task. DPO then ranks among valid answers instead of teaching the alphabet.

questions.q: Format-valid is 80%. Should you start DPO for tone?
questions.a: Not yet. Finish SFT (or constraints) until validity is in band. Tone pairs among invalid JSON will not yield a parser-stable model.

questions.q: Pairs were written by a 70B, reference is your 3B SFT. Risk?
questions.a: Off-policy: the 3B assigns nonsense likelihoods to 70B prose. Prefer pairs sampled from the 3B, or accept a weaker update.

questions.q: What do you freeze as the DPO reference in the standard setup?
questions.a: The SFT checkpoint you started from. Not a random base and not a moving average unless you have a reason.

questions.q: Can DPO replace SFT if you have lots of pairs?
questions.a: Rarely for tasks with a unique gold. Pairs without a valid-band model waste the method. Use SFT for the gold mapping, DPO for the ranking.

what-preference-tuning-is-for.explain:
## What it is

Preference tuning is for **qualities that are hard to write as a single correct string**: **tone**, **helpfulness**, **refusal calibration** (not too much, not too little), **concision**, politeness vs firmness. Several answers can be "correct"; you want a better one.

It is not for facts, not for schema, not for "add the wiki". Those have gold or tools. If you can unit-test it, you probably should not DPO it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this keeps DPO off the JSON ticket and on the brand-voice ticket. Misapplication is expensive labelling.

Interviews: list the soft qualities and explicitly exclude schema and facts.

Qualities hard to write as one gold string: tone, helpfulness, refusal style, concision.

## How it works + one small example

Use a one-line test: **could two employees write different acceptable answers?** If yes, preferences can rank them. If no, write the gold.

Example. Refusal: the SFT model refuses too often (over-refusal) or too rarely. You pair a good calibrated refusal with a lecture or with an unsafe compliance. DPO moves the boundary. You still keep a safety probe so you do not DPO your way into a jailbreak.

Helpfulness: chosen answers the question; rejected hedges. Watch length. Concision: chosen is shorter at equal facts. Tone: chosen matches the brand paragraph in the spec.

If you can write the exact JSON, SFT. If two JSONs are valid and one is kinder/shorter, DPO. Example: support tone after a correct SFT router. You did not DPO the labels.

## Failure modes

1. **DPO for exact labels.** Use SFT.

2. **DPO for changing facts.** Use RAG.

3. **DPO for safety with no probe.** You will over- or under-refuse in the dark.

4. **DPO for facts.**

Translate what preference tuning is for into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for what preference tuning is for than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used what preference tuning is for, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of what preference tuning is for in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate what preference tuning is for more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-5.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for what preference tuning is for more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used what preference tuning is for more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of what preference tuning is for more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use preference tuning for tone, calibrated refusals, helpfulness, and concision — qualities with many valid strings. If I can write one gold or a unit test, I stay on SFT or a checker.
keyPoints: Preferences fit many-valid-answers qualities.
Tone, helpfulness, refusal calibration, concision.
Not for facts, schemas, or unique labels.
If a unit test exists, prefer that signal.
Always keep probes when you touch refusals.
SFT gets you valid; DPO ranks valid.

questions.q: Name three qualities preference tuning is for.
questions.a: Tone/brand voice, helpfulness versus hedging, refusal calibration, and concision. Each has many acceptable strings you can rank.

questions.q: Wrong JSON schema — DPO or not?
questions.a: Not. Teach the schema with SFT and constrained decoding. DPO among invalid objects is the wrong instrument.

questions.q: You DPO'd refusals and the jailbreak probe collapsed. What was missing?
questions.a: A safety probe gate and pairs that include 'must still refuse' as chosen. You calibrated only toward helpfulness.

questions.q: Why is 'many valid answers' the test?
questions.a: Because demonstrations need one gold. When several golds exist, a pairwise ranking matches the job. When one gold exists, pairs add noise.

questions.q: Can DPO make answers shorter on purpose?
questions.a: Yes if concision is the named quality, facts are matched, and you report token counts. Otherwise it usually makes them longer.

when-sft-is-enough.explain:
## What it is

**SFT is enough** when the remaining error is a **unique mapping** you can write: labels, templates, extractors, "always this outline". Preference optimisation **adds value** when, after SFT, humans still argue among valid outputs about a soft quality and you can measure that argument with pairs.

If SFT already hits the target and probes are green, **stop**. DPO is not a prestige layer.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, extra DPO is extra labelling, extra drift risk, and another artefact to rebase. Teams add it because a paper did.

Interviews: say you would skip DPO on a closed labeler that already clears the bar.

If the residual is 'emit this string', SFT. Ship DPO only when it beats SFT on the same held-out pairs.

## How it works + one small example

Decision after SFT eval:

- Unique-gold metric at target, probes hold → ship SFT.
- Unique-gold at target, tone/refusal still failing a written rubric → collect pairs, DPO, A/B.
- Unique-gold not at target → more SFT/data, not DPO.

Example. Router F1 93% vs 92% target, format 99.6%, probes hold. A PM wants DPO "for quality". You decline; there is no pairwise quality left that money cares about. A writer-bot at 93% factuality but 40% "too stiff" on a tone rubric: DPO is in play.

Write the skip in the decision record so the next intern does not add DPO for décor.

A/B the SFT checkpoint vs SFT+DPO on the same prefs and the task set. Example: DPO +0.2 on tone, −1 on schema. You keep SFT. A ritual DPO stage is not a virtue.

## Failure modes

1. **DPO as default second stage.**

2. **DPO to fix underfit SFT.** Wrong instrument.

3. **No A/B.** You cannot show DPO added value.

4. **Always adding DPO** to look complete.

Time-box when sft is enough to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on when sft is enough', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether when sft is enough would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for when sft is enough that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box when sft is enough more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on when sft is enough more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether when sft is enough more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for when sft is enough more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

SFT is enough when the gold mapping hits the target. I add DPO only when a soft quality still fails a written rubric, and I ship SFT if the A/B does not win.
keyPoints: Unique-gold tasks that hit the bar do not need DPO.
DPO is for leftover soft qualities among valid answers.
Do not use DPO to fix underfit SFT.
Require an SFT-versus-DPO A/B on the same pairs.
