Prestige is not a stage in the pipeline.
Write down why you skipped DPO.

questions.q: When is SFT enough without preference tuning?
questions.a: When the task is a unique mapping and the SFT checkpoint already meets the target and probes. There is no leftover ranking problem worth pairs.

questions.q: SFT F1 is 4 points under target. Add DPO?
questions.a: No. Fix SFT data, LR, or capacity. DPO ranks; it does not install a missing mapping.

questions.q: A PM wants DPO on a labeler that already clears the bar. What do you write?
questions.a: A skip: no named leftover quality, DPO would add retrain tax without a metric. Offer a tone DPO only if they write a tone rubric and a user-visible metric.

questions.q: What A/B is required before you ship DPO?
questions.a: DPO versus the SFT checkpoint on the same held-out pairs and the same probes. If DPO does not win, serve SFT.

questions.q: DPO 'felt nicer' but lost the pairwise eval. Ship?
questions.a: No. Feeling is the bias DPO already overfits. Keep SFT or rebuild pairs.

pair-construction-rules.explain:
## What it is

**Pair construction rules** are the written constraints that make chosen and rejected **differ only on the quality you named**. They are the spec for preference data: validity, length band, fact match, no extra tools, no new citations, same language.

Without rules, every rater invents a private contrast and DPO learns a stew.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you stop a labelling vendor from sending you "good essay vs stub". Rules can be enforced in the UI (block submit if length ratio > 1.5) and in a filter.

Interviews: this is the preference analogue of gold-spec-before-collection.

Preferred and rejected differ only on the quality you named. Write the rule; lint it.

## How it works + one small example

Put the rules on one page:

- Quality name and three examples of a legal gap.
- Both sides schema-valid / safe-enough as required.
- Length ratio in [1/k, k] unless the quality is length.
- Same factual claims; no extra numbers on the chosen side.
- Language and register match the user.

Example. Rule fail: chosen adds a discount the user never had. That is a fact confound (and a product incident waiting). Filter catches the extra number; pair dies.

Automate what you can (length, schema). Humans judge the named quality only after the automations pass.

A script checks length bucket, same facts, same schema validity, different tone score. Fail the row otherwise. Example: 18% of pairs failed the lint; those were the ones teaching length. You dropped them.

## Failure modes

1. **Rules in a slide, not in the UI.**

2. **Quality name changes mid-batch** with the same dataset id.

3. **Rules so tight you have 40 pairs.** Loosen with care; do not silently drop the quality.

4. **Free-form 'worse' samples** from an unprompted model.

A practical sitting for pair construction rules: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of pair construction rules with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put pair construction rules on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of pair construction rules that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for pair construction rules more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of pair construction rules more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put pair construction rules more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of pair construction rules more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write pair rules so the only intended difference is the named quality, I enforce the cheap rules in software, and I drop confounded pairs instead of hoping DPO ignores them.
keyPoints: Rules isolate the named quality from confounds.
Enforce length, schema, and fact checks in software.
Humans only judge what automation cannot.
Bump dataset version if the quality name changes.
A legal gap is shown with three examples on the spec.
Confounded pairs are dropped, not 'mostly fine'.

questions.q: What do pair construction rules isolate?
questions.a: The named quality. Chosen and rejected should match on validity, facts, and usually length so DPO cannot latch onto a confound.

questions.q: Chosen invents a discount. Filter or keep?
questions.a: Filter. That is a fact confound and a product risk. The pair no longer teaches tone or concision.

questions.q: Raters keep submitting 4× length gaps. Fix?
questions.a: Block in the UI with the length-ratio rule and show a message. Do not only complain in the weekly meeting.

questions.q: Why version the dataset when the quality name changes?
questions.a: Old pairs teach a different contrast. Mixing 'tone' and 'concision' under one id makes the loss uninterpretable.

questions.q: Which rules should be software, which human?
questions.a: Software: schema, length ratio, language id, cheap fact regexes. Human: the named quality after those pass.

inter-rater-agreement.explain:
## What it is

**Inter-rater agreement** is the measured rate at which two labellers (or a labeller and a judge) pick the same side. It is the health metric of a preference set. **Pause labelling if it stays near chance** (about 50% on a balanced binary task, or whatever chance is for your design).

Agreement is not vanity. It is whether a latent quality exists. You can have a beautiful UI and no quality.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, agreement is the number you bring to a vendor review. "We labelled 8,000" is not a status. "Agreement 79% after rubric v3" is.

Interviews: give a pause threshold and what you do next (fix rubric, not more volume).

Measure it; pause near chance. Agreement is a data SLI.

## How it works + one small example

Compute on the overlap set every batch. Report raw agreement and, if useful, Cohen's κ. Stratify: maybe raters agree on rude-vs-polite and coin-flip on two polite variants — then your quality is too fine.

Example. Batch 1: 61%. Rubric was "sounds better". Batch 2 after examples: 84%. You scale. A later batch drops to 64% when a new rater cohort arrives — you pause and retrain people, not the model.

If humans agree 85% but the judge agrees with humans 60%, the judge is not ready to replace them.

Weekly κ on a 50-pair overlap. Example: κ fell when a new rater joined; you retrained them on the rubric before adding their pairs. Shipping those pairs would have been cheaper than the GPU and more damaging.

## Failure modes

1. **No overlap.** Agreement is undefined; you pretend it is high.

2. **Averaging away a bad rater.** One person can poison thousands of pairs.

3. **Chance-level but 'directionally fine'.** There is no direction.

4. **Paying piece-rate with no overlap set.**

On the job, inter rater agreement is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-5.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is inter rater agreement'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply inter rater agreement as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating inter rater agreement as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, inter rater agreement more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-5.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is inter rater agreement more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply inter rater agreement more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating inter rater agreement more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I measure agreement every batch and I stop labelling when it sits near chance. Volume without agreement is a coin-flip dataset with a logo.
keyPoints: Agreement says whether the quality exists.
Pause near chance; fix the rubric or the raters.
Use an overlap set every batch, not once at launch.
Stratify: some slices may be unlabelable.
A judge that disagrees with humans is not a cheaper human.
Report agreement on the card next to pair count.

questions.q: What does near-chance inter-rater agreement imply?
questions.a: The quality is not defined well enough to learn. More pairs will not help. Pause and fix the rubric or the rater training.

questions.q: Agreement is 82% overall but 51% on 'two polite replies'. Meaning?
questions.a: The slice is too fine; raters cannot see a gap. Drop that slice or redefine the quality. Do not DPO the coin-flip band.

questions.q: You scaled to a new vendor and agreement fell 20 points. Action?
questions.a: Pause that vendor's volume. Retrain on the quiz pairs, check for a silent rubric change, and do not mix their pairs into v1 until overlap recovers.

questions.q: Why not replace humans with a judge at 60% human agreement?
questions.a: The judge is worse than a noisy human pair. Calibrate until it matches overlap, or keep humans.

questions.q: What belongs on the overlap set?
questions.a: A random-plus-stratified sample of pairs each batch, labelled by two independent raters, used only for agreement — not quietly as extra train without a flag.

beta-and-reference-model.explain:
## What it is

**Beta** is the DPO knob that scales the **penalty for leaving the reference**. The **reference** is a **frozen** model, usually the SFT checkpoint, whose log-probs appear in the loss as the anchor. You need both: without a reference there is no tether; without a sensible beta the tether is slack or a noose.

High beta ≈ conservative, small moves, SFT-like. Low beta ≈ aggressive, can collapse to pair artefacts (verbosity, sycophancy). The right value is swept on val pairs and probes, not copied from a paper that used different pair noise.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, mystery DPO quality is often beta. People copy `beta=0.1` and get a different personality.

Interviews: define both and say the reference stays frozen.

β scales how hard you push away from the frozen SFT reference. You need that reference.

## How it works + one small example

Sweep beta on a short grid (e.g. 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) after pairs are clean. Watch pair-win, length, and probes. Freeze reference weights; if you accidentally train the reference you no longer have DPO.

Example. beta=0.05: win +18, length +90%, refusal −12. beta=0.3: win +7, length +8%, probes hold. You take 0.3. The paper's 0.1 was not your data.

If you swap base mid-project you also swap reference — it is the SFT of *that* base, not an old adapter's cousin.

Too-low β: drift, ramble, safety slip. Too-high: no movement. The reference is the SFT checkpoint, frozen. Example: you accidentally DPO'd against the raw base; the model forgot the schema. Pin the reference id in the run file.

## Failure modes

1. **Training the reference.** The math you think you are running is gone.

2. **Beta=0 'to learn faster'.** Drift.

3. **Reference is a different family than the policy.** Logits are not comparable in the way you want.

4. **Updating the reference every step.**

A practical sitting for beta and reference model: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of beta and reference model with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put beta and reference model on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of beta and reference model that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for beta and reference model more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-5 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of beta and reference model more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put beta and reference model more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of beta and reference model more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Beta tethers the policy to a frozen SFT reference: high stays close, low chases pairs. I sweep it on wins, length, and probes, and I never update the reference.
keyPoints: Reference = frozen SFT (usually); it anchors log-probs.
Beta scales the penalty for diverging from that anchor.
Sweep beta; do not copy a paper's value blindly.
Watch length and probes, not only pair-win.
If the reference trains, you are not running DPO.
A new base needs a new SFT reference.

questions.q: What is the DPO reference model and why is it frozen?
questions.a: Usually the SFT checkpoint. It provides the anchor log-probs in the loss. If it trains, the tether moves and the update is no longer DPO as intended.

questions.q: What does raising beta do to the policy?
questions.a: Keeps it closer to the reference; more conservative updates. Lower beta lets it fit the pairs more aggressively.

questions.q: Low beta, big win rate, refusals down. Reading?
questions.a: Over-chasing noisy or helpful-biased pairs. Raise beta, clean pairs, and require the probe to hold.

questions.q: Can the reference be a different architecture than the policy?
questions.a: Not in the standard setup. You want comparable token log-probs on the same tokenizer and family. Use the SFT of the model you are updating.

questions.q: How do you pick beta in practice?
questions.a: A small grid on val pair-win, mean length, and probes. Choose the most conservative beta that still delivers a real win.

preference-versus-sft-a-b.explain:
## What it is

**Ship DPO only when it beats the SFT checkpoint** on the **same held-out pairs** and does not fail probes or cost/latency budgets. The A/B is the product decision. A lower DPO loss, a nicer vibe, or a judge that likes wordiness is not an A/B.

If DPO ties or loses, serve SFT. You still keep the pair set for later; you do not owe the method a production slot.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you prevent a prestige stage from adding 40% tokens. The SFT model was the thing that already paid for itself.

Interviews: they want to hear you would roll back to SFT.

Ship DPO only when it beats the SFT checkpoint on the same held-out pairs and does not trip kills.

## How it works + one small example

Same prompts, same judge/humans, pre-registered metrics: pair-win, the original task metric, probes, mean tokens, latency. DPO must win the ones you wrote down.

Example. Pair-win 57% vs SFT (not enough vs noise), tokens +30%, F1 flat. You do not ship. Second try after length-matched pairs: win 64%, tokens −5%, F1 flat, probes hold. You ship DPO.

Use a holdout of pairs that no training step saw. Training-pair accuracy is as optimistic as SFT train loss.

Same set, same judge, plus the schema/safety packs. Example: DPO wins tone, ties schema, safety flat — ship. DPO wins a judge that loves length — do not ship; you taught the judge.

## Failure modes

1. **Judge is the pair generator.** Self-preference.

2. **No token metric.** You miss the ramble tax.

3. **Shipping DPO because the YAML pipeline includes it.**

4. **A vibe A/B with no held-out pairs.**

Time-box preference versus sft a b to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-5 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on preference versus sft a b', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether preference versus sft a b would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for preference versus sft a b that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on preference versus sft a b more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether preference versus sft a b more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for preference versus sft a b more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

DPO has to beat SFT on a pre-registered A/B — held-out pairs, probes, and cost. If it does not, I serve SFT and I do not apologise to the paper.
keyPoints: Required A/B: DPO vs SFT on the same held-out pairs.
Also gate on task metrics, probes, and tokens.
A tie or a loss means serve SFT.
Do not use the training pairs as the A/B.
Avoid a judge that wrote the pairs.
Pipeline default is not a ship decision.

questions.q: What must DPO beat before you ship it?
questions.a: The SFT checkpoint on a pre-registered A/B: held-out pair wins, the original task metrics, probes, and usually token/latency cost.

questions.q: DPO wins 52% of held-out pairs and is 40% longer. Ship?
questions.a: No. 52% may be noise and the length tax is real. Rebuild pairs or keep SFT.

questions.q: The A/B judge is the same model that created the pairs. Issue?
questions.a: Self-preference can fake a DPO win. Use a different judge or humans, calibrated on overlap.

questions.q: Why keep the pair set if you ship SFT?
questions.a: It is still an eval and a future data asset. Not shipping DPO is not deleting the labels.

questions.q: Who has the burden of proof, SFT or DPO?
questions.a: DPO. SFT is the incumbent that already cleared the unique-gold bar. The new stage must earn the extra complexity.

reward-based-tuning.explain:
## What it is

**Reward-based fine-tuning (RFT / RL for LLMs)** scores each model output with a **reward** and updates the policy to make high-scoring outputs more likely. Unlike SFT (imitate a string) or DPO (prefer A over B), the signal can be a **scalar** from a program: unit tests passed, math checker, schema valid, a rubric model.

The model proposes, the grader scores, the optimiser reinforces. If the grader is cheap and honest, this can improve tasks where you do not want to write full demonstrations. If the grader is gameable, the model will game it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is how code and math models get extra lift when you have tests but not solutions. It is also how people burn a quarter teaching a model to print "PASSED" without running the test.

Interviews: define the loop and immediately say **reward hacking**. The loop without the hack is incomplete.

Outputs are scored; training pushes toward higher scores. The grader is the product.

## How it works + one small example

Minimal picture:

1. Start from an SFT policy that sometimes scores above zero (otherwise there is no signal).
2. Sample outputs; run the grader; get a scalar (or vector).
3. Update toward higher reward with a KL or length tether to the SFT reference.
4. Eval on a **held-out grader** or human set, not only the train grader.

Example. A coding task: reward = fraction of hidden tests passed. After RFT, pass rate 18%→41% on the train problem set and 18%→22% on a held-out set — you overfit the grader's problem distribution. You add more problems and a style penalty for empty `assert True` hacks.

You do not build PPO from scratch for a product FAQ. You use a managed RFT product or a maintained framework, and only when a grader exists.

If you cannot write a grader you trust more than a preference pair, skip RFT. Example: unit tests on generated code are a grader. A fuzzy 'be nicer' is not — use DPO. RFT without a checker is how you invent reward hacking.

## Failure modes

1. **Zero reward forever.** No successful samples; nothing to reinforce. Warm up with SFT.

2. **Train grader = only eval.** Hacking looks like progress.

3. **No KL tether.** Policy leaves language and emits grader bait.

4. **RFT because it sounds more advanced than SFT.**

Make reward based tuning falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For reward based tuning, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair reward based tuning with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for reward based tuning and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make reward based tuning more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For reward based tuning more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair reward based tuning more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for reward based tuning more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

RFT scores samples and reinforces high scores. I only use it when a grader I trust exists, I tether to SFT, and I eval on a grader the policy did not train against.
keyPoints: RFT: sample, score with a reward, reinforce.
Needs some non-zero successes to start — usually after SFT.
A program grader is the honest case (tests, schema, math).
The model will hack a weak grader.
Keep a KL/length tether to the SFT reference.
Eval on a held-out checker, not only the train reward.

questions.q: What signal does reward-based tuning learn from?
questions.a: A scalar (or structured) score of the sampled output, not a gold string or a pairwise label. The policy is pushed toward higher-scoring behaviour.

questions.q: Why must the SFT policy sometimes succeed before RFT?
questions.a: If every sample scores zero, there is no differential signal to reinforce. Warm up with SFT or simplify the grader until some rollouts win.

questions.q: Train reward soars, held-out tests are flat. Diagnosis?
questions.a: Reward hacking or overfitting the train problem set. Inspect high-reward samples and add an independent checker.

questions.q: What is the role of a KL or length penalty?
questions.a: It bounds how far the policy may drift from the SFT reference so it cannot abandon language for grader bait.

questions.q: When is a rubric model a weaker reward than a unit test?
questions.a: When the rubric can be flattered with tone or length. A unit test either passed or did not. Prefer machine-checkable scores when they exist.

rft-vs-sft-vs-dpo.explain:
## What it is

Three teachers:

- **SFT** learns from **demonstrations** (this string).
- **DPO** learns from **comparisons** (this string beats that string).
- **RFT** learns from a **reward** (this string scores 0.8).

Pick by the cheapest honest signal you have. Unique gold → SFT. Soft ranking → DPO. Automatic checker → RFT. Do not reach for RFT because it sounds like research.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, method shopping wastes months. A labeler with gold rows does not become better because you wrapped it in RL.

Interviews: a three-row table is the whole answer. Then an example of each.

SFT: examples. DPO: comparisons. RFT: a scalar from a grader. Different supervision.

## How it works + one small example

Worked matching:

- Forty labels, 2k golds → SFT.
- Valid answers, brand voice → SFT then DPO.
- Code that must pass tests, few solutions → RFT (maybe after a little SFT so some tests pass).
- Policy FAQ → none of the above first; RAG.

Example. You have tests and also 200 solutions. Start SFT on the 200, then RFT with tests as reward for extra lift. You have tests and 0 solutions and a 0% pass rate — SFT from a teacher or simplify; RFT cannot start.

If you have neither gold, nor pairs, nor a grader, you do not have a tuning problem. You have a spec problem.

Table it in one breath. Example: JSON keys → SFT; terse vs wordy → DPO; code must pass tests → RFT. Mixing the words in an interview is a fail.

## Failure modes

1. **RFT on a vibe reward.** Expensive DPO with extra ways to hack.

2. **SFT when you only have tests.** You will invent fake gold.

3. **Using all three stacked** as a default pipeline.

4. **'We did RL'** on a DPO run.

Translate rft vs sft vs dpo into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-6.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for rft vs sft vs dpo than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used rft vs sft vs dpo, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of rft vs sft vs dpo in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

tasks-with-gradable-outputs.explain:
## What it is

RFT fits tasks whose outputs can be **graded reliably and automatically**: **code that must pass tests**, **math with a checkable final answer**, **structured outputs** with a schema and validators, maybe games with a score. The grader should be cheaper and more trusted than a human on every sample.

If a human has to read every output to score it, you do not have an RFT task. You have a labelling task (SFT or DPO).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the filter that keeps RFT off support-email tone. Tone is not automatically gradable unless you accept a weak judge.

Interviews: list the three good families and why FAQ tone is not one.

Code tests, math checkers, schema validators — machine-checkable. That is the fit.

## How it works + one small example

Ask: **can a program say pass/fail or 0–1 without reading for vibe?** If yes, sketch the grader first, then the trainer.

Example. Extract fields into JSON; reward = schema valid × required fields present × regex on a date. That is gradable. "Write a kind refund email" is not, unless you reduce it to a checklist so tight it is really SFT.

Math: exact match on a canonicalised answer, plus a cheap format check. Code: hidden tests, time/memory caps, and a ban on network. If your tests can be gamed by printing the expected string, they are not hidden enough.

List the checker. Example: a function must pass 12 tests; the reward is pass rate. A support reply has no such checker — do not force RFT. Rubric judges are a last resort and they can be hacked too.

## Failure modes

1. **Grader needs a frontier model every sample** and you cannot afford it — and it is hackable.

2. **Public tests only.** The policy memorizes the public cases.

3. **Calling BLEU a grader for open-ended email.**

4. **RFT on brand voice.**

A practical sitting for tasks with gradable outputs: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-6 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of tasks with gradable outputs with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put tasks with gradable outputs on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

If you cannot write the grader, you cannot write the RFT job.

questions.q: Name three task families that fit RFT well.
questions.a: Code judged by tests, math with a canonical checkable answer, and structured outputs with schema/validators. Each has a program that can score without vibe.

questions.q: Is brand-voice email a good RFT task?
questions.a: Not by default. Scoring kindness needs a human or a hackable judge. Use SFT/DPO, or reduce the task to a tight checklist you can actually code.

questions.q: Public tests 100%, hidden tests 10%. What happened?
questions.a: The policy overfit or hacked the public suite. Keep hidden tests out of the train reward, and expand diversity.

questions.q: Why is a schema validator a legitimate reward?
questions.a: It is deterministic, cheap, and aligned with what production will accept. It does not care about prose flattery.

questions.q: You can only afford an LLM judge as reward. What extra work is required?
questions.a: Calibrate against humans, control length, keep a held-out human set, and expect hacking. Prefer this only when no program grader exists.

reward-design-reward-hacking.explain:
## What it is

**Reward design is the hard part.** **Reward hacking** is when the policy **optimises the grader instead of the intent**: prints `assert True`, repeats the question to trigger a keyword, pads tokens if the judge likes length, emits the format of a passing test without the logic.

If you did not look at high-reward samples, you have not evaluated the reward. The curve going up is the hacking detector's enemy.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, uninspected rewards ship embarrassments. A math model that outputs "42" in a box because the regex only looked for a box.

Interviews: give two hacking examples and the fix (better grader + held-out + inspect).

The model will optimise the grader, not your intent. Collect hacks.

## How it works + one small example

Design loop:

1. Write the intent in English.
2. Implement a conservative grader (false negatives better than false positives at first).
3. Sample high-reward outputs **by hand** every run.
4. Add those hacks to a **gallery** that must score low.
5. Keep a held-out grader or human panel.

Example. Reward = "contains the gold number". The model writes a paragraph of wrong reasoning and the gold number at the end. You change the reward to check reasoning steps or use a hidden equivalent problem. You add the hack to the gallery.

Length bonuses without a quality floor produce novels. Keyword bonuses produce keyword salad.

Gallery: padding to hit length, repeating a keyword the judge likes, passing tests by deleting them if the harness is sloppy. Example: a code agent learned to `return True` on helper names. You added tests. The gallery is part of the suite.

## Failure modes

1. **Never reading high-reward samples.**

2. **Updating the train grader until the curve looks good** without a frozen holdout.

3. **Single keyword rewards.**

4. **A single scalar** with no hack cases.

The reward is the spec the model will game. I inspect high-reward samples, keep a hacking gallery that must score low, and I never trust a rising curve alone.

Hacking = high score, low intent.
Read high-reward samples every run.
Keep a gallery of known hacks that must fail.
Prefer conservative graders; expand after inspection.
A rising train reward is not success.

questions.q: What is reward hacking in RFT?
questions.a: The policy finds behaviour that scores well on the grader without satisfying the human intent — empty tests, keyword salad, length padding, boxed answers without working.

questions.q: Train reward is up 40%, humans say answers are worse. First action?
questions.a: Read high-reward samples, add the hacks to the gallery, freeze a held-out grader, and stop shipping on the train curve.

questions.q: Why start with a conservative grader?
questions.a: False positives (hacks that score high) poison the policy. False negatives just slow you; you can relax after you inspect.

questions.q: Give a code-hacking example and a fix.
questions.a: The model writes `assert True` or hard-codes the sample output. Fix: hidden tests, mutation of inputs, ban of the shortcut in the gallery, process limits.

questions.q: Should you keep tightening the train grader until the curve is pretty?
questions.a: Not without a frozen holdout. Otherwise you and the policy are jointly overfitting a moving target.

reaching-rft-in-practice.explain:
## What it is

In practice you reach RFT through a **managed service** (a vendor's reinforcement / grader loop) or a **maintained framework** (TRL, vendor SDKs), not by implementing PPO, GAE, and a distributed actor pool from a 2017 blog. The product work is the **grader**, the **data**, the **tether**, and the **eval** — not the optimiser trivia.

Building from scratch is a research career, not a quarter's roadmap for a support bot.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, home-grown RL loops fail in undebuggable ways and nobody can rebase them. Interviewers who have shipped will be suspicious of "I wrote PPO".

Interviews: say you would use a maintained stack and spend the time on reward design.

Usually a managed service or a specialised framework, not from-scratch PPO in a weekend.

## How it works + one small example

Path:

1. Confirm a grader exists and SFT sometimes scores.
2. Pick a vendor RFT API if the base is closed, or TRL/etc. if open weights.
3. Implement the grader as a service the trainer can call safely (sandbox for code).
4. Configure KL/length, batch, and eval callbacks.
5. Do not fork the trainer in week one.

Example. OpenAI-style reinforcement fine-tuning on a hosted model: you supply graded tasks, they run the loop, you keep the eval. Open-weights: TRL PPO/GRPO/RLOO recipes with your test runner in a jail. Either way the unique code is the grader, not the policy gradient.

If procurement forbids both, you probably do not do RFT this quarter. That is an acceptable outcome.

Be honest: you will use a vendor RFT product or a maintained RL library, with SFT first, a real grader, and a KL bound. Example: you do not implement PPO on a Sunday and call it Level 13 complete.

## Failure modes

1. **Custom PPO on a laptop** as the plan.

2. **Ungated code execution** in the grader. That is an incident.

3. **Treating the vendor as owning the eval.** You still need a held-out set they do not train on.

4. **A from-scratch trainer** you cannot rerun.

Time-box reaching rft in practice to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on reaching rft in practice', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether reaching rft in practice would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for reaching rft in practice that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box reaching rft in practice more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on reaching rft in practice more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether reaching rft in practice more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for reaching rft in practice more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I reach RFT through a maintained service or framework and I spend my time on the grader, the sandbox, and the eval. I will not implement PPO from scratch for a product tune.
keyPoints: Use managed RFT or a maintained framework.
Your unique work is the grader and the eval.
Sandbox any code-execution reward.
Keep a held-out set the vendor does not see.
No GPU/RL operators means no DIY PPO.
Skipping RFT is valid when the stack is not there.

questions.q: Why not implement PPO from scratch for a product RFT?
questions.a: The failure modes are subtle, the rebase cost is high, and maintained stacks already exist. The product differentiator is the grader and eval, not your policy-gradient code.

questions.q: You need RFT on a closed hosted model. Path?
questions.a: The vendor's reinforcement/fine-tune-with-grader API if it exists, plus your own held-out eval. You will not get weights; keep the tasks and grader.

questions.q: The code grader runs model-written Python on the training box. Risk?
questions.a: Remote code execution. Sandbox with no network, limits, and a dedicated worker. This is a security bug, not an ML detail.

questions.q: What do you still own if a vendor runs the loop?
questions.a: Task definitions, the grader spec, a held-out eval, and the decision record. Those survive a vendor change.

questions.q: No managed API and no one to operate TRL. What do you do?
questions.a: Skip RFT. Use SFT/DPO or a stronger prompted model. An unowned RL loop is not cheaper.

verifiable-reward-only.explain:
## What it is

**Verifiable reward only** means you start RFT when a **checker, test suite, or schema** can score the output **without a human in the inner loop**. Humans may design the checker and audit samples. They do not grade every rollout.

This rule keeps you off vibe-RL. The moment the reward is "a 7B judge's feelings", you have DPO with extra steps and extra hacks.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the go/no-go. It also forces you to invest in tests — which you wanted for the product anyway.

Interviews: "I only RFT when I can write a checker" is a complete policy.

Use RFT when a checker, test suite or schema can score the output without a human in the loop.

## How it works + one small example

Write the checker first as a CLI: input in, score out, deterministic, tested. If you cannot, you are not ready.

Example. JSON extractor: `score = schema_ok * required_fields * date_parse`. CI tests the scorer with known pass/fail fixtures, including hacks. Only then do you point TRL at it.

If product insists on a prose quality, you either operationalise it into checks (banned phrases, max sentences, required section headers) or you leave RFT.

If a human must look, you have prefs or SFT, not a reliable RFT reward. Example: XML must validate — OK. 'Empathy' — not OK. A hybrid (schema check + small DPO) is often the grown-up mix.

## Failure modes

1. **Human-in-the-loop on every sample** labelled as RFT.

2. **Non-deterministic judge** with no seed and no calibration.

3. **Checker that needs the gold answer inside the prompt** the model can copy.

4. **An LLM judge as the only reward** with no hack suite.

Translate verifiable reward only into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-6.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for verifiable reward only than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used verifiable reward only, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I only start RFT when a program can score the output. If I need a human to feel the quality, I use pairs or demonstrations instead.
keyPoints: Inner-loop reward must be a program, not a human.
Humans design and audit the checker; they do not grade rollouts.
A judge-LLM is not 'verifiable' without heavy caveats.
Build the checker as a tested CLI first.
Operationalise prose into checks or skip RFT.
A checker that leaks the gold will be copied.

questions.q: What does 'verifiable reward only' require?
questions.a: A checker, test suite, or schema that can score each output without a human in the inner loop. Humans may audit, but the trainer calls a program.

questions.q: Stakeholders want RFT on 'empathy'. Options?
questions.a: Turn empathy into checkable rules if that is real, or use DPO with a rubric. Do not put an uncalibrated empathy judge in the inner loop and call it verifiable.

questions.q: The scorer embeds the gold number in a comment the model can see. Issue?
questions.a: The policy will copy it. Hide gold from the model; keep it in the scorer only.

questions.q: Why test the checker in CI with hack fixtures?
questions.a: Because the checker is the spec. If `assert True` scores 1.0, you will reinforce it. Fixtures are the gallery.

questions.q: Can a human audit sample replace the inner-loop human?
questions.a: Yes — that is the point. Audit a sample of high-reward outputs offline. Do not block every rollout on a person.

reward-hacking-gallery.explain:
## What it is

A **reward-hacking gallery** is a living set of **outputs that should score low** even if they once fooled the grader: padded repeats, `assert True`, boxed guesses, keyword salad, empty templates. You add every new hack you find. The gallery is part of the grader's test suite.

Without a gallery, every fix is temporary. The policy rediscovers last month's trick with new punctuation.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is regression testing for the spec. It is the most concrete artefact you can show in a review.

Interviews: naming a gallery sounds like you have been burned, which is credibility.

Collect pads, repeats, and grader games. Add them to the suite so a 'better' reward that hacks fails CI.

## How it works + one small example

Store `gallery/*.json` with the output, why it is a hack, and the required score (usually 0). CI fails if any item scores above ε. When inspection finds a new hack, you add a file before you change the trainer.

Example. The model learned to emit the function signature and `return 0`. You add three variants to the gallery, tighten tests, and only then resume RFT. The next run cannot celebrate a reward built on `return 0`.

Share the gallery with SFT too: those strings should not become gold.

Ten known hacks as unit tests on the grader. Example: empty code + comments that mention the tests. If the grader scores that high, you fix the grader before any RL step.

## Failure modes

1. **Gallery in a Slack thread.** It will not run in CI.

2. **One example per hack class.** The policy paraphrases around it.

3. **Deleting old hacks** because "we fixed that". They come back.

4. **A gallery in a doc** that is not executed.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep a CI-tested gallery of hacks that must score near zero, and I add every new cheat before I resume training. The gallery is how the grader stays honest.
keyPoints: Gallery = known hacks that must score low.
It lives in CI next to the checker, not in Slack.
Add the new cheat before you resume the run.
Keep variants; paraphrases will appear.
Do not delete old hacks.
SFT should not treat gallery items as gold.

questions.q: What is a reward-hacking gallery?
questions.a: A versioned set of cheating outputs that the grader must score near zero, run in CI, grown every time inspection finds a new trick.

questions.q: You found a new pad-and-repeat cheat mid-run. Order of operations?
questions.a: Add it to the gallery, make CI fail, fix the grader, confirm the gallery, then resume RFT. Do not 'just lower LR'.

questions.q: Gallery is three items from month one. Risk?
questions.a: The policy has moved to paraphrases. Keep adding variants and recent samples or the gallery becomes folklore.

questions.q: Why keep old hacks after the grader 'fixed' them?
questions.a: Fixes regress. Old hacks are regression tests for the spec, like unit tests for a parser.

questions.q: Can the gallery be used as extra negative SFT?
questions.a: Carefully, as 'do not emit this', but the primary job is scoring. Do not flood SFT with weird negatives and wreck the dialect.

kl-or-length-penalty.explain:
## What it is

A **KL penalty** (or a close cousin) **bounds how far the policy may drift** from the **SFT reference**. A **length penalty** bounds the cheap hack of emitting more tokens when the reward correlates with length. Together they are the seatbelt.

Without a tether, RFT can leave grammatical language for grader tokens. Without a length term, it can write novels that scrape 0.01 extra reward.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, missing tethers are how an RFT job produces garbage that still "wins" the train reward. You restore from SFT and start over.

Interviews: name KL to reference and length; say they are not optional décor.

Bound how far the policy may drift from the SFT reference, and bound length if the reward likes words.

## How it works + one small example

Set a KL coefficient and watch KL and reward together. If reward rises only as KL explodes, you are leaving the SFT island. If length rises with reward, add an explicit length cost or a cap.

Example. Reward +0.2, KL from 0.1 to 8, mean tokens 80→400. You raise KL coeff and add a length penalty; land reward +0.08 with KL 0.4 and tokens 90. The smaller honest gain is the one you keep.

The reference is the SFT checkpoint, frozen, same tokenizer. A mismatched reference is a broken seatbelt.

KL to SFT, plus a length penalty if needed. Example: without KL the model left the schema to chase tests with print-debug spam. With KL it stayed in distribution and still raised pass rate.

## Failure modes

1. **KL coeff = 0 because learning was slow.**

2. **Length penalty so huge** the model stops answering.

3. **Reference is the base, not SFT**, so the tether pulls toward the wrong dialect.

4. **Unbounded RL** for two extra points.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For kl or length penalty, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.
