## What you would say in 30 seconds

I tether RFT to the SFT reference with a KL (or equivalent) and I penalise length when the reward loves tokens. A reward gain that explodes KL is not a gain I will serve.
keyPoints: KL bounds drift from the frozen SFT reference.
Length penalty fights verbosity hacks.
Watch reward, KL, and tokens on one plot.
A reward-up / KL-explode run is a fail.
Reference must be the SFT you actually like.
Zero tether is how language collapses to grader bait.

questions.q: What does a KL penalty do in RFT?
questions.a: It penalises the policy for moving far from a frozen reference (usually SFT), so high reward cannot be bought by abandoning the language you started with.

questions.q: Reward up, KL 0.1→8, tokens 5×. Ship?
questions.a: No. Raise the tether, add a length cost, inspect samples. You bought grader points with drift.

questions.q: You set KL to 0 to 'let it learn'. What happens?
questions.a: The policy can collapse to whatever the grader accidentally likes, including nonsense tokens. Restore a non-zero tether.

questions.q: Why is the SFT model the usual reference, not the raw base?
questions.a: SFT already speaks the task dialect. Tethering to the raw base pulls you away from the format you paid to teach.

questions.q: When is a length penalty the wrong tool?
questions.a: When the task truly needs long outputs (explanations, code). Then cap pathological length but do not punish necessary tokens. Use a budget, not a war on length.

rubric-versus-unit-test-rewards.explain:
## What it is

Prefer **machine-checkable scores** (unit tests, exact match, schema). Use a **rubric judge** only when a test **cannot exist**. A rubric is a structured human or model score (0–4 on criteria). It is more honest than a vibe but still gameable — especially by length and by models that share a family with the judge.

The order is: unit-test-like, then rubric with humans in calibration, then "please score this" as a last resort you probably skip.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, rubric-only RFT is how you rediscover length bias with more GPUs. Unit tests are the gift you should not refuse.

Interviews: state the preference order clearly.

Prefer machine-checkable scores. A rubric judge is last resort and needs its own hack suite.

## How it works + one small example

If any part of the task is checkable, score that part with a program and only send the residue to a rubric. Hybrid rewards beat a single LLM score.

Example. Code+explanation: tests score the code (weight 0.8); a short rubric scores the explanation (0.2) after length control. The policy cannot ignore tests by writing a lovely essay.

If you must use a rubric-only judge, freeze it, calibrate on humans, length-control, and keep a human holdout. Treat it as DPO-adjacent, not as a unit test.

Tests > schema > rubric. Example: you moved from a judge rubric to a real parser+tests and the 'gain' shrank — the judge had been flattered. That is a win for honesty.

## Failure modes

1. **Rubric for something a regex could do.**

2. **Same-family judge and policy** without calibration.

3. **Equal weights on essay and tests** so the essay can dominate.

4. **A 20-line rubric** you never adversarial-tested.

Time-box rubric versus unit test rewards to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on rubric versus unit test rewards', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether rubric versus unit test rewards would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for rubric versus unit test rewards that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box rubric versus unit test rewards more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-6 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on rubric versus unit test rewards more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether rubric versus unit test rewards more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for rubric versus unit test rewards more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I prefer unit-test and schema rewards. I use a rubric judge only for the residue a program cannot score, and I never let the essay outvote the tests.
keyPoints: Prefer program scores over rubric judges.
Rubrics are for qualities no checker can see.
Hybrid: tests on the checkable part, rubric on the rest.
Calibrate and length-control any judge.
Do not let prose weight dominate a testable task.
A rubric is closer to DPO than to a unit test.

questions.q: When may you use a rubric judge as an RFT reward?
questions.a: Only when a machine-checkable score cannot exist for that quality. Even then calibrate, length-control, and keep a human holdout.

questions.q: Code+explanation task. How do you weight rewards?
questions.a: Put most weight on hidden tests. Use a small, length-controlled rubric for the explanation. The essay must not outvote failing tests.

questions.q: The judge is the same family as the policy and loves long answers. Issue?
questions.a: Self-preference and length bias. Swap the judge, calibrate, or drop to tests-only.

questions.q: Why is a schema check better than a 1–5 'structuredness' rubric?
questions.a: It is deterministic and aligned with the parser. A 1–5 score can be flattered. Use the parser.

questions.q: You can write tests for 80% of the spec. RFT on a 100% rubric anyway?
questions.a: No. Score the 80% with tests and only rubric the rest. Do not throw away the honest signal.

when-not-to-reach-for-rl.explain:
## What it is

**Skip RFT** if you **cannot write a grader you trust more than a preference pair** (or a demonstration). RL adds variance, hacks, and ops. It is not a promotion from DPO. If pairs already capture the quality, DPO is enough. If gold exists, SFT is enough. If nothing exists, write a spec.

Also skip if you cannot sandbox the grader, cannot tether, or cannot staff the loop.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "we should try RL" is a meeting that needs a grown-up. The cost is not the GPU; it is the hack-and-chase cycle.

Interviews: a crisp skip policy scores well. Zeal for PPO does not.

Skip RFT if you cannot write a grader you trust more than a preference pair.

## How it works + one small example

Skip list:

- No program grader, only vibes.
- Grader less trusted than two humans comparing answers.
- Policy never scores above zero and you refuse to SFT first.
- Cannot isolate code execution.
- Success metric is already met by SFT/DPO.

Example. A PM saw a lab blog. Your task is brand tone. You write: no verifiable reward, DPO is the method if anything, SFT already at 90% on the unique parts. RL is out of scope. That memo is the deliverable.

If they still want a story, offer a **grader design spike** with no trainer — if the spike cannot score 50 fixtures cleanly, RL is cancelled with evidence.

Decision: no checker → SFT/DPO. Checker exists but data is tiny → maybe still SFT. Checker exists, volume high, hacks collected → RFT is in play. Example: you said no to RFT on tone in a meeting and offered DPO instead. That is seniority.

## Failure modes

1. **RL as culture.** Every task gets a loop.

2. **Skipping the spike.** You discover the grader is junk after a week of GPU.

3. **Trusting a vendor 'RL' button** with no held-out eval.

4. **RL as a prestige layer.**

Make when not to reach for rl falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For when not to reach for rl, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair when not to reach for rl with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for when not to reach for rl and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make when not to reach for rl more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-6.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For when not to reach for rl more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair when not to reach for rl more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for when not to reach for rl more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I skip RFT unless I have a grader I trust more than a pair, a sandbox, and a tether. If SFT or DPO already matches the signal, RL is theatre.
keyPoints: No trusted grader → no RFT.
If pairs are more honest than the grader, use DPO.
If gold exists and suffices, use SFT.
No sandbox or no staff → skip.
A grader-only spike can cancel RL cheaply.
RL is not a prestige upgrade from DPO.

questions.q: When do you skip RFT even if someone asks for RL?
questions.a: When you cannot write a grader more trusted than pairs or gold, when you cannot sandbox or staff it, or when SFT/DPO already meet the metric.

questions.q: Tone task, good pairs, no checker. Method?
questions.a: DPO (after SFT), not RFT. A niceness judge is a worse signal than the pairs.

questions.q: A vendor offers an 'RL fine-tune' button with no eval export. Risk?
questions.a: You cannot verify hacking or hold out data. Decline or demand a held-out eval you control.

questions.q: What is a grader design spike?
questions.a: A short project that scores a fixture set (including hacks) with no trainer attached. If it fails, RFT is cancelled before GPUs.

questions.q: SFT already hits the test-pass target. Add RFT?
questions.a: Only if a leftover checkable gap remains and an A/B shows lift. Hitting the target is a skip, not a reason to stack RL.

teacher-student.explain:
## What it is

**Distillation** here means a **stronger teacher** produces outputs that **train a smaller student** on one narrow workload. It is SFT (sometimes DPO) where the gold is **teacher text**, not a human original. The bet: the student keeps enough of the mapping to serve cheaper and faster, possibly on hardware you control.

The teacher can be a frontier API or a larger open model. The student is usually an 1–8B you can host. You are not transferring "intelligence" in the abstract. You are copying a **workload-specific** input–output map.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the cost story after a prompted giant already works. You do not distil as step one. You distil when the teacher path is good and the bill or latency hurts.

Interviews: teacher → student, narrow workload, filter the teacher, check terms.

A stronger teacher writes outputs that train a smaller student on one workload. Not 'transferring intelligence'.

## How it works + one small example

Sequence: freeze a teacher prompt that already hits the eval; generate on **real traffic-like** inputs; filter; SFT the student; compare both on the **same human-labelled** set (not only teacher labels).

Example. A 70B-class teacher routes tickets at 93% on a human set and costs too much at 80k/day. You generate on 20k historical tickets, drop rows that fail the spec or disagree with a human sample, train a 3B, land 90% at a tenth the unit cost. You route low-confidence student calls back to the teacher.

Do not distil a teacher that is still failing the task. You will copy the failure cheaper.

Freeze a teacher prompt that already hits the eval; generate on real-like inputs; filter; SFT the student; compare both on a **human** set. Example: 70B teacher 93% at high $; 3B student 90% at 1/10. You route low-confidence student calls back to the teacher. You do not distil a failing teacher.

## Failure modes

1. **Distilling a bad teacher.** Cheaper wrong.

2. **Evaluating only against teacher labels.** You measure imitation, including mistakes.

3. **Broad 'general assistant' distillation** with no workload boundary.

4. **Distilling as step one** before the teacher works.

Make teacher student falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For teacher student, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair teacher student with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for teacher student and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make teacher student more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For teacher student more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair teacher student more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for teacher student more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I distil a teacher that already wins a narrow workload into a smaller student, I filter the teacher’s answers, and I score both on human labels — not on the teacher’s own keys.
keyPoints: Teacher writes; student is SFT'd on those outputs.
Narrow workload, not generic intelligence transfer.
Teacher must already hit the eval.
Filter before the student treats text as gold.
Compare on human labels, not teacher self-labels.
A cheap copy of a failing teacher is still a fail.

questions.q: What is teacher-to-student distillation in this playbook?
questions.a: A stronger model generates outputs on a narrow workload that become training data for a smaller model you can serve cheaper or locally. It is imitation of a working teacher, not a new pretrain.

questions.q: The teacher is at 71% on the human set. Distil?
questions.a: No. Fix the teacher path first (prompt, retrieval). Distilling 71% yields a cheaper 71%-ish student and hardens the mistakes.

questions.q: Student matches the teacher 99% but human accuracy is 70%. What did you measure?
questions.a: Imitation of teacher errors. Add a human-labelled holdout and filter the train set against it.

questions.q: Why keep the workload narrow?
questions.a: A small student cannot absorb a frontier model's whole personality. It can absorb one mapping (labels, a template, a tool-calling style) well.

questions.q: How does a confidence fallback change the economics?
questions.a: Most traffic hits the cheap student; hard cases go to the teacher. You keep quality on the tail without paying teacher prices on the body.

generating-filtering-teacher-outputs.explain:
## What it is

Teacher data must be **generated on inputs that look like production** and **filtered** by your evals before it becomes truth. Generation on the teacher's favourite demo prompts yields a student that only handles demos. Unfiltered generation yields a student that loves the teacher's mistakes and catchphrases.

Filter = spec predicates, task metrics, diversity checks, PII/licence, and a human audit sample — the same bar as any SFT set.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "we dumped 100k teacher rows" is how students collapse. The dump was cheap; the serve failure is not.

Interviews: on-policy inputs + filter-then-train is the pair they want.

Generate on traffic-like prompts; drop rows that fail your evals before they become truth.

## How it works + one small example

Pipeline:

1. Sample prompts from logs or a realistic simulator (typos, empty, tail labels).
2. Run the teacher with the production prompt (retrieval included if prod has it).
3. `accept()` the outputs; drop fails.
4. Diversity and leak scans.
5. Audit 50; then train.

Example. 40k generated, 11k fail schema, 6k are greeting clones, 2k leak near the test set → 21k accepted. Those 21k beat the 40k dump on human eval.

If retrieval is in the teacher path, store the retrieved context with the row or the student will be asked to know facts the teacher was handed.

Filter: schema, spec, disagreement with a human sample. Example: 20k generated, 14k after filter. The 6k would have taught mistakes cheaper. You never train on unfiltered teacher dumps.

## Failure modes

1. **Demo-only prompts.** 

2. **Filter-after-train.** The student already ate the junk.

3. **Teacher without the retrieval the student will lack.** You ask the student to be the corpus.

4. **Trusting the teacher** because it is bigger.

On the job, generating filtering teacher outputs is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-7.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is generating filtering teacher outputs'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply generating filtering teacher outputs as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating generating filtering teacher outputs as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, generating filtering teacher outputs more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-7.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is generating filtering teacher outputs more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply generating filtering teacher outputs more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating generating filtering teacher outputs more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I generate teacher answers on real-looking traffic, I filter them with the same spec and evals I use for humans, and only then do they become the student’s gold.
keyPoints: Prompts from real traffic or a realistic simulator.
Teacher uses the production prompt (and retrieval if any).
Filter with accept(), diversity, leak, audit.
Do not train on the raw dump.
If the teacher saw retrieved context, record it or drop the fact.
Demo prompts make a demo student.

questions.q: Why generate teacher outputs on real traffic prompts?
questions.a: The student must handle the messy distribution you serve. Demo prompts under-represent typos, empties, and tail labels, so the student fails in production.

questions.q: Teacher path uses retrieval. Student will not. What do you store?
questions.a: Either include the retrieved passages in the student’s prompt at train and serve, or strip fact-bearing answers and keep only style. Do not ask the student to recall documents it will not see.

questions.q: You trained on all 100k raw teacher rows. Student repeats a wrong catchphrase. Cause?
questions.a: No filter. The catchphrase was common in teacher dumps. Filter and diversity-check, then retrain.

questions.q: What filters apply to teacher data?
questions.a: The same as human SFT: spec predicates, schema, PII, licence, near-dupe leak, n-gram diversity, and a 50-row audit.

questions.q: When is a simulator acceptable instead of logs?
questions.a: When logs are thin or restricted. The simulator must include tail and messy cases, not only happy paths, or you are back to demos.

capability-for-cost-latency.explain:
## What it is

You distil to **trade a little capability for cost, latency, and control**. The honest report is a **three-column table**: quality, latency, cost per request (or per 1k) for teacher, student, and any fallback design. "The student is almost as good" without dollars and milliseconds is a slogan.

Self-hosting can win even at equal API token prices if you need residency or a reserved-capacity shape.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, finance will ask for this table. If you cannot produce it, you are not ready to distil.

Interviews: say what you are willing to lose (2–4 quality points, illustrative) for a 5–10× unit-cost drop — and that you measured both.

Trade a little quality for $ and ms, and for a model you can host.

## How it works + one small example

Measure on the same set, same hardware story.

Example. Teacher API: 93% F1, 900ms p95, $12/1k. Student GPU: 90% F1, 120ms p95, $1.2/1k. Fallback 8% of traffic to teacher: blended 92.4%, 180ms, $2.1/1k. You ship the blend.

If the student is 88% and there is no acceptable fallback, you may keep the teacher. Distillation is allowed to lose the A/B.

Report both models on the same set: score, p95, $/1k. Example: −3 points, −8× cost, −4× latency, in-VPC. The gate allows −3. You ship the student. A −3 that also misses the safety pack you do not.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality-only report.**

2. **Student latency measured on a laptop, teacher on a cold API.** Unfair.

3. **Ignoring GPU idle cost** when volume is low. Unit cost explodes.

4. **Quality-only distillation slides.**

Time-box capability for cost latency to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-7 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on capability for cost latency', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether capability for cost latency would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for capability for cost latency that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

Time-box capability for cost latency more to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-7 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on capability for cost latency more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether capability for cost latency more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for capability for cost latency more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I report quality, latency, and cost for teacher, student, and fallback on the same set. Distillation is a trade, and I will keep the teacher if the trade fails.
keyPoints: The point is capability-per-dollar and per-second, plus control.
Always table quality, latency, and cost together.
A small quality drop can be fine if the unit cost falls a lot.
Blended fallback often beats a pure student.
Low volume can erase GPU savings via idle cost.
The trade is allowed to lose; then you do not ship the student.

questions.q: What three numbers belong in a distillation report?
questions.a: Quality on a shared set, latency (p50/p95), and cost per request or per 1k, for teacher, student, and any fallback blend.

questions.q: Student is −3 F1, 8× cheaper, 5× faster. How do you decide?
questions.a: If −3 is inside the written budget and a fallback can recover the tail, ship the blend. If −3 is on a critical slice, do not.

questions.q: Unit cost assumed 100% GPU utilisation but you have 2k requests/day. Issue?
questions.a: Idle GPU dominates. Recompute with reserved-hour cost. The API teacher may be cheaper at low volume.

questions.q: Why measure both models on the same hardware story?
questions.a: A cold API vs a warm local GPU (or the reverse) lies about latency. State the conditions.

questions.q: When does self-hosting win besides token price?
questions.a: Data residency, predictable capacity, or adapter control. Those can justify a student even if API tokens look similar.

copied-mistakes-low-diversity.explain:
## What it is

Two structural risks: the student **copies teacher mistakes** (and becomes confidently wrong), and **low-diversity synthetic** text **narrows** what the student can handle. Repeated synth-on-synth training is how you get **model collapse**: tails of the distribution vanish.

Diversity checks and human labels are not optional extras on teacher data. They are the whole defence.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a student that only understands teacher-polished English fails the first angry, bilingual, truncated ticket.

Interviews: name copied error and collapse. Mention a human holdout.

The student copies teacher errors and cloned phrasing. Filter and diversify.

## How it works + one small example

Defences:

- Filter teacher errors with the spec and a human sample.
- Diversity caps and n-gram drops.
- Mix in real edited logs, not only teacher prose.
- Never train a new teacher on the student’s outputs and loop.
- Eval on human gold, messy prompts, and a slice the teacher never saw.

Example. After two synth generations, unique openings collapse from 800 to 40. You stop, inject log_edit rows, and reset the teacher prompt. The student recovers tail labels.

A copied systematic miss (always swapping two labels) must be fixed in the teacher or the filter, not by hoping the student "generalises past" it.

Diversity checks + human sample. Example: the teacher always said 'Happy to help!' and the student could not stop. You filtered that n-gram and you added expert rows. A student that only speaks Teacher is brittle on real logs.

## Failure modes

1. **Synth-on-synth loops.**

2. **Human eval only on teacher-like prompts.**

3. **Keeping known teacher bugs because volume.**

4. **No human set** — only teacher-vs-student on teacher labels.

A practical sitting for copied mistakes low diversity: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-7 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of copied mistakes low diversity with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put copied mistakes low diversity on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of copied mistakes low diversity that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for copied mistakes low diversity more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-7 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of copied mistakes low diversity more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put copied mistakes low diversity more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of copied mistakes low diversity more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I assume teacher data is biased and incomplete: I filter mistakes, enforce diversity, mix real logs, and I will not train on the student’s own outputs in a loop.
keyPoints: Students copy teacher errors, often more confidently.
Low-diversity synth narrows the tails.
Synth-on-synth loops collapse the distribution.
Mix real edited logs into the student set.
Human eval on messy prompts the teacher did not polish.
Fix systematic teacher bugs at the source.

questions.q: What is model collapse in distillation?
questions.a: Repeated training on model-generated text that drops the tails of the real distribution. The student (and later teachers) only handle a few templates.

questions.q: The teacher systematically swaps two labels. What does the student do?
questions.a: Copies the swap, often more consistently. Filter or fix the teacher; do not hope the student unlearns a majority error.

questions.q: After a second synth generation, tail accuracy dies. Cause?
questions.a: Diversity collapse. Inject real logs, drop clones, and stop feeding the student its teacher-of-a-student.

questions.q: Why mix log_edit rows into a teacher-heavy set?
questions.a: They carry messy phrasing and true tails the teacher never writes. Without them the student is polite and brittle.

questions.q: How do you eval for copied mistakes?
questions.a: A human-labelled set, plus a slice of known teacher failure modes. If the student matches the teacher on those, you copied the bug.

teacher-terms-of-use.explain:
## What it is

Some providers **restrict using their outputs to train competing or replacement models**. Distillation can be a **contract** problem, not only a technical one. You check the teacher’s terms (and your counsel) **before** you generate 100k rows you cannot keep.

"The outputs are public on the user’s screen" is not a licence to train. Internal use versus a competing hosted model also differ. This is the same family of issue as licensed documents in SFT.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is a stop-the-line check. A legal surprise after you have a student in prod is a bad week.

Interviews: mention terms unprompted. It reads as production sense.

Some APIs forbid using outputs to train a competing or replacement model. Read them.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist:

- Read the teacher API terms and the "no model training / no competing model" clauses.
- If forbidden, pick a permissively licensed teacher, human data, or a vendor that allows it.
- Record the decision and the date; terms move.
- Do not hide origin in the dataset card. Opacity is not compliance.

Example. Provider A forbids training competing models. You use provider B or an open teacher whose licence allows it, or you hire humans for the 3k rows you actually need. You do not "anonymise" A’s outputs and hope.

If terms allow internal tuning but not a public rehost, that constraint belongs in the serve plan.

Legal reads the ToS before you generate. Example: a frontier API bans training a public competing model; an internal student behind your login may still be allowed — or not. You do not find out at launch. Open-weight teachers have licences too.

## Failure modes

1. **Asking engineering to decide licence.** Call legal.

2. **Generating first, asking later.** You may have to delete the set.

3. **Assuming open-weight teacher ⇒ free to do anything.** Check that licence too.

4. **Generating 20k rows first.**

Time-box teacher terms of use to a morning: one hour to measure, one hour to write the decision, one hour to put a test in CI or a drill on the calendar. m13-7 items that cannot fit that box are either too vague or too large — split them.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on teacher terms of use', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether teacher terms of use would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for teacher terms of use that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

When they ask you to 'go deeper on teacher terms of use more', do not add jargon. Add a constraint (region, ACL, $ cap, slice) and say what you would refuse. Refusal is the senior move.

Example you can reuse: pick a single customer-facing flow and ask whether teacher terms of use more would have changed the path, the log line, or the rollback. If the answer is 'not really', you may be over-weighting the topic for that flow.

Failure: a checklist for teacher terms of use more that lives in a personal note and never became a gate. Gates are how teams remember; notes are how individuals forget.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read the teacher’s terms before I generate training data. If they forbid training a replacement model, I change teacher or use humans — I do not hide the origin.

Check before you generate a lake you cannot keep.
Public on a screen is not a training licence.
