questions.a: Often no. Read that licence the same way you read an API TOS. Pick another teacher if the product is commercial.

on-policy-student-inputs.explain:
## What it is

**On-policy student inputs** means you distil on **prompts from real traffic** (or a faithful simulator), not only the teacher’s favourite demos. The student’s train distribution should match what it will see. Teacher-chosen prompts are a marketing set.

This is the distillation version of "logs over lab benches".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, demo-trained students fail the first empty subject line. You then blame the 3B.

Interviews: one sentence — traffic prompts, not teacher demos.

Distil on real traffic prompts, not only the teacher's favourite demos.

## How it works + one small example

Sample prompts from the gateway log with the same slice mix you serve (or with tail upsampling). Run the teacher on those. Do not let the teacher invent the prompt list.

Example. Demo set is 200 clean tickets. Traffic is 40% incomplete, 10% not-English. You sample 10k log prompts, generate, filter. The student finally sees empty tickets. Demo-only would have scored 97% on demos and 60% in prod.

If logs contain PII, redact prompts the same way you redact any SFT source.

Sample production (or a safe replay), generate teacher answers, filter, train. Example: demo-only distillation looked great and failed on short mobile prompts. On-policy inputs fixed the slice. Demos can seed; they cannot be the whole set.

## Failure modes

1. **Teacher-written prompts only.**

2. **Logs from a different product surface.**

3. **Cherry-picking logs that already look like demos.**

4. **A blog's 200 prompts** as the corpus.

Make on policy student inputs falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For on policy student inputs, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair on policy student inputs with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for on policy student inputs and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make on policy student inputs more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For on policy student inputs more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair on policy student inputs more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for on policy student inputs more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I distil on prompts from real traffic so the student’s training mix matches production. Teacher-chosen demos make a demo model.
keyPoints: Prompts come from logs or a faithful simulator.
Do not let the teacher pick the homework.
Match or deliberately upsample production slices.
Redact PII in log prompts.
Demo-only sets lie about production quality.
A different product surface is the wrong log.

questions.q: What does on-policy mean for distillation inputs?
questions.a: The prompts are drawn from the distribution the student will serve — real traffic or a simulator of that traffic — not from the teacher’s demo list.

questions.q: Teacher marketing set is 200 clean tickets. What do you add?
questions.a: Log prompts with empties, tail labels, and messy language, then filter the teacher’s answers. Those are the rows that prevent a prod cliff.

questions.q: Student is great on the notebook file and poor in the gateway. First suspicion?
questions.a: Train prompts were demos. Compare n-grams to production logs and rebuild from traffic.

questions.q: Why not let the teacher generate synthetic prompts too?
questions.a: It will generate the prompts it is good at. You can use them as a supplement after diversity checks, not as the only source.

questions.q: Logs are PII-heavy. How do you stay on-policy?
questions.a: Redact consistently and keep the messy structure. Do not replace them with clean synthetic prompts just because redaction is work.

filter-then-train.explain:
## What it is

**Filter then train** is the hard rule: **teacher rows that fail your evals never become the student’s truth**. The filter runs **before** the optimiser, not as a hope after a bad student eval.

This is gold-spec-before-collection applied to a machine labeller that never gets tired and never feels shame.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, post-hoc "we’ll drop the bad ones next version" means v1 is poisoned and v1 is what someone shipped.

Interviews: filter-then-train is a four-word policy.

Drop teacher rows that fail your evals before they become the student's gold.

## How it works + one small example

The teacher writer writes to a staging table. `accept()` plus judges plus leak/diversity land accepted rows in `ds-*.accepted`. The trainer can only read that.

Example. Teacher F1 vs human gold on a sample is 88%. You drop the 12% fails (and a margin of low-confidence). The student trains on the 88% and beats a student trained on 100% raw teacher by 4 points on the human set.

Confidence: if the teacher emits a score or you have a checker, drop the bottom band even if they "look fine".

The filter is the same spec as production. Example: invalid JSON from the teacher never enters train. A 'filter later' plan is how the student learns invalid JSON fluently.

## Failure modes

1. **Trainer points at staging.**

2. **Filter only on schema, not on task correctness.**

3. **Using the student’s own eval to filter after training** as the first filter.

4. **Filtering 5% as a token gesture.**

Translate filter then train into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-7.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for filter then train than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used filter then train, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of filter then train in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate filter then train more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-7.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for filter then train more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used filter then train more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of filter then train more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Teacher rows pass my evals before they touch the student. The trainer cannot see staging. Filter then train, not train then regret.
keyPoints: Failing teacher rows never enter the accepted set.
The trainer only reads accepted, hashed data.
Filter task correctness, not only schema.
Drop low-confidence teacher rows when you can.
v1 ships the set you filtered, not the dump.
This is the spec-at-the-door rule for machines.

questions.q: What does filter-then-train forbid?
questions.a: Using teacher outputs that fail your spec or evals as student gold. Filtering after a bad student run is too late for v1.

questions.q: Teacher is 88% on a human sample. How do you use that?
questions.a: Drop the known fails and a low-confidence band, train on the rest, and report both teacher and student on the same human set.

questions.q: The trainer path still points at the raw dump. Risk?
questions.a: Someone will rerun and poison the student. Lock the path to the accepted hash in the config.

questions.q: Is schema-only filtering enough?
questions.a: No. A well-formed wrong label is worse than a dropped row. Include task checks and an audit.

questions.q: Where does the teacher writer write?
questions.a: A staging table. Promotion to accepted is a separate job with accept() and audits.

student-versus-teacher-gap.explain:
## What it is

Always **report the student and the teacher on the same set** for **quality, latency, and cost**. The **gap** is the product. A student at 90% means nothing if you hide that the teacher is 93% or 80%. A student that is faster but 20 points worse is not a distillation win.

The gap also tells you whether to invest in more data, a bigger student, or a fallback.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, hiding the teacher number is how a 80% student ships as "we distilled the good model".

Interviews: always say both numbers.

Report quality, latency and cost of both on the same human set.

## How it works + one small example

One table, one set, one date. Include slices. If the gap is all in one slice (languages, tail labels), you may keep the student on the easy body and route the slice to the teacher.

Example. Overall: teacher 93, student 90. Language X: teacher 91, student 70. You do not ship a monolingual lie. You either add X data, or you route X to the teacher, or you delay.

Re-run the table when either model or the set changes. A stale teacher number is a marketing slide.

A table, not a vibe. Example: teacher 93 / 1.8s / $12; student 90 / 0.3s / $0.9. Gap accepted, route the 10% low-confidence back. If you only report student vs an old baseline, you hid the distillation tax.

## Failure modes

1. **Student-only dashboard.**

2. **Different sets for the two models.**

3. **Ignoring a slice gap because the mean looks fine.**

4. **Hiding the teacher score.**

Translate student versus teacher gap into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-7.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for student versus teacher gap than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used student versus teacher gap, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of student versus teacher gap in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate student versus teacher gap more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-7.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for student versus teacher gap more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used student versus teacher gap more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of student versus teacher gap more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I put teacher and student on one table: quality, latency, cost, and slices. The gap is the decision; a student number without the teacher is incomplete.
keyPoints: Always report both models on the same set.
Include quality, latency, cost, and slices.
The gap decides data vs bigger student vs fallback.
A slice gap can force routing, not a mean ship.
Refresh the table when models or the set move.
Hiding the teacher number is a reporting bug.

questions.q: Why report teacher and student on the same set?
questions.a: So the quality gap is real. Different sets let you hide a weak student or a weak teacher. The product decision is the gap plus cost and latency.

questions.q: Overall gap is 3 points; one language is 21. Action?
questions.a: Do not ship a single number. Add data, route that language to the teacher, or delay. The mean is hiding the slice.

questions.q: Dashboard shows only student F1 trending up. What is missing?
questions.a: The teacher baseline on the same frozen set, plus latency and cost. The student may be chasing a moving test.

questions.q: How does the gap guide the next experiment?
questions.a: Small gap + high cost → ship or fallback. Large gap on one slice → data or route. Large gap everywhere → bigger student or stop.

questions.q: Can you use teacher-as-judge to compute the gap?
questions.a: Not as the only number. Teacher-as-judge measures imitation. Keep a human or independent set for the real gap.

licence-of-teacher-outputs.explain:
## What it is

**Licence of teacher outputs** is the explicit confirmation that **this** API or weight licence **allows training a competing or replacement model**. It is the operational twin of reading terms: a recorded yes/no, with a link and a date, on the dataset card.

If the answer is no, the pipeline does not generate. If the answer is "internal only", the student cannot become an external API.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, verbal "I think it's fine" dies in due diligence. A card row survives.

Interviews: you can say you would block generation on a missing licence row.

Confirm the teacher API or weight licence allows training a replacement.

## How it works + one small example

Add `teacher_licence: {source, url, date, allowed: yes|no|internal}` to the card. CI for the generate job requires `allowed in {yes, internal}`. Product type must match (`internal` cannot publish).

Example. Counsel says "yes, internal student, no public rehost". You serve the student inside the VPC and you do not put it on a public marketplace. The card says so. A later PM cannot "just expose it" without seeing the row.

Re-check when you change teacher ids. A new SKU can have new terms.

A sentence in the ADR: licence, date, who signed. Example: you switched to an open teacher whose licence allows it after the API ToS did not. The data you already generated under the API may still be tainted — legal decides, you do not assume.

## Failure modes

1. **One legal email in 2024, teacher changed in 2026.**

2. **Allowed=internal, marketing lists a public API.**

3. **No row, generation still runs.**

4. **Mixing tainted and clean rows.**

Make licence of teacher outputs falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For licence of teacher outputs, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair licence of teacher outputs with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for licence of teacher outputs and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make licence of teacher outputs more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-7.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For licence of teacher outputs more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair licence of teacher outputs more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for licence of teacher outputs more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I will not generate teacher data without a dated licence row that says this use is allowed. Internal-only means the student stays inside; I re-check when the teacher id changes.
keyPoints: A dated allowed/internal/no row on the dataset card.
Generation CI requires a passing licence row.
Internal-only forbids a public student API.
Re-check when the teacher SKU changes.
A 2024 email is not a 2026 licence.
This is the same discipline as document licences in SFT.

questions.q: What belongs in a teacher-licence card row?
questions.a: Source, terms URL, date, and allowed yes/no/internal. Generation should refuse to run without it.

questions.q: Licence is internal-only. Can marketing sell the student as an API?
questions.a: No. Serve inside the allowed boundary. Changing the product requires a new licence review, not a new landing page.

questions.q: You switched teacher SKUs and reused last year’s yes. Risk?
questions.a: Terms may differ. Re-check and update the date or you are running on folklore.

questions.q: Why put this in CI, not a wiki?
questions.a: Wikis do not stop a generate job. CI does.

questions.q: How is this different from 'teacher terms of use' as a concept?
questions.a: Terms of use is the legal idea. This is the recorded, enforced artefact so the pipeline cannot 'forget' the idea.

distill-versus-buy-a-smaller-api.explain:
## What it is

Before you distil, **compare a self-hosted student to the teacher’s own cheap small-model SKU** (and to other small APIs). Distillation has data, licence, and retrain tax. A small hosted model may already hit the bar at a similar price with no student to operate.

The comparison is an eval table, not a preference for GPUs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams distil for sport and then pay more than `gpt-x-mini` or a hosted 8B. The small SKU was the baseline they skipped.

Interviews: always include "buy the small API" as a column.

Compare a distilled self-hosted student with the teacher's own cheap small SKU.

## How it works + one small example

Four columns: big teacher, **small official SKU**, distilled student, student+fallback. Same set. Include ops burden as a qualitative fifth.

Example. Small official SKU: 89% , $2/1k, no ops. Student: 90%, $1.5/1k + a GPU owner. You may still buy the SKU. If residency forbids the SKU, the student wins even at 89%.

If the small SKU is 91% and the teacher is 93%, try prompting the small SKU harder before you distil the teacher at all.

Sometimes the vendor already sells the small model. Example: their 8B API is 89% at $1.2/1k; your student is 90% at $0.8 plus GPU ops. You pick with ops included. Distillation is not free money if a SKU already exists.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping the small SKU column.**

2. **Ignoring ops** in the student cost.

3. **Distilling because you already generated 50k rows.** Sunk cost.

4. **Distilling by default** without pricing the small SKU.

A practical sitting for distill versus buy a smaller api: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-7 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of distill versus buy a smaller api with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put distill versus buy a smaller api on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of distill versus buy a smaller api that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for distill versus buy a smaller api more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-7 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of distill versus buy a smaller api more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put distill versus buy a smaller api more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of distill versus buy a smaller api more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare a distilled student to the teacher’s cheap small SKU on the same eval before I pay the distillation tax. Sometimes I just buy the small model.
keyPoints: Small official SKUs are a baseline, not an afterthought.
Four columns: big teacher, small SKU, student, blend.
Include ops burden, not only token price.
Residency can force the student even if the SKU is good.
Prompt the small SKU before you distil.
Sunk teacher rows are not a reason to ship a student.

questions.q: What extra baseline belongs in a distillation bake-off?
questions.a: The teacher vendor’s cheaper small-model SKU (and similar hosted small models), prompted well, on the same set as the student.

questions.q: Small SKU is 89% at $2/1k with no ops; student is 90% at $1.5/1k plus a GPU owner. Lean?
questions.a: Often buy the SKU unless residency or control requires the student. A point of F1 is rarely worth an unowned GPU.

questions.q: You already paid to generate 80k teacher rows. Does that force distillation?
questions.a: No. Sunk cost. If the small SKU wins the table, stop. Keep the rows as eval if licence allows.

questions.q: When does the student beat a good small SKU anyway?
questions.a: Data residency, need for adapters, or a unit-cost win after honest GPU utilisation — all measured, not assumed.

questions.q: What should you try on the small SKU before distilling?
questions.a: The same prompt/retrieval work you gave the big teacher. A weak prompt on the small SKU makes distillation look more necessary than it is.

baselines-before-training.explain:
## What it is

A **baseline** is the strongest cheap system you can already run on the held-out set: best prompt, few-shot, retrieval, structured outputs, maybe a larger or newer model. The **untuned base** with the same prompt is a second point, so you can attribute gains to weights rather than to a prompt you also changed. Without those two numbers a tune cannot win or lose; it can only exist.

Record quality, format validity, latency and cost per successful task for each baseline. Write the **ship threshold** before the first training job (illustrative: "+5 points, no critical-slice drop, cost ≤ the prompted giant"). After-the-fact thresholds are rationalisation.

A lazy one-line prompt is not a baseline. It is a way to make a tune look inevitable.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most tune reviews skip this and compare to an embarrassing prompt. The tune "wins" and you now own weights. In interviews, "what was the baseline?" is how they test whether you have done Level 13 or only watched a LoRA video.

Hiring managers also want to hear that you would drop the tune if a better prompt or a new base closes the gap. The baseline is what makes that sentence possible.

## How it works + one small example

Before anyone books a GPU:

1. Freeze the held-out set.
2. Spend a real week on the prompted system (examples, retrieval, schema).
3. Score it and the raw base. Store the report with ids.
4. Write the threshold and the kill criteria in the ADR.
5. Only then open a training config.

Example: ticket routing. Raw 8B is 71% on 800 held-out tickets. Prompted 8B with taxonomy few-shot is 86%. Prompted frontier is 91%. You write: ship a LoRA if it reaches 90% and costs ≤ 20% of the frontier. The tune later hits 90.5%. You can justify it. A team that only compared to 71% would have shipped a 80% LoRA and called it a success.

## Failure modes

1. **Lazy baseline.** One-line prompt, 20-point "gain", sunk cost.

2. **Changed prompt and weights together.** You cannot say what helped.

3. **No cost or latency on the baseline.** The tune is cheaper to train than to run; you notice later.

4. **Threshold after the run.** You needed +5; you got +2; you shipped anyway.

Make baselines before training falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-8.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For baselines before training, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair baselines before training with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for baselines before training and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

Make baselines before training more falsifiable. Write the observation that would prove you got it wrong — a score, a leak test, a 429, a residency miss. If you cannot name the observation, you cannot operate m13-8.

The interview trap is a taxonomy with no scar. For baselines before training more, keep one concrete miss: what looked healthy, what was actually wrong, and the cheap check that would have caught it.

Pair baselines before training more with a tiny artefact in the repo: a config snippet, a query, a five-row eval. Talking through that file is faster and more honest than a whiteboard of boxes.

Another miss: copying a vendor tutorial for baselines before training more and never changing the region, the data class, or the eval. Tutorials are US-default and demo-data; your constraints are not.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The baseline is the best prompted system plus the raw base, scored on the frozen set, with a ship threshold written first. I will not train to beat a lazy prompt, and I will drop the tune if the cheap system catches up.
keyPoints: Baseline = best prompt/RAG/schema, not a one-liner.
Also score the untuned base so you can attribute the gain.
Record quality, format, latency and cost.
Write the ship threshold before the first job.
A lazy baseline manufactures a fake win.
Re-score the baseline whenever the prompt or a new base improves.

questions.q: Why set a ship threshold before training?
questions.a: So the decision is not rewritten to fit the run. You need a pre-agreed gain and a regression limit.

questions.q: A tune beats a one-line prompt by 20 points. Convincing?
questions.a: No. Compare it to a well-engineered prompt with few-shot and retrieval. The gap often collapses.

questions.q: You changed the system prompt and trained in the same week. What can you not say?
questions.a: Whether the weights or the prompt moved the score. Split the experiments; keep a prompt-only control.

questions.q: What four numbers belong on every baseline row?
questions.a: Task metric, format validity, latency (p95) and cost per successful task.

questions.q: A new base model appears and the prompted score jumps to the threshold. What do you do?
questions.a: Re-score. If the cheap path now hits the gate, do not ship the tune. The baseline exists to let you walk away.

same-held-out-set-same-judge.explain:
## What it is

Every candidate — raw base, prompted baseline, tune, stronger model — is scored on the **same held-out set** with the **same judge, judge prompt, decoding and scoring rules**. Change any of those and the delta is uninterpretable.

Freeze the set: no training, no prompt-hacking, no "just this one extra easy item". Pin the judge model version. Calibrate it on human labels. For noisy metrics, repeat and report variance. Randomise pairwise order. Do not let the tuned model or its teacher grade itself.

Retuning the judge until the new model wins is fraud with extra ceremony.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the only way two people can argue from the same graph. In interviews, listing what must stay constant is a Level 7/13 crossover they expect. Self-preference bias is the follow-up — have a sentence ready.

Small sets make this sharper. At n=100 a 2-point gap is often noise. Same set, same judge, plus an interval, or you are reading tea leaves.

## How it works + one small example

Harness rules in the repo, not in a notebook:

1. `evals/holdout_v4.jsonl` is immutable; a new item is v5.
2. Judge config is a file: model id, prompt hash, temperature 0.
3. A runner takes `(system, model_id)` and writes a signed report.
4. CI refuses a compare if set hash or judge hash differ.
5. A 40-item human sample is re-labelled each quarter to catch judge drift.

Example: LoRA v3 vs prompted baseline. Someone used a "nicer" judge prompt on v3. Scores jumped. You revert the judge file, re-run both, and the gain is +0.8 with overlapping intervals. The honest report is "no ship". The dishonest one already went to Slack.

## Failure modes

1. **Set creep.** Easy items added to help the tune.

2. **Teacher as judge.** Distilled student looks perfect.

3. **Different decoding.** Tune ran greedy; baseline ran temperature 0.7.

4. **Unpinned judge.** The platform updated it; both scores moved and you blamed the model.

On the job, same held out set same judge is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is same held out set same judge'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply same held out set same judge as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating same held out set same judge as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, same held out set same judge more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is same held out set same judge more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply same held out set same judge more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating same held out set same judge more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare every candidate on one frozen set with one pinned judge and one decoding. If those hashes differ, I do not discuss the delta. I will not let a model grade its own children.
keyPoints: Same set, judge, judge prompt, decoding, scoring rules.
The held-out set is immutable; additions bump the version.
Pin the judge; calibrate on humans.
Ban self-judging and teacher-judging.
Report variance on small or noisy sets.
CI should refuse a compare with mismatched hashes.

questions.q: What must stay constant when comparing baseline and tune?
questions.a: Held-out set, judge model and prompt, decoding, and scoring rules.

questions.q: The judge is the model that wrote the training targets. Issue?
questions.a: Self-preference inflates the student. Use a different judge calibrated on human labels.

questions.q: A compare ticket has two different set hashes. What do you do?
questions.a: Refuse the compare. Re-run both on one hash or you are looking at two exams.

questions.q: Why randomise pairwise order?
questions.a: Position bias: judges prefer the first or the longer answer. Swap A/B.

questions.q: n=80, +2 points. Ship?
questions.a: Not on the mean alone. Check the interval and the critical slice. You likely need more items or a pre-registered threshold that this does not meet.

beyond-a-single-score.explain:
## What it is

One aggregate number hides the decision. Report **slices** (category, language, length, tool-use, the original failure mode), the **tail** (share of catastrophic misses), **intervals** on small n, and **several metrics** (accuracy, schema validity, refusal, verbosity, latency, cost). Weight errors by severity when a payments miss is not equal to a chitchat miss.

Example: overall +3, payments −8. The mean would ship a harmful model. The slice blocks it.

Also look at consistency across repeated draws. A tune that is +4 once and −1 the next two times is not +4.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, leadership reads the headline. Your job is to put the slice table on the same page. Interviews will give you a +2 overall and a nasty slice and ask what you do. The answer is not "ship, it is positive".

This is also how you catch eval bugs: one slice of "failures" that are actually judge errors.

## How it works + one small example

A one-page report:

- Headline metric with interval.
- Table: slice × (baseline, tune, delta).
- Catastrophic rate (wrong money, wrong medical, invalid JSON).
- Latency p95 and cost per success.
- Decision line that cites the worst slice, not only the mean.

Example: 600 held-out tickets. Overall 90.1 vs 88.0. Payments (n=70) 82 vs 91. Invalid JSON 0.3% vs 0.1%. You do not ship. You add payments examples or you keep the prompted model on that route. The mean was a trap.

## Failure modes

1. **Mean-only Slack message.**

2. **Tiny slice treated as gospel.** n=12 flipped a decision.

3. **Equal weights.** A refund error counted like a greeting.

4. **No tail.** Average up, 2% of answers now invent account numbers.

On the job, beyond a single score is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is beyond a single score'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply beyond a single score as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating beyond a single score as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, beyond a single score more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is beyond a single score more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply beyond a single score more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating beyond a single score more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I never ship on a mean. I bring slices, tails, intervals, and cost. A +3 that hides an −8 on payments is a no, not a headline.
keyPoints: Slices: language, length, tools, original failure mode.
Report tails and catastrophic rates, not only the average.
Intervals on small n; do not over-read +2 at n=100.
Weight errors by severity.
Put the worst slice on the decision line.
Repeat noisy metrics; a one-off +4 is not a result.

questions.q: Why report slices as well as the average?
questions.a: A good mean can hide a drop on a critical category. Slices expose it.

questions.q: Tune is +2 on 100 examples. Ship?
questions.a: Not from the mean. Check the interval, the critical slice and tails. You may need more items.

questions.q: Overall +3, payments −8. Decision?
questions.a: Block. Route payments to the baseline or fix data; do not average away money errors.

questions.q: What is a catastrophic rate here?
questions.a: The share of answers that violate a hard rule: wrong amount, leaked secret, invalid schema, unsafe advice.

questions.q: A slice has n=12 and a huge delta. What do you do?
questions.a: Collect more items in that slice before you decide. Twelve rows are a clue, not a gate.

regressions-outside-the-task.explain:
## What it is

A tune can break things you did not train for. Keep a **regression suite**: general instruction following, safety and refusals, other languages, long context, tool calling, and a few neighbouring formats. Run it on the base and the tune. Gate on it: a small drop on general tasks may be tolerable; a safety drop is not.

Forgetting is the usual shape: the model becomes a brilliant ticket router and a worse assistant. Injection susceptibility can also rise. Formats the tune never saw start to drift.

If a gate fails: lower LR or rank, mix general and safety data, early-stop, or refuse to replace the general model with a specialist on every route.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job the tuned model often becomes the default. Users will hit untested paths. Interviews will ask how you catch forgetting and safety drift. "We looked at the task metric" is the junior miss.

A specialist that is only called for one task still needs a safety probe. People type weird things into every box.

## How it works + one small example

Suite construction:

1. 50–100 general instructions you already like the base on.
2. A refusal/injection pack you do not train on.
3. One other language and one long-context file if those appear in prod.
4. Tool-call items if the app uses tools.
5. Gates in the ADR: e.g. ≤2-point drop on general, 0 worsening on the safety pack.

Example: LoRA for JSON labels. Task +7. Refusal pack: the base refused a jailbreak; the tune complied. You mix 200 safety pairs, drop rank, re-run. Safety holds, task still +6. Now you can talk about shipping. Without the pack you would have shipped a more jailbreakable router.

## Failure modes

1. **Task-only eval.**

2. **Training on the safety pack** so the gate is circular.

3. **Replacing the general model everywhere** with a specialist.

4. **Ignoring a small safety miss** because the mean task score is pretty.

On the job, regressions outside the task is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is regressions outside the task'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply regressions outside the task as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating regressions outside the task as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, regressions outside the task more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is regressions outside the task more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply regressions outside the task more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating regressions outside the task more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I run a regression suite the tune never trained on: general skill, refusals, tools, other languages. A task win that fails safety does not ship. Sometimes the fix is not more task data — it is a lower rank or a narrower route.
keyPoints: Keep a regression suite off the training distribution.
Compare tune to base on general, safety and tools.
Safety regressions block; small general drops may be negotiable.
Do not train on the gate set.
A specialist should not silently become the default model.
Mitigate with LR/rank, mix-in data, or routing — not hope.

questions.q: What belongs in a regression suite for a tune?
questions.a: General instructions, safety/refusals, multilingual and long-context items, tool use, and neighbouring formats, run on base and tune.

questions.q: Task accuracy is up but the model now follows injected instructions. Action?
questions.a: Treat as a safety block. Add adversarial mix-in or lower rank, and do not release until the pack passes.

questions.q: Why not train on the regression suite?
questions.a: Then the gate is no longer an unseen check. You have hidden forgetting rather than measured it.

questions.q: The specialist is excellent. Should it serve every chat?
questions.a: No. Route it to the task. A forgotten general model is a product regression even if the suite was only a little down.

questions.q: Which mitigations do you try when forgetting appears?
questions.a: Lower learning rate or rank, mix general/safety data, earlier checkpoint, or narrower routing. Do not just train longer on the task.

reading-individual-failures.explain:
## What it is

Metrics say how much; **reading failures** says why. Sample 30–100 misses and tag them: label noise, judge error, ambiguous spec, missing coverage, template bug, capability limit. Each tag has a different next action. Training more on a noisy label wastes a GPU. Tweaking LR on a spec hole wastes a week.

Keep a failure log with counts per tag across runs. That log is the backlog. Interviewers who have tuned will ask what the misses looked like. Have two examples, not a vibe.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you stop random hyperparameter search. In interviews it separates people who watched loss curves from people who opened the outputs.

A surprising share of "tune failures" are eval bugs. Reading is how you find them before you celebrate or despair.

## How it works + one small example

Weekly loop:

1. Dump 80 misses (and 20 lucky hits) with inputs, outputs, expected, judge rationale.
2. Two people tag independently; discuss disagreements (that is spec work).
3. Tally. If ≥30% are judge or label errors, fix the eval and rescore **both** systems before you touch weights.
4. If coverage: write 50 new gold examples of that shape.
5. If capability: consider a bigger base, RAG, or accept.

Example: 40% of "wrong" routing labels are actually outdated gold — the taxonomy changed. You relabel, rescore, and the tune's "gain" shrinks to +1. You just saved a pointless rank sweep.

## Failure modes

1. **Only reading the worst 5.** They are not the distribution.

2. **One tagger.** Their theory becomes the dataset.

3. **Fixing the tune when the eval is wrong.**

4. **No log.** Next month you rediscover the same three bugs.

Translate reading individual failures into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for reading individual failures than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used reading individual failures, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of reading individual failures in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate reading individual failures more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for reading individual failures more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used reading individual failures more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of reading individual failures more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read a sample of misses and tag causes before I change rank or data. If the eval is dirty I fix it and rescore both sides. The failure log is the plan; the loss curve is not.
keyPoints: Sample misses; tag cause; act by tag.
Judge and label errors: fix eval, rescore both.
Coverage gaps: targeted gold, not a higher LR.
Two taggers expose spec holes.
Keep a counted failure log across runs.
Be ready to describe two real misses in an interview.

questions.q: Why read failures by hand?
questions.a: To separate eval bugs, spec holes, coverage gaps and true capability limits — which metrics cannot name.

questions.q: 40% of failures are actually correct. Now what?
questions.a: Fix labels or the judge, rescore baseline and tune, then decide. Do not train against a dirty exam.

questions.q: What is the next step for a coverage-gap tag?
questions.a: Write targeted gold examples of that shape, version the set, retrain or re-prompt, and re-eval.

questions.q: Why use two taggers?
questions.a: Disagreement is usually an ambiguous spec. One person will silently pick a side and bake it into the data.

questions.q: You only opened the five ugliest outputs. Risk?
questions.a: Those are not the miss distribution. You will fix a rare horror and miss the common tag that actually moves the metric.

simpler-alternatives-one-last-time.explain:
## What it is

After you learn from the failures, **re-run the cheap path** with that knowledge: a better prompt, better few-shots, retrieval, constrained decoding, a router that sends hard cases to a giant, or a newer base. Sunk cost will tell you to ship the tune because you already trained. Discipline says the tune must still beat the *new* cheap system on the same set, after maintenance cost.

A 1.5-point win that needs a retrain every quarter usually loses to a prompt. A 1.5-point win that also cuts tokens 5× might still ship. Write both numbers.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the last chance to avoid a pet model. In interviews, admitting you killed a tune is a seniority signal. "We always ship what we train" is the opposite.

Failure analysis is prompt research in disguise. Use it twice.

## How it works + one small example

Last-week checklist:

1. Take the top three failure tags.
2. Spend a day on prompt/retrieval/schema aimed at those tags.
3. Re-score that improved baseline.
4. Compare tune vs improved baseline on quality, cost, latency, maintenance.
5. Decide. If you still ship the tune, say why the cheap path lost.

Example: the tune fixed format drift. A JSON schema on the baseline now does the same. Quality ties; the tune has a retrain tax. You keep the schema and archive the adapter. The week of training was tuition, not a product.

## Failure modes

1. **Sunk-cost ship.**

2. **Not giving the baseline the same insights.**

3. **Ignoring maintenance.** +2 points, two retrains a year, one engineer.

4. **A new base you did not re-prompt.** The cheap path was never given a chance on the new id.

A practical sitting for simpler alternatives one last time: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of simpler alternatives one last time with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put simpler alternatives one last time on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of simpler alternatives one last time that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for simpler alternatives one last time more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of simpler alternatives one last time more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put simpler alternatives one last time more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of simpler alternatives one last time more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Before I ship a tune I re-run the best cheap system with everything I learned. If the gap is small and the retrain tax is real, I keep the prompt. Killing a tune is a valid outcome.
keyPoints: Re-apply failure insights to the prompt/RAG path.
Compare against the improved baseline, not the old one.
Weigh gain against retrain and serving cost.
Sunk cost is not a reason to ship.
A schema or a new base can erase a tune's reason to exist.
Write why the cheap path lost if you still ship weights.

questions.q: Why revisit simple alternatives after a tune?
questions.a: Failure analysis often yields prompt or retrieval fixes that close the gap, and the tune must still justify its maintenance.

questions.q: The tune is +1.5 over the improved prompt. Decision?
questions.a: Usually do not ship unless cost or latency gains pay for retrains. A small quality edge is not enough.

questions.q: A schema constraint now matches the tune on format. What do you do?
questions.a: Archive the adapter if format was the residual error. Keep the schema. Do not serve weights you no longer need.

questions.q: What sentence belongs in the ADR if you still ship?
questions.a: Why the improved cheap path lost, with numbers, and when you will re-check it.

questions.q: A newer base arrives during the project. Last step?
questions.a: Prompt it well and score it. It may retire both the old baseline and the tune.

writing-the-decision-down.explain:
## What it is

A **fine-tune decision record** is a page: problem, baselines, method, base and dataset versions, eval design, results with slices, regressions, cost to train and serve, risks, decision, rollback, and **what would change the decision**. Link run ids. Two pages maximum or nobody will read it.

This is how a later engineer retrains when the base dies, how an auditor sees why a custom model exists, and how you stop folklore ("we tuned because quality was bad") from replacing numbers.

A model in production that nobody can reproduce is an incident that has not happened yet.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people leave. The adapter remains. The record is the difference between a 2-day retrain and a 6-week archaeology. Interviews will ask you to "write the decision down" as the last Level 13 habit. Treat it like an ADR, not like a blog.

## How it works + one small example

Template headings:

1. Residual failure and why cheaper rungs lost.
2. Data: version, n, licence, PII check.
3. Recipe: base revision, PEFT, LR, steps, template hash.
4. Eval: set hash, judge hash, slices, intervals.
5. Regressions and safety pack.
6. Serve cost vs baseline.
7. Decision + revisit triggers (new base, drift, spec change).
8. Rollback alias.

Example: you ship LoRA v4 for routing. Six months later the base is deprecated. A new hire follows the page, retrains, hits the same gates, flips the alias. Without the page they would start from a Slack thread and a missing dataset.

## Failure modes

1. **A notebook as the record.** It does not open next year.

2. **No revisit triggers.** The tune lives forever without a question.

3. **Missing hashes.** You cannot reproduce.

4. **A novel.** If it is 12 pages it will not be updated.

Translate writing the decision down into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for writing the decision down than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used writing the decision down, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of writing the decision down in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate writing the decision down more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for writing the decision down more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used writing the decision down more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of writing the decision down more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write a one-page decision: failure, data, recipe, eval, regressions, cost, rollback, and what would change my mind. The adapter is not the asset; the page plus the dataset is.
keyPoints: Page: problem, baselines, versions, results, regressions, cost, decision.
Include rollback and revisit triggers.
Link dataset hash, run id, template hash.
Keep it short enough to update.
This is what makes a retrain possible after the base dies.
A notebook is not a decision record.

questions.q: What should a tuning decision record contain?
questions.a: Problem, baselines, method, versions, eval design, slices, regressions, cost, risks, decision, rollback and revisit triggers.

questions.q: Why include 'what would change the decision'?
questions.a: It sets triggers — new base, volume, drift, spec — so the tune is not immortal by default.

questions.q: The only write-up is a training notebook. Risk?
questions.a: It will not run, it has no hashes, and a new hire cannot retrain. Promote the facts to a page with links.

questions.q: Which hashes belong on the page?
questions.a: Dataset, eval set, judge config, template, base revision, and the training run.

questions.q: Who is the page for besides you?
questions.a: The person who retrains after you leave, the auditor, and future-you during a deprecation.

slice-metrics-not-only-mean.explain:
## What it is

**Slice metrics** break the score by language, length, tool-use and the original failure mode — the cuts that can hide a regression. You choose slices from how the product fails, not from a default dashboard. A mean is a convenience; a slice is a decision.

Pre-register the slices in the eval spec so you cannot invent a flattering cut after the run. Report n per slice. A beautiful delta on n=9 is a hint.

When a slice is the reason you tuned (tone on angry tickets, JSON on long inputs), that slice is a **gate**, not a decoration.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, means get screenshotted; slices get ignored unless you make them the headline. Interviews will hand you a mean and wait to see if you ask for slices. Ask.

This is the same habit as Level 7, applied to a tune that is trying to look like a single win.

## How it works + one small example

1. List slices in the eval spec: language, token bucket, tool/no-tool, original failure tag.
2. Require n ≥ a floor (illustrative: 40) before a slice can gate; otherwise it is exploratory.
3. Put the original-failure slice on the decision line.
4. Watch for Simpson: every slice flat, mean up because mix shifted.

Example: you tuned for terse tone. Overall +1. The "angry, long" slice — the reason you started — is −4. You do not ship. You add 80 gold replies of that shape. The mean was never the question.

1. **Slices after the fact** to find a win.

2. **Gating on n=10.**

3. **Omitting the failure mode you tuned for.**

4. **Mix shift.** New traffic is easier; the mean lies.

A practical sitting for slice metrics not only mean: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pre-register slices — language, length, tools, the original failure — and I gate on the slice I came to fix. A mean is not a decision. Small-n slices are clues, not gates.

Pre-register slices; do not hunt after the run.
Report n; small slices are exploratory.
The slice you tuned for is a gate.
Watch mix shift that moves the mean without moving slices.
Put the worst material slice on the decision line.

questions.q: Which slices should a fine-tune report include?
questions.a: At least language, length, tool-use and the original failure mode, with n and a pre-registered gate on the one you tuned for.

questions.q: Overall +1, original-failure slice −4. Ship?
questions.a: No. That slice was the reason to train. Fix data or routing first.

questions.q: A new slice appears after you saw the scores. Problem?
questions.a: Post-hoc cutting. You can explore it, but you cannot use it as the official win without a new pre-registered eval version.

questions.q: Why report n per slice?
questions.a: So you do not gate on nine rows. Below the floor, treat the number as a hint and collect more.

questions.q: Mean up, every slice flat. What might be true?
questions.a: The traffic mix got easier (Simpson). Check slice weights versus last month.

safety-and-format-probes.explain:
## What it is

Re-run **refusal** and **schema** probes after every tune, even when the task looks unrelated. Preference and SFT both move the model; they can soften refusals, invent fields, drop end-of-turn, or start matching a jailbreak it used to ignore. A routing LoRA is not exempt.

Probes are small, frozen, and never trained on. Safety: must-refuse and must-answer items. Format: valid JSON, required keys, no extra keys, stop tokens. Fail the run if either pack regresses past the written gate.

This is cheaper than a user finding it, and cheaper than an auditor asking why you never checked.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "it's just labels" is how a helpful-to-a-fault model ships. In interviews, saying you re-run safety and schema after an unrelated tune is a crisp senior habit.

Format probes also catch template mismatch: the notebook was fine, serving invented a second JSON wrapper.

## How it works + one small example

1. Keep `probes/safety_v2.jsonl` and `probes/schema_v2.jsonl` next to the task eval.
2. Runner always executes all three.
3. Gates: 0 worsening on must-refuse; schema validity ≥ baseline.
4. On fail: inspect template first, then rank/LR, then mix-in.

Example: a tone LoRA. Task eval is up. Schema probe: 7% of outputs add a commentary line before the JSON. Serving would break the parser. You add a stop rule and 40 clean examples, re-run. Safety pack still clean. Now the tone win is real.

## Failure modes

1. **"Unrelated task" skip.**

2. **Training on the probe set.**

3. **Only testing in the notebook**, not through the serve template.

4. **Softening refusals** to raise a helpfulness score and not noticing.

Translate safety and format probes into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for safety and format probes than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used safety and format probes, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of safety and format probes in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

Translate safety and format probes more into a control someone else can audit: a setting, a test, a hash, a budget. Auditors and hiring managers both relax when they can see the control, not only hear the phrase, especially on m13-8.

Interview close: 'I would rather show you the test for safety and format probes more than talk about it'. Then describe that test in two sentences — input, expected, fail action.

Keep a dated example next to the note: the week you used safety and format probes more, the number you saw, the change you made. Dated examples survive model-catalog churn; abstract advice does not.

Last failure: optimising the wording of safety and format probes more in a design doc while the production path still does the old thing. The doc is not the system. Diff the config.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every tune re-runs frozen safety and schema probes, including tunes that are 'just tone' or 'just labels'. A task win that breaks JSON or a refusal does not ship.
keyPoints: Safety and schema probes run after every tune.
Never train on the probe sets.
Run them through the serving template, not only the trainer.
0 worsening on must-refuse is a typical hard gate.
Format drift is often a template or EOS issue.
Unrelated tasks are not exempt.

questions.q: Why re-run refusal tests after a tone-only LoRA?
questions.a: SFT and DPO move global behaviour. Helpfulness pressure can soften refusals even when you never trained on unsafe items.

questions.q: Schema probe fails only on the server, not in the trainer. First check?
questions.a: Chat template, stop tokens and any gateway wrapper. Then compare greedy outputs token-for-token.

questions.q: May you add failing probe items to the training set?
questions.a: You may add *similar* gold items. Keep the probe set itself held out or the gate becomes circular.

questions.q: What is a reasonable safety gate?
questions.a: No increase in must-refuse misses versus the base, on a frozen pack, before any task metric can ship.

questions.q: A helpfulness judge loves the tune; the refusal pack drops. Decision?
questions.a: Block. Do not trade a judge point for a refusal miss. Mix safety data or lower the preference pressure.

cost-normalized-quality.explain:
## What it is

Report **quality per dollar** and **quality per second**, not quality alone. A tune that matches a frontier model at 1/10 the unit cost can win with a slightly lower score. A tune that ties quality and doubles p95 or needs a dedicated GPU at 5% utilisation can lose.

Compute **cost per successful task** (retries, invalid JSON, human escalations included). Use p95, not average latency. Include hosting idle if you reserved hardware. Illustrative numbers only; re-check current prices.

A quality-only ADR is how you ship a slower, dearer specialist.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, GPUs and tokens are the visible bill; quality is the visible chart. Interviews want you to put them on one axis. "We improved 2 points" without cost is incomplete. "We held quality and cut cost 8×" is a product sentence.

This is also how distillation and small LoRAs justify themselves when they are slightly worse.

## How it works + one small example

Table every candidate:

| | Score | p95 | $ / 1k successes | GPU idle? |
| Prompted frontier | 91 | 1.8s | 12.00 | no |
| Prompted 8B | 86 | 0.4s | 1.10 | no |
| LoRA 3B | 90 | 0.3s | 0.80 | yes, 40% util |

You ship the LoRA if utilisation stays honest; you do not if nights are empty and the $0.80 becomes $4. You might also route easy traffic to the 8B and hard traffic to the frontier.

Recompute at 10× volume; reserved capacity may then win.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality-only slide.**

2. **Per-call cost** ignoring retries and invalids.

3. **Average latency** hiding a terrible p95.

4. **Ignoring idle** on a reserved GPU.

On the job, cost normalized quality is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is cost normalized quality'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply cost normalized quality as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating cost normalized quality as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

On the job, cost normalized quality more is a thirty-minute artefact, not a definition. Write the owner, the metric, the ticket you would file, and the first query you would run. If those four are blank, you have vocabulary and not an operating habit for m13-8.

Interviewers who have shipped will not stop at 'what is cost normalized quality more'. They want a number, a miss, and the first incident move. Prepare a 20-second story that includes a failure, not only a win, and name the control you would check.

Drill: take last week's traffic or a synthetic stand-in and apply cost normalized quality more as a checklist. Record one decision that would have changed. That note is what you walk through on a whiteboard when they say 'tell me about a time'.

One more failure: treating cost normalized quality more as a slide you memorised and never running it against a real region, a real eval set, or a real on-call. The first production week then becomes the tutorial you skipped.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I report quality per dollar and per second, using cost per successful task and p95, including idle. A slightly worse cheap model can win; a tied specialist on an empty GPU can lose.
keyPoints: Normalise quality by dollar and by second.
Use cost per successful task, not per call.
Quote p95, not the mean latency.
Include reserved-GPU idle in the unit cost.
A small quality drop can be a win at 10× cheaper.
Recompute at 10× volume; the winner can flip.

questions.q: Why not report quality alone for a tune?
questions.a: Serving cost and latency can erase the gain. Decision-makers need quality per dollar and per second.

questions.q: The LoRA ties the frontier but sits on an idle GPU. Risk?
questions.a: Unit cost includes idle. At low utilisation the API frontier may still be cheaper. Measure utilisation or use a host that scales to zero.

questions.q: Which latency number do you put on the scorecard?
questions.a: p95 (and TTFT if streaming), at production token lengths — not the mean of a lab batch.

questions.q: A cheaper model retries twice as often. What metric catches that?
questions.a: Cost per successful task, which folds retries and invalid outputs into the denominator.

questions.q: When can a slightly worse student still ship?
questions.a: When quality stays above the gate and cost or latency drops enough to pay for data and retrains.

kill-criteria-in-writing.explain:
## What it is

**Kill criteria** are the regressions that reject the tune **before you see the numbers**: safety pack worsening, critical-slice drop beyond X, schema validity below baseline, forgetting past a threshold, cost above the prompted option, eval-set leakage, or a missing reproducibility file. You write them in the ADR with the ship threshold.

Without kill criteria, every ugly number becomes a story. With them, a run can simply fail. That is a feature.

Kill criteria are not optional stretch goals. If you later waive one, you write a new ADR; you do not quietly ignore the line.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this protects you from sunk cost and from a VP who saw a pretty mean. In interviews, pre-committing the reject rules is the same discipline as pre-registering slices. It reads as scientific rather than theatrical.

It also speeds training: a run that trips a kill stops; you do not "just try one more epoch".

## How it works + one small example

Example block in the ADR (illustrative):

- Safety must-refuse: no increase vs base.
- Payments slice: ≥ −1 point vs prompted baseline.
- Schema validity: ≥ baseline.
- General probe: ≥ −2 points.
- $ / 1k successes: ≤ 0.3× frontier.
- Missing dataset hash or template: automatic kill.

A run hits +6 overall and −5 on payments. It is dead on arrival. You do not schedule a "review". You add data or you stop.

Waivers require the same people who signed the ADR, in writing.

## Failure modes

1. **Criteria after the run.**

2. **Soft language** ("we will consider safety").

3. **Waiving in Slack.**

4. **So many kills that no run can pass** — then you are avoiding a decision.

A practical sitting for kill criteria in writing: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of kill criteria in writing with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put kill criteria in writing on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of kill criteria in writing that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for kill criteria in writing more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-8 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of kill criteria in writing more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put kill criteria in writing more on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of kill criteria in writing more that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write kill criteria with the ship threshold, before any loss curve. Safety, critical slices, schema, forgetting, cost and missing hashes can reject a pretty mean. Waivers are a new ADR, not a Slack shrug.
keyPoints: Pre-commit the regressions that reject the tune.
Safety, critical slice, schema, forgetting, cost, missing hashes.
Write them next to the ship threshold.
A tripped kill stops the run; it does not start a debate.
Waivers need a new signed record.
Too many kills is avoidance; too few is theatre.

questions.q: What are kill criteria in a fine-tune project?
questions.a: Pre-written regression rules that reject the tune regardless of the headline metric — safety, slices, schema, forgetting, cost, missing artefacts.

questions.q: Overall +6, payments −5, payments was a kill. What happens?
questions.a: The run is rejected. You do not 'review' it into a ship. Fix data or stop.

questions.q: Why write kills before you train?
questions.a: So an ugly number cannot be story-told into a pass, and so you can stop a bad run early.

questions.q: A VP wants to waive a safety kill in Slack. Response?
questions.a: A waiver is a new signed ADR, not a chat message. The original signers must accept the new risk in writing.

questions.q: Name two automatic kills that are not quality scores.
questions.a: Missing dataset or template hash, and a cost-per-success above the prompted option you already run.

separate-adapter-or-merged-weights.explain:
## What it is

A LoRA can stay a **separate adapter** loaded onto a frozen base at serve time, or you can **merge** `W' = W + (α/r)BA` into a full checkpoint. Adapters are tiny, swappable, and let many variants share one base (multi-LoRA). Merge removes adapter overhead and works with any stack, including GGUF/Ollama, but each variant becomes a full-size artefact.

Keep the unmerged adapter even if you ship merged. It is the cheap source of truth. A merged file without the adapter is how teams lose the ability to swap or to re-merge after a base patch.

Choose adapters when you iterate or multi-tenant; merge when you have one frozen model for a simple or edge runtime.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is a storage and rollback question disguised as a file format. Interviews will ask when you merge. "Always merge" wastes disk on twenty tenants. "Never merge" blocks Ollama and some engines.

The senior add-on: I keep the adapter either way, and I re-eval after merge because merge-plus-quant is not bit-identical.

## How it works + one small example

Decision:

- 20 tenant tones, one 8B base → separate adapters on vLLM.
- One house classifier, ship to laptops → merge, then GGUF.
- Weekly iteration → stay unmerged until the version is boring.

Example: you merge for an Ollama demo, then delete the adapter folder to "clean up". A week later you need a second tone. You cannot cheaply fork. You still have the merged 16-bit blob, but not the BA matrices. Restore from backup if you are lucky; otherwise retrain.

Always `diff` a handful of greedy outputs before and after merge.

## Failure modes

1. **Deleting the adapter after merge.**

2. **Merging twenty variants** and paying twenty full copies.

3. **Serving unmerged on an engine that does not support LoRA.**

4. **Not re-evaluating** after merge or quant.

A practical sitting for separate adapter or merged weights: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-9 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of separate adapter or merged weights with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.

Worked habit: put separate adapter or merged weights on the ADR as a row with an owner and a revisit date. Example language: 'we do this because X; we revisit if Y'. Without the revisit, the habit dies at the next reorg.

Failure to add: a beautiful write-up of separate adapter or merged weights that nobody can execute when the owner is on leave. A deputy and a page in the runbook are part of the design.

A practical sitting for separate adapter or merged weights more: open the production region, the bill, and the eval pack, and write what would be true on Monday if you owned this. m13-9 work that cannot survive that sitting is still a blog post.

In interviews, follow the definition of separate adapter or merged weights more with 'here is how I would know it was broken'. Name a dashboard, a threshold, and who gets the page. That sequence is the seniority signal.
